entries.title: What design is
entries.summary: Design is deciding how something should work for the people who use it.
entries.tags: principle intro guide what design deciding how something should work people who use looks part last helps think three layers problem
entries.search_text: What design is Design is deciding how something should work for the people who use it. How it looks is part of that, but it’s the last part. It helps to think of three layers. The problem comes first, and each layer after it rests on the one before. - The problem : Who is this for, and what are they trying to get done? If this is wrong, nothing built on it can save the design. - The behavior : What happens when people act: what they see, what they can undo, and what happens when something fails. - The surface : Layout, type, color and motion. It makes the behavior easy to read, but it can’t fix the wrong behavior. Most of what people call bad design is a wrong call about the problem or the behavior, not the surface. The demo shows one parking app, changed at each layer, and in every version you park for what turns out to be 1 hour 20 minutes. - Original - New surface - New behavior - New problem Only the new problem removes the ticket altogether, because it answers the real question. That is why this book starts with judgment about problems and gets to components last.

entries.title: What design engineering is
entries.summary: A design engineer designs in the material the product is made of: code.
entries.tags: principle intro guide what design engineering engineer designs material product made code instead handing over pictures build thing try change until
entries.search_text: What design engineering is A design engineer designs in the material the product is made of: code. Instead of handing over pictures, they build the thing, try it, and change it until it works. The role exists because many design decisions only show up when something runs. How long should a spinner wait before it appears? What happens to a 40-character name? Where does focus go when a dialog closes? A mockup rarely answers these, but a prototype in code answers them in minutes. - Prototypes : Quick working versions that answer a design question, so the team decides on evidence instead of opinions. - The details : States, timing, motion, edge cases and the keyboard path. Mockups skip them, but people notice all of them. - What ships : Keeping what was designed and what ships the same, through components, tokens and review of the built thing. It sits between two roles that already exist. The three differ mostly in where each one starts and what each one is judged on. Designer Design engineer Frontend engineer Starts from A problem and the people who have it A design question, or a design that has to work for real A spec and a codebase Produces Flows, mockups, the design system Working prototypes, interface details, components Features that ship, are tested and can be maintained Judged on Whether it solves the right problem clearly Whether the built thing feels as intended, in every state Whether it works, is fast and lasts The rest of the book follows that work, from judging the problem to shipping the solution.

entries.title: Hierarchy of needs
entries.summary: The hierarchy of needs is an order for building a feature.

rules.title: Make it work before you polish it
Check more than the happy path
Make room for delight once it holds
Don’t cover a failure with a joke

entries.tags: principle problem guide hierarchy needs order building feature first work every time easy use only after delight count like small animation
entries.search_text: Hierarchy of needs The hierarchy of needs is an order for building a feature. First it has to work, then work every time, then be easy to use. Only after that does delight count, like a small animation or a friendly line of text. Each layer rests on the ones below it, so a pleasant touch on a feature that sometimes fails doesn’t feel pleasant: it feels like nobody checked. Easy to use includes people who use a keyboard or a screen reader, so accessibility belongs in that layer and can’t wait for the polish. Rules Four rules keep the layers in order. 1. Make it work before you polish it When the animation is done before the feature, people get the nice moment and then find nothing behind it. The polish makes the failure feel worse, because it promised something. Build from the bottom up, and add the polish last. 2. Check more than the happy path A feature can work when everything goes right and still fail people often, because networks are slow, lists are empty and servers return errors. If those cases show a blank screen, people can’t tell whether to wait or leave. Try each case before you call the feature done, and give each one a clear state. 3. Make room for delight once it holds There is always another bug, so delight can wait forever. The product then works but feels flat: finishing something feels the same as nothing happening. Once the base holds, plan small moments of care, like a friendly confirmation or a smooth transition, as part of the work. 4. Don’t cover a failure with a joke A cheerful message on a failed payment leaves people with no idea what went wrong, and it can feel like the product doesn’t take their money seriously. Say plainly what failed and what they can do about it. Keep the playful touches for moments that went well. In real products Notice that each product shows its base is dependable before it adds anything playful. - Dropbox: each file in the synced folder shows a small icon, arrows while it syncs and a check once it’s up to date. People trust it with work files because they can see that each one is safe. - WhatsApp: a message shows a clock until it has really left the phone, then one tick when it’s sent and two when it’s delivered. It never claims a message went out when it didn’t. - Asana: finishing a task now and then sends a cartoon creature across the screen. It’s a small, rare treat on top of a task list that already works. - Duolingo: the cheerful end-of-lesson screen also shows the XP you earned and your accuracy. The fun celebrates progress that was really counted.

entries.title: Problem framing
entries.summary: Framing the problem means writing down who has it, what they’re trying to do and what stops them, before anyone draws a screen.

rules.title: Restate the request as a problem
Name the person, the moment and the obstacle
Keep the answer out of the frame
Leave what you don’t know empty

entries.tags: principle problem guide framing means writing down who what trying stops before anyone draws screen also says how know got
entries.search_text: Problem framing Framing the problem means writing down who has it, what they’re trying to do and what stops them, before anyone draws a screen. It also says how you’ll know the problem got smaller, which success criteria then spell out. When a request arrives as a solution, the frame turns it back into the problem behind it, so the team can compare more than one answer. Name the person closely enough to include how they work, for example with a keyboard only or on a small phone. Rules Five rules keep a problem frame useful. 1. Restate the request as a problem A ticket often names its own answer, like “add an Export to PDF button”, and if the work starts there, the only question left is where the button goes. The request is a hint about what hurts, not a spec, so write down the problem behind it first, then look for answers. 2. Name the person, the moment and the obstacle A frame like “make settings easier to use” fits almost any design: two people can read it, picture different screens, and both feel right. Say who it is, when it happens and what gets in their way. If two readers still picture different things, narrow it again. A who that’s only a group, like “users” or “everyone”, is always too broad. The brief check lists the words to watch for. 3. Show where you saw it A problem nobody has seen is a guess: the team can’t tell how often it happens or how much it hurts, so the talk turns into opinions. Point to where it came from: a support message, a session you watched, a count. One real example is worth more than a paragraph of reasons. 4. Keep the answer out of the frame “People can’t find the Sort button” already holds its answer: only one design fits it, so the frame just repeats the request. Any control name in the problem, like a button, a dialog or a toggle, is the sign to look for. Describe what people are trying to get done, without naming a control. Then sketch at least two different answers. 5. Leave what you don’t know empty A frame filled with guesses reads like fact, so nobody checks it, and the team builds for a problem that may not exist. Say where each part came from: something people told you, something you read or saw, or your own guess. Look before you guess, in the support threads, tickets and notes that already exist. When nobody knows yet, leave the part empty and add it to a list of things to check. Label any guess with how you’ll check it, and when two sources disagree, show both. In real products Notice how narrow each problem is: who, what they want, and what stops them. The frames are this book’s summary, not the companies’ own notes. - Gmail: Undo send holds each email for a few seconds and offers Undo in the corner. It solves the moment of regret without an “Are you sure?” before every send. - Slack: threads move the replies to one message into a side panel. The channel stays readable, and the side conversation still has a home. - Uber: shows the car moving on the map, the minutes until pickup, and the car and its plate. Waiting becomes something riders can plan around. - Spotify: Discover Weekly is a fresh playlist picked for each listener every week. It removes the search step instead of making search better.

entries.title: Success criteria
entries.summary: Success criteria say what you would see or count if a change worked.

rules.title: Count people who got it done
Write them down before you build
Turn feelings into things you can see

entries.tags: principle problem guide success criteria say what would see count change worked where frame says solve done looks like good
entries.search_text: Success criteria Success criteria say what you would see or count if a change worked. Where the problem frame says what to solve, they say what “done” looks like. Good criteria describe what people do, not how the design feels. “People find Export without help” can be checked, but “Export is more intuitive” can’t. Include the other ways people work too, for example “people using only a keyboard can finish checkout”. Rules Four rules keep success criteria useful. 1. Count people who got it done Views, clicks and time on page can all go up when a design gets worse, because a confusing page makes people click around and stay longer. Count what people came to do instead: how many finished the task, how long it took and how many errors they hit. 2. Watch people, not only numbers A number tells you that something changed, not why: a drop in sign-ups could come from any field on the form. Watch a few people use it. Five short sessions often show the exact place where people stop, which no dashboard will. 3. Write them down before you build Without criteria, a change is done when it ships: nobody can say whether it helped, and the review only checks that it looks fine. Write the criteria in the ticket or the brief before work starts, so the review can test the change against them. 4. Turn feelings into things you can see Words like easier, cleaner and more intuitive sound like goals, but nobody can check them, so after a test people argue about whether it felt easier. Turn each feeling into something you can watch: found without help, finished on the first try, fewer questions to support. The demo at the top of this entry marks these words, and the brief check in Part 4 flags the same ones. Fill the slots with your own task and numbers. Table: Vague word Write instead, for example easy, easier, simple, simpler, intuitive, user-friendly People find X without help, in under N clicks. good, better, improve, improved, improves, improvement, nice, nicer Fewer support questions about Y , or fewer retries when people do it. clean, cleaner, clearer, modern People spot the main action in a five-second look at X . seamless, smooth, smoother Nobody gets stuck or asks for help between X and Y . somehow, etc List what you mean: X , Y and Z . In real products - GitHub: a repo can require named checks to pass before a pull request can merge, and every change is held to them. - YouTube Studio: next to views, it shows how long people watched and where they dropped off. Views can climb while most people leave in the first seconds. - Apple Watch: each Activity ring is a daily goal you can count, like minutes of exercise. One glance shows how close you are, with nothing left to judge by feel.

entries.title: Visual hierarchy
entries.summary: Visual hierarchy is the order in which people notice things on a screen.

rules.title: Keep to three or four levels

entries.tags: principle clarity guide visual hierarchy order which people notice things screen size weight color position space set region one thing should
entries.search_text: Visual hierarchy Visual hierarchy is the order in which people notice things on a screen. Size, weight, color, position and space set that order. In each region, one thing should clearly lead and the rest should step down from it. When the order is clear, people find what matters in one glance and read the rest only if they need it. Build the same order into the markup, with real headings and lists, so people using a screen reader can move through the page the same way. Rules Four rules keep visual hierarchy clear. 1. Let one thing lead When everything is bold, big or bright, nothing stands out, and people have to read every line to find the one they need. Pick one focal point per region, usually the outcome or the next step, and make everything else quieter. 2. Don’t rely on color alone Like any meaning carried by color alone , a title set apart only by its color blends into the text around it in grayscale, in bright sun or for people who see color differently. Set the order with size, weight, position and space, and let color add to it. 3. Keep to three or four levels Eight sizes and four weights, each a little different, don’t read as an order: people can’t tell which level a line is on, so the page looks uneven instead of organized. Three or four levels are enough, for example a title, key facts, body text and small print. Make each step big enough to see at a glance. 4. Keep one primary button Two filled buttons side by side ask for the same attention, so people stop to work out which one is the next step, and some press the wrong one. Keep one primary action per view and make the others secondary, as in Button hierarchy . In real products Notice the one thing that leads in each, marked with a dashed outline, and how far everything else steps down from it. - iOS Weather: the current temperature is by far the largest thing on screen. The place, the conditions and the forecast step down below it, so one glance tells you how warm it is. - Airbnb: on a listing, the booking card has one filled button, Reserve, with the nightly price in bold above it. Dates, guests and fine print stay quieter. - Linear: an issue’s title is the largest, darkest text on the page. Status, priority and assignee sit in a side panel in smaller, lighter text. - Gmail: in the compose window, Send is the only filled button. Formatting, attachments and delete are small gray icons, so the next step is never in doubt.

entries.title: Proximity
entries.summary: Proximity means that things close together look like they belong together.

rules.title: Use more space between groups than inside them
Try space before boxes and lines
Put a control next to what it changes
Keep help text tight under its field

entries.tags: principle clarity guide proximity means things close together look like belong people read space between items before words gaps screen tell
entries.search_text: Proximity Proximity means that things close together look like they belong together. People read the space between items before they read the words, so the gaps on a screen tell them what goes with what. Space only groups things for people who can see it, so give assistive tech the same groups: a real label for every field, and a named group around each set of fields. Rules Four rules keep spacing honest. 1. Use more space between groups than inside them When every gap is the same, people can’t tell where one group ends and the next begins, so a caption between two photos could belong to either. Make the space between groups clearly bigger than the space inside them. About twice as much is a good start. 2. Try space before boxes and lines Borders and divider lines around every group give people a lot of lines to read past: the page looks busy, and the lines compete with the content. Group with space first, and add a line or a box only when space alone isn’t enough, like in a long, dense list. 3. Put a control next to what it changes When a setting sits at the top and the button that applies it sits far below, people don’t see that they belong together: they change the setting and nothing happens, or they hunt for the button. Keep a control next to the thing it changes, and its action next to the control. 4. Keep help text tight under its field A message that sits closer to the next field than to its own seems to be about the next field, so people fix the wrong thing or miss the message. Keep help and error text close under their field, with the bigger gap after them, as in Text field . In real products Notice where the bigger gaps fall: between groups, never inside them. - iOS Settings: rows sit in rounded groups, with a clear gap between groups. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth read as one set and Notifications starts the next, with no heading needed. - Slack: messages one person sends in a row stack under a single name, with tight spacing. A new person gets a name, a picture and more space above. - Instagram: under a post, like, comment and share sit together on the left, and save sits alone on the right. The gap says save is a different kind of action. - YouTube: a video’s thumbnail, title, channel and view count sit tight together, with wider gaps between videos. The grid reads as separate cards without any borders.

entries.title: Spacing rhythm
entries.summary: Spacing rhythm means every gap on a screen comes from a short scale of sizes, such as 4, 8, 16, 24 and 32 pixels, and the edges of things line up.

rules.title: Take every gap from one scale
Line edges up, or offset them clearly

entries.tags: principle clarity guide spacing rhythm means every gap screen comes short scale sizes such pixels edges things line people never measure
entries.search_text: Spacing rhythm Spacing rhythm means every gap on a screen comes from a short scale of sizes, such as 4, 8, 16, 24 and 32 pixels, and the edges of things line up. People never measure the gaps, but they notice when gaps vary for no reason: the screen looks untidy, and it takes longer to see what belongs together. It works together with Proximity : Proximity decides which gaps should be small and which large, and rhythm decides which sizes those gaps can be. Set the steps in rem, so the gaps grow when people make their text larger. Rules Three rules keep spacing steady. 1. Take every gap from one scale When each gap is picked by eye, a screen ends up with many sizes that are almost the same. People can’t tell 11 from 13, so the small differences only look like mistakes. Give the team a short scale and use only its steps, so a review can ask “which step?” instead of “why 13?”. 2. Line edges up, or offset them clearly Edges that sit a few pixels apart look like an error, so people see a ragged column and trust the screen a little less. Put shared edges on the same line. When something should stand apart, like a note under a price, indent it by a full step or more so it reads as a choice. 3. Choose density on purpose When each panel gets its own padding, one list is cramped and the next one is roomy, so people have to adjust at every panel and the cramped rows are harder to tap. Pick a density for each kind of screen, such as compact for a busy settings page and roomy for a welcome dialog, and build both from the same steps. In real products Notice the few gap sizes that repeat, and the edges that line up. Dashed lines mark the shared edges. - Notion: every block, from headings to to-dos, starts on the same left edge. The + and the drag handle appear in the margin on hover, so the edge never moves. - GitHub: its design system, Primer, takes every gap from a short spacing scale. Lists, cards and dialogs use the same few steps, so pages feel related. - iOS Mail: the unread dot sits in the margin, and each divider line starts where the text starts. Every row shares one text edge. - Pinterest: pins have different heights, but every column is the same width and every gap is the same size. The steady gutters keep a busy grid calm.

entries.title: Contrast
entries.summary: Contrast is how clearly text and controls stand apart from what’s behind them.

rules.title: Don’t carry meaning with color alone
Pick colors that differ in lightness

entries.tags: principle clarity guide contrast how clearly text controls stand apart what behind too little people squint miss things read screen all
entries.search_text: Contrast Contrast is how clearly text and controls stand apart from what’s behind them. With too little, people squint, miss things, or can’t read the screen at all in sunlight. WCAG asks for at least 4.5 : 1 for body text, and 3 : 1 for large text and for the edges and icons people need to see. The second half of the idea is about meaning. Color can make a status quicker to spot, but it can’t be the only clue, because some people can’t tell certain colors apart and some screens show everything in gray. Pair every color with a shape, an icon or a word. Rules Four rules keep text readable and meaning clear. 1. Give text enough contrast Pale gray text looks calm in a mockup on a good monitor, but on a phone in sunlight, or for someone with weaker eyes, it fades away. Give body text at least 4.5 : 1 against its background, and large text at least 3 : 1. Check the quiet text too: captions, placeholders and hints. 2. Don’t carry meaning with color alone A green or red amount only tells something to people who see the color. For everyone else, money in and money out look the same. Add a sign, an arrow or a word, such as “+” and “Received”, so color still helps people scan and the meaning stays when the color is gone. 3. Pick colors that differ in lightness Many people can’t tell red from green, especially when the two are equally light, so a seat map in those colors becomes one muddy shade. Choose colors that are also clearly lighter and darker than each other, and add a mark and a word to each state. 4. Check both themes A gray that passes on white can fail on dark gray. This happens when colors are picked in the light theme and copied into the dark one, which leaves dim text on a dim background. Measure every text and background pair in each theme, and give the dark theme its own values. In real products Notice that every state has its own shape or word. Each sketch is shown twice, the second time without color. - Linear: each issue status has its own icon shape, from a dashed circle for backlog to a half-filled one in progress and a check for done. Without color, the shapes still tell them apart. - GitHub: a pull request’s state is a colored label with an icon and a word: Open, Merged, Closed or Draft. Without color, the word and the icon still say it. - Slack: an active person gets a filled dot and an away person an empty ring. Filled versus hollow carries the meaning, not just green versus gray. - Duolingo: after you check an answer, the panel turns green with a check and praise, or red with a cross and the right answer written out. The icon, the words and a sound carry the meaning too, so color is never alone.

entries.title: Internal & external
entries.summary: Consistency means one action has one look, one concept has one name, and the same buttons sit in the same order everywhere.
entries.tags: principle consistency guide internal external means one action look concept name same buttons sit order everywhere people learn product noticing
entries.search_text: Internal & external Consistency means one action has one look, one concept has one name, and the same buttons sit in the same order everywhere. People learn a product by noticing patterns, so when the patterns hold, what they learned on one screen works on the next. When they don’t, people slow down and wonder whether two things that look different do different things. There are two kinds. Internal consistency is about your own product: the same thing looks and works the same on every screen. External consistency is about everything else people use, the platform and other common products, as in Jakob’s law . Keyboard and screen-reader users lean on both, because they can’t take in a whole screen at a glance. Rules Three rules keep a product consistent. 1. Give one action one look When Add to cart is a filled button on one page and a plain link on another, people wonder whether the two do different things: a link usually opens a page, so some expect to see the item rather than add it. Build the action once as a component and use it everywhere. If two places really need different styles, they probably need different names too. 2. Give one thing one name When one thing has two names, people assume there are two things, so they look in the wrong place or doubt that their action worked. Pick one word for each concept and keep a short glossary. Use the same word in buttons, menus, messages and help. 3. Follow the platform’s conventions People bring habits from every other app they use. Most dialogs put the main button at the right end, with Cancel just before it, so when a product flips that order, people press by position and hit the wrong button. Follow the convention unless you can show a clear win for a real task, and if you do break it, break it the same way everywhere. In real products Notice what stays the same from screen to screen, and which habits people bring from other products. - Google Docs: Docs, Sheets and Slides share one menu order and keep Share in the top-right corner. Only a few menus differ, so learning one teaches the others. - macOS: dialogs put the main button at the right end, with Cancel just before it. Apps that keep the platform’s order let people answer without rereading the buttons. - Linear: Cmd+K opens a command menu, the same shortcut Slack and GitHub use to jump around or run commands. People bring that habit from tool to tool. - YouTube: every video in a feed or search results has the same ⋮ menu beside its title, with the same actions. Learn it once and it works on every video.

entries.title: Design tokens
entries.summary: A design token is a shared value with a name, such as a corner radius, a spacing step, a color or a text size.
entries.tags: principle consistency guide design tokens token shared value name such corner radius spacing step color text size components point instead holding
entries.search_text: Design tokens A design token is a shared value with a name, such as a corner radius, a spacing step, a color or a text size. Components point at the name instead of holding their own number, so when the token changes, every component that uses it changes with it. Tokens are how Spacing rhythm and consistency hold up in a large team. They can carry contrast too: give every background token a matching text token, like “accent” and “on-accent”, and check each pair once, so no component can pick a pair that fails. Kinds of tokens Most systems have three layers of tokens: base, role and component. Each layer points at the one before it, so a change happens in one place. - Base. Raw values, like blue-600 = 2F5DA8. Components never use them directly. - Role. A name for a job, like accent or danger. This is the layer components use. - Component. For one component that has to differ from its role, like a play button in the text color. Rules Three rules keep tokens useful. 1. Point components at tokens When each component holds its own numbers, a change has to be made in every component. Someone always misses one, and the product drifts: a 6 px corner here, an 8 px corner there. Point every component at a token instead, so a change in one place reaches all of them. 2. Name tokens by their job A token named after its value, like blue-500, can’t change without becoming wrong: to rebrand, you either edit every component, or make blue-500 green and turn everything else that used it green too. Name tokens by their job, such as accent or rain. Only the job token knows which blue it is, so a rebrand changes one line. 3. Keep the set small Tokens that are close, like radius-7, radius-8 and radius-9, look the same on screen. People can’t choose between them, so they pick one at random, and the product drifts anyway. Keep a few clear steps, each with a job. When two tokens are close and used for the same job, merge them. In real products - Figma: layers can point at a variable, like accent, instead of a raw color. Change the variable once and every layer that uses it updates. Modes, like Light and Dark, swap a whole set of values at once. - VS Code: every part of the window reads a named theme color, like editor.background or statusBar.background. A theme only fills in those names. Extensions use the same names, so they follow every theme too. - iOS: apps set text by role, like Headline, Body and Caption, not by pixel size. Move the Text Size slider in Settings and every app that uses these roles scales all its text together. - X (Twitter): the display settings let you pick one accent color, and buttons, links and highlights across the app switch to it at once.

entries.title: Break it on purpose
entries.summary: Consistency doesn’t mean everything looks the same.
entries.tags: principle consistency guide break purpose doesn mean everything looks same one thing really different such action destroys work should look
entries.search_text: Break it on purpose Consistency doesn’t mean everything looks the same. When one thing really is different, such as an action that destroys work, it should look different, and it should be the only thing that does. People notice the one element that breaks a pattern, but only while the pattern holds everywhere else. This is the other half of Internal and external consistency . Like any meaning carried by color , an exception needs a second cue: an icon, a divider, a place at the end of the list, or the word itself, like “Delete”. Rules Three rules keep exceptions meaningful. 1. Keep exceptions rare When every action gets its own color, weight or badge, nothing stands out, and people have to read every item to find the one they need, as on a screen where everything is bold . Keep about one exception per screen, for the one thing that really differs, and give everything else the normal style. 2. Write down the reason An exception without a reason looks like any other style choice, so the next person copies it to places where it doesn’t belong, and soon it means nothing. Write the reason next to the rule, like “red only for actions that destroy data”. If you can’t write a reason, follow the rule. 3. Audit for drift Not every difference is a choice: someone copies an old screen or picks a value that’s close enough, and small variants pile up release after release. Check the product now and then. Fold drift back into the system, and if a variant has a real job, give it a name and add it. In real products - GitHub: a repository’s settings page stays plain until the bottom. The few actions that are hard to undo, like Archive and Delete, sit together in a red-bordered “Danger Zone” with its own heading. - Gmail: Compose is the only big filled button in the sidebar. Inbox, Starred, Sent and the rest are plain rows, so the one way to start something new is easy to find. - Spotify: a playlist page has one big round Play button. Save, download and more options are small plain icons next to it, because playing is what most people came for. - iOS: in a photo’s long-press menu, every item is plain except Delete. It’s red, has a trash icon and comes last, so it stands apart even without the color.

entries.title: Labels
entries.summary: A button label should say what happens when people press it: a verb, and the thing it acts on.

rules.title: Name the action, not the answer

entries.tags: principle words guide labels button label should say what happens people press verb thing acts save draft delete photos yes don
entries.search_text: Labels A button label should say what happens when people press it: a verb, and the thing it acts on. “Save draft” and “Delete 3 photos” do that, and “OK” and “Yes” don’t. Labels are the smallest case of plain language , and they matter more on a button, because pressing it changes something. Rules Four rules keep labels clear. 1. Name the action, not the answer “OK”, “Submit” and “Yes” only make sense next to the question above them. People who skim read the buttons first, and so do screen-reader users who jump between buttons, so they have to go back to the text to learn what a button does, or guess. Use a verb and an object, like “Delete draft”, so the button makes sense on its own. 2. Use people’s words Words like “Execute query” describe what the code does, not what people want to do, so people stop to translate them and some give up. Use the words people use for their own tasks, like “Search” and “Add contact”. Labels in people’s words covers how to find those words. 3. Pick one capital style When “Add To Cart” sits next to “Save for later”, the page looks like it was put together from different apps, and people notice the mismatch before they read the words. Pick one style and use it on every button, menu item and title. Sentence case is a common choice: only the first word and names get a capital. 4. Keep one verb per action If the menu says “Remove” and the dialog it opens says “Delete”, people can’t tell whether it’s the same action, and often it isn’t: removing a photo from an album keeps it, deleting it doesn’t. Give each action one name everywhere , so the confirm button repeats the verb from the menu item that opened it. In real products Read only the buttons in each sketch: they still tell you what will happen. - macOS: closing an unsaved document asks with Don’t Save, Cancel and Save, not Yes, No and Cancel. - GitHub: the merge button names the method you picked, like “Squash and merge”, and the confirm step repeats it. - WhatsApp: deleting a message offers “Delete for me” and “Delete for everyone”, so each button says who loses the message. - Spotify: a song’s menu is a list of verbs with their objects, like Add to playlist, Add to queue and Go to album.

entries.title: Error messages
entries.summary: A good error message says what happened, why if you know, and what to do next, in plain words that don’t blame anyone.

rules.title: Describe the problem, not the person
Match the tone to the stakes

entries.tags: principle words guide error messages good message says what happened why know next plain don blame anyone people read bad
entries.search_text: Error messages A good error message says what happened, why if you know, and what to do next, in plain words that don’t blame anyone. People read it at a bad moment, when something they wanted didn’t work, and the message decides whether they fix it in a few seconds or give up. This entry is about the words. Where the message goes, next to a field or across the page, is covered in Inline message and Error state . Rules Four rules keep error messages helpful. 1. Describe the problem, not the person “You entered an invalid value” tells people they did something wrong, but not what, so they feel blamed and still have to guess the rule. Describe the thing in neutral words and include the rule, like “Quantity needs a number from 1 to 99”, so people can fix it in one try. 2. Lead with plain words A code like “Error 0x80070002” means nothing to most people, who can’t tell whether the problem is theirs, the app’s or the network’s, and screen readers read it out one character at a time. Say what happened in plain words first. Keep the code small, or behind “Show details”, for support and developers. 3. Offer the next step A message that explains the problem and offers only “OK” leaves people where they started: once it closes, they have to find the fix on their own. Put the action that fixes it on the message, on a button that names it, like “Give Sam access” or “Try again”. 4. Match the tone to the stakes Red capitals and words like “fatal” make people think their work is lost. Most errors aren’t like that: the problem can be fixed, or the app will try again on its own. Use calm words that fit what happened, and say what still works: “Your changes are saved on this device.” In real products - VS Code: if a file changed on disk after you opened it, saving stops and says why. The message offers Compare and Overwrite, so both ways forward are right there. - GitHub: a pull request that can’t merge says the branch has conflicts, lists the files, and puts a Resolve conflicts button right there. No error code, no blame. - Gmail: a bounced email leads with “Address not found” and one plain sentence about which address failed. The server’s code comes last, in small print, for whoever needs it. - Google sign-in: a wrong password gets a short, neutral message right under the field, with both ways forward: try again, or reset the password.

entries.title: Plain language
entries.summary: Plain language means the words people already use, in short sentences, with the main point first and one name for each concept.
entries.tags: principle words guide plain language means people already use short sentences main point first one name concept read fast often
entries.search_text: Plain language Plain language means the words people already use, in short sentences, with the main point first and one name for each concept. People read fast and often read only part of the text, so plain words let them understand it the first time. It helps everyone, and most of all people reading in a second language, people with cognitive or learning disabilities, and anyone tired or stressed. Labels apply the same rules to buttons. Rules Four rules keep writing plain. 1. Use everyday words Words like “utilize” and “initiate” make people slow down and translate. Some stop reading, and people reading in a second language may not know them at all. Use the words people use, like “use” and “start”. If a technical term can’t be avoided, explain it the first time it appears, including where to find it. 2. Put the point first When a message opens with background and conditions, people have to read to the end to learn what it means for them, and many stop before they get there. A notification preview may show only the first line. Lead with what people need to know or do, and put the reason and the details after it. 3. One idea per sentence A long sentence makes people hold several ideas at once, so they lose track, read it again, or miss the part that mattered to them. Give each idea its own sentence, and split any sentence that needs “and” twice. 4. Give each thing one name If a shop says “bag” in one place, “basket” in another and “cart” in a third, people wonder whether these are different places and look for their items in the wrong one. Pick one term, keep it in a short glossary, and use it everywhere, help pages included, as one thing, one name explains. In real products - Google Docs: the menu, the side panel and the button all use the same word: Version history, Name current version, Restore this version. - Uber: the main field asks “Where to?”, the way a driver would, instead of “Enter destination address”. Saved places use people’s own names, like Home and Work. - iOS: a setting has a plain name, and the line under it says what it does with everyday examples. Low Power Mode names what it cuts back, like downloads and mail, and for how long.

entries.title: Motion
entries.summary: Motion should explain a change, like where a panel came from or where a deleted item went, and then get out of the way fast.

rules.title: Animate to explain, not to decorate
Match the easing to the direction

entries.tags: principle craft guide motion should explain change like where panel came deleted item went get out way fast explains nothing only
entries.search_text: Motion Motion should explain a change, like where a panel came from or where a deleted item went, and then get out of the way fast. Motion that explains nothing only makes people wait. Two settings shape every animation: how long it takes, and its easing, which is how its speed changes along the way. The demo below lets you change both on the same panel. Rules Four rules keep motion useful. 1. Keep it short An animation that takes 600 ms looks smooth the first time, but by the tenth time people are waiting for it, and if it blocks clicks while it plays, the app feels broken. Keep most interface motion around 150–300 ms: small moves get less, big ones a little more, and nothing should block the next click. 2. Animate to explain, not to decorate When everything bounces, fades and slides, motion stops meaning anything, because people can’t tell which movement is about the thing they just did. Use motion to show a change, such as where something came from, where it went or what was added, and cut any animation that explains nothing. 3. Respect reduced motion Large movement on screen can make some people dizzy or sick, so they turn on the reduce motion setting on their device, and an app that ignores it keeps sliding and zooming anyway. Check prefers-reduced-motion and test with the setting on. Swap slides and zooms for an instant change or a short fade: the change still happens, only the movement goes. 4. Match the easing to the direction Linear motion looks mechanical. Ease-in starts slow, so something that arrives with it feels late, and something that leaves with ease-out seems to linger. Ease out for things that enter, so they arrive fast and settle, and ease in for things that leave. Keep overshoot for rare, playful moments. In real products - iOS: an app opens by growing out of its icon and shrinks back into it when you leave, so you see where it lives. With Reduce Motion on, it fades instead. - macOS: a minimized window shrinks down into the Dock. The motion shows where the window went, so you know where to click to get it back. - Gmail: swipe an email and it slides off the side, then the rows below move up to close the gap. You see that it left and what took its place, and a bar offers Undo. - Instagram: double-tap a photo and a big heart pops up on it, then fades, while the small heart below fills in. A little bounce suits this one quick, light action.

entries.title: Edge cases
entries.summary: Real data is long, missing, huge and empty.

rules.title: Test with the extremes from the start
Keep the part that tells items apart
Reserve space for what loads later

entries.tags: principle craft guide edge cases real data long missing huge empty names run past images fail load counts reach millions fields
entries.search_text: Edge cases Real data is long, missing, huge and empty. Names run past the edge, images fail to load, counts reach the millions, and fields come back blank. A design made only with tidy sample data breaks on the first day of real use, and people see those cases every day after that. For every field, decide what happens when it is very long, missing, very large, empty, or squeezed into a narrow space. Checking more than the happy path covers slow, empty and failed loads. This entry is about the data itself. Rules Four rules keep a design working with real data. 1. Test with the extremes from the start A mockup filled with a short name, a perfect image and a tidy number always looks finished, so the problems show up only after launch, when real people bring real data. Put the extremes in the mockups, the stories and the test data from the start, so they get designed instead of discovered. 2. Keep the part that tells items apart When long names are cut at the end, items that differ only at the end look the same: three files all read “Quarterly report dra…”, and people pick the wrong one. Cut the middle to keep the end, or let the text wrap to two lines. Keep the full text in the page so screen readers read it, and show it on hover and on focus. 3. Reserve space for what loads later When something loads late, it pushes everything below it down, and a click aimed at a button lands on the wrong thing. Reserve the space before the content arrives: give images a fixed aspect ratio, and make skeletons the same size as the content they stand in for. 4. Format values for people Raw values like “1234567”, “null” and “undefined” show that nobody planned for this case: a long number is hard to read at a glance, and “null” looks like a bug. Format numbers and dates for reading, like “1.2M followers”, with the exact value one step away, and write a fallback for every field that can be empty. In real products - VS Code: when two open tabs have the same file name, each tab adds the part of its path that tells them apart, in lighter text. Tabs with unique names stay short. - macOS Finder: long file names are cut in the middle, not at the end. The start and the ending both stay visible, so “final v2.pdf” and “final v3.pdf” still look different. - YouTube: big view counts are rounded, like “1.2M views”, and dates are relative, like “3 years ago”. Long titles wrap to two lines before they’re cut. The exact count and date show when you open the description. - Airbnb: a listing without enough reviews shows “New” where the star rating goes. There’s no zero-star rating and no empty gap.

entries.title: Keyboard and focus
entries.summary: Every control should work from the keyboard alone, focus should move in the order people read, and a visible ring should always show where it is.

sections.title: Ways to move with the keyboard

rules.title: Make focus order match reading order
Move focus with what opens and closes

entries.tags: principle craft guide keyboard focus every control should work alone move order people read visible ring always show where who use
entries.search_text: Keyboard and focus Every control should work from the keyboard alone, focus should move in the order people read, and a visible ring should always show where it is. People who can’t use a mouse depend on this, and so do screen reader users and people who type fast. Focus is the keyboard’s pointer. Tab moves it, and Enter or Space act on what it points at. If people can’t see focus, or it jumps around, they can’t tell what the next key will do. Ways to move with the keyboard There are four main ways to move with the keyboard. Most apps need Tab and arrow keys, a skip link helps on long pages, and shortcuts help in apps people use all day. - Tab. Tab moves to the next field, button or link in reading order, and Shift+Tab goes back. click Name, then press Tab. - Arrow keys. A group of options, such as tabs, a radio set or a menu, is one Tab stop, and arrow keys move inside it. People don’t have to tab through every option to get past the group. click Week, press the arrow keys, then press Tab. - Skip link. The first Tab on the page shows a “Skip to main content” link. Enter jumps past the header, so people don’t tab through the same eight links on every page. press Load the page, then press Tab and Enter. - Shortcuts. Single keys run frequent actions. They add to Tab and never replace it, and a ? key lists them so people can learn them. click the inbox, then press j, k and e. Rules Four rules keep the keyboard path usable. 1. Keep the focus ring visible Focus rings are often removed because they look out of place, so keyboard users press Tab, see nothing change, and can’t tell which button Enter will press until it’s too late. Restyle the ring to fit the design instead of removing it. :focus-visible shows it for keyboard use and hides it on most mouse clicks. 2. Make focus order match reading order People expect Tab to follow the layout: left to right, top to bottom. When CSS moves things around, or a positive tabindex sets its own order, focus jumps to a field they haven’t reached yet, so they type into the wrong field or skip one. Put elements in the DOM in reading order, and use only tabindex="0" and tabindex="-1" . 3. Use real buttons and links A div or span with a click handler works with a mouse and nothing else: Tab skips it, Enter does nothing, and a screen reader doesn’t call it a button. Use a button for actions and a link for going somewhere, because they get focus, the keys and a role for free. See Link vs button . 4. Move focus with what opens and closes When a dialog opens and focus stays behind it, keyboard users keep tabbing through a page they can’t see. When it closes and focus goes back to the top, they have to find their place again. Move focus into the dialog when it opens, and when it closes, put focus back on the control that opened it. In real products Notice where focus lands in each one, and how it’s marked. - VS Code: the Command Palette opens with focus already in its search box, arrows move the highlight, and Esc puts focus back where you were typing. - GitHub: the first Tab press shows a “Skip to content” link at the top. Keyboard users jump past the long header in one key instead of tabbing through every link. - Gmail: with keyboard shortcuts turned on in settings, j and k move through the inbox and a marker shows the current conversation, so you always know what Enter will open. - YouTube: on a video, k pauses, j and l jump 10 seconds, m mutes and f goes full screen. The player flashes an icon when you pause or mute, so you can tell the key worked.

entries.title: Critique against the goal
entries.summary: A critique judges work against what it is for.

rules.title: Tie each comment to the goal
Name the problem before the fix
Ask what feedback is wanted first

entries.tags: principle critique guide against goal judges work what starts says serves doesn only suggests fix designer gets something act still
entries.search_text: Critique against the goal A critique judges work against what it is for. It starts from the goal, says what serves the goal and what doesn’t, and only then suggests a fix, so the designer gets something to act on and still chooses the fix. That is what separates it from a reaction: “I don’t like it” says how you feel, not what to change. Put needs like access into the goal too, such as “works with a keyboard alone”, so a missing focus ring counts against the goal and nobody can wave it off as polish. Kinds of critique Work at different stages needs different feedback, so there is one kind of critique for each stage. Each kind wastes time when it comes at the wrong stage, so ask which one is wanted . If you can’t ask, go by how finished the work is. Table: Kind When Look at Direction Early sketches, while the idea can still change Whether it solves the right problem Flow The steps exist as rough screens Whether people can get from start to finish without getting stuck Polish The flow is settled and the screens are close to done Contrast, alignment and wording - Direction. Two early sketches of a shopping list. - Flow. Three rough screens, from a recipe to the list. - Polish. A shopping list that’s close to done. Rules Four rules keep critique useful. 1. Tie each comment to the goal “I don’t like it” leaves the designer guessing, so they either defend the design or change something at random. Say what the design does, or fails to do, for the people it’s for. A reaction is still useful as a clue: look closer at what caused it, then name that. 2. Name the problem before the fix “Make the button bigger” is a fix without a problem. The designer can only do it or argue, and the fix may not solve anything. Name the problem first, such as “people can’t find Checkout”, so the designer can judge your fix and may find a better one. 3. Ask what feedback is wanted first Notes on spacing and colors don’t help an early sketch, because the idea may still change and take the details with it. Ask first whether the designer wants feedback on direction, flow or polish. For early work, ask about the idea and leave the details for later. 4. Hear their read first When the reviewer speaks first, the designer’s view bends toward theirs: they defend the design or take every note, and the doubt they already had never comes up. Ask the designer what works for them and what worries them, then give your critique, and say where the two agree and where they don’t. The same goes for an agent’s review: get the designer’s read before you show it. In real products Notice that each one ties feedback to a goal or to one spot, and leaves the fix to the owner. - Grammarly: you set goals such as audience and formality first. Each suggestion then names the problem before it offers a rewrite, and you can accept or dismiss it. - Figma: a comment is pinned to the exact spot on the canvas, so feedback is about one specific thing. The thread is resolved once it’s dealt with. - GitHub: a review comment sits on the exact line and can carry a suggested change. The reviewer explains the problem, and the author decides whether to commit the fix. - Airbnb: guests rate cleanliness, accuracy, check-in, communication, location and value separately. A host learns what to fix, not just that the stay got four stars.

entries.title: Heuristic review
entries.summary: A heuristic review checks a design against a short list of rules of thumb.

rules.title: Say what a mock can’t show

entries.tags: principle critique guide heuristic review checks design against short list rules thumb best-known jakob nielsen ten usability heuristics one person run
entries.search_text: Heuristic review A heuristic review checks a design against a short list of rules of thumb. The best-known list is Jakob Nielsen’s ten usability heuristics. One person can run it in an hour, before anyone outside the team sees the design. It finds likely problems, not proven ones, which separates it from a usability test, where you watch real people use the design. The ten heuristics also leave out accessibility, so add a separate pass for keyboard, focus, contrast and screen readers. The dialog in the demo breaks six of the ten. Here are all ten, each with a question to ask and the entries that cover it. Table: Heuristic Ask In this book 1 · Visibility of system status Does the screen always show what’s happening, and how long it will take? Instant feedback , Progress bar 2 · Match between the system and the real world Does it use the words people use, in the order they think of things? Labels in people’s words , Plain words, one term per concept 3 · User control and freedom Can people back out of every step, even halfway through? Undo instead of “Are you sure?” , Dialog 4 · Consistency and standards Does the same thing look and work the same here and in the apps people already use? Internal and external consistency , Jakob’s law 5 · Error prevention Does the design stop the mistake before it happens? Constraints that prevent errors , Forgiving input 6 · Recognition rather than recall Can people see their options instead of remembering them? Labels that say what happens , Search with filters and recents , Command palette 7 · Flexibility and efficiency of use Do frequent users get faster paths that newcomers never have to learn? Keyboard shortcuts and accelerators , Layered interface 8 · Aesthetic and minimalist design Does anything on the screen compete with what matters? Visual hierarchy , Rams’ ten principles 9 · Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors Does each error say what went wrong and what to do next, in plain words? Error messages that help , Error state 10 · Help and documentation Is the help right where the question comes up? Contextual hints over tours Then make the accessibility pass. A mock shows only some of it, so most of these checks need a running build. Table: Check Passes when Shows in a mock? In this book Keyboard You can finish the whole task with the keyboard alone, in reading order. No, it needs a running build Keyboard paths are craft Focus Focus is always visible, moves into a dialog when it opens and back when it closes. No Move focus with what opens and closes Contrast Body text is at least 4.5 : 1 against its background; large text, edges and icons people need are at least 3 : 1. Yes Contrast, and never color alone Color No meaning is carried by color alone. Yes Don’t carry meaning with color alone Names Every control says what it does, and is a real button or link that a screen reader can name. Partly: the words show, the roles only in code Labels that say what happens , Use real buttons and links Announcements Errors, toasts and finished work appear in text that screen readers announce. No Instant feedback Motion With reduce motion on, slides and zooms become an instant change or a short fade. No Respect reduced motion Rules Four rules keep a heuristic review useful. 1. Pair it with watching people A review finds what reviewers expect to go wrong, but real people trip over things no list predicts and breeze past some problems the review rated high. If the review is the only test, the team fixes guesses. Watch a few people try the same flow, and let what they do decide which findings matter. 2. Ask three to five reviewers One reviewer finds only part of the problems, because each person notices different things. Ask three to five people to review on their own, then merge the lists. Past five, each new reviewer adds little. An agent’s review counts as another reviewer only if it looks through a different lens or runs on a different model, because one model asked twice repeats its own blind spots. 3. Rate each problem by severity A flat list of problems gives the team no order, so they fix the quick ones first and the problem that stops people from paying waits. Rate each problem from 0 to 4 and fix from the top. The rating weighs how many people hit the problem, how much it hurts and whether it gets in their way every time. Table: Severity Means Example 0 · Not a problem Not a usability problem after all. Drop it and write down why. “I’d make it blue”, with no problem behind it 1 · Cosmetic Fix it if there’s time left. A typo: “Delivey fee” 2 · Minor Low priority: people notice it but get past it. Prices are low contrast 3 · Major High priority: people struggle or lose work. The basket empties when you switch restaurant 4 · Catastrophe Fix it before release: people can’t finish the task. Card payment fails if the address has an accent 4. Say what a mock can’t show A review of a static mock can only judge what’s drawn. Timing, focus, screen readers and real data don’t show, so a clean review reads as a pass for things nobody checked. List what the mock can’t show next to the findings, and check those parts in a running build. The table shows what each stage of a prototype can show. Table: What you check Sketch Static mock Clickable page Branch in the app Whether it solves the problem Yes Yes Yes Yes Hierarchy and layout Roughly Yes Yes Yes Words and labels If written Yes Yes Yes Contrast and color No Yes Yes Yes States: loading, empty, error Only if drawn Only if drawn Only if built Yes Real data: long names, empty lists No Only if drawn Sample data only Yes Timing and motion No No Yes Yes Keyboard, focus and screen readers No No With real controls Yes Speed with real data No No No Yes In real products Each one gets a different heuristic right. Naming the heuristic when you see it done well makes it easier to spot when it’s missing. - Uber: after you book, the map shows the car moving toward you and the arrival time keeps updating, so you never wonder whether anything is happening. Heuristic 1, visibility of system status. - Gmail: if a message mentions an attachment but has no file, Gmail asks before sending. It catches the slip at the last moment it can still be fixed. Heuristic 5, error prevention. - macOS: menus list every command by name with its shortcut beside it. People find a command by looking instead of remembering, and pick up the faster key along the way. Heuristics 6 and 7. - Google Search: a misspelled query gets results for the likely spelling, with a link to search for exactly what you typed. Heuristic 9, help users recognize, diagnose and recover from errors.

entries.title: Rams’ principles
entries.summary: Dieter Rams designed radios, record players and shelves for Braun and Vitsœ.

rules.title: Ask them as questions, not rules
Cut what doesn’t serve the goal

entries.tags: principle critique guide rams principles dieter designed radios record players shelves braun vits his ten good design still among most quoted
entries.search_text: Rams’ principles Dieter Rams designed radios, record players and shelves for Braun and Vitsœ. His ten principles of good design are still among the most quoted in design. He summed them up as “Less, but better.” He wrote them about physical products, and in software they work best as questions to ask of a screen. The readings in the cards below are one translation, so argue with them and write your own. Rules Three rules keep the principles useful. 1. Ask them as questions, not rules Read as rules, some of the ten pull against each other. “Unobtrusive” says hide the toolbar, “understandable” says label every tool, and a checklist can’t say which one wins. Ask each one as a question about the goal, and the tension leads you to a design that serves both. 2. Cut what doesn’t serve the goal “As little design as possible” is often read as minimal styling: gray, flat, no labels. The screen looks simple, but people have to hunt for what they need. Remove what doesn’t serve the goal instead, and keep a visible label or a clear button, because it is often the essential part. 3. Treat “honest” as a design rule “Honest” sounds like a rule for advertising, so teams skip it, and a sign-up gets a fake countdown, a pre-ticked add-on and a price that grows later. People find out after they pay and stop trusting the product. Show the full cost before people commit, and leave add-ons unticked. See Smart defaults . In real products Each one serves a principle by leaving something out, or by caring about a detail most people never notice. - Notion: a new page is a title and an empty line. Every kind of block waits behind the / key, so the page stays plain until you need more. As little design as possible. - Photoshop: press Tab and the panels hide, leaving only the image. Press it again and they come back. The tool steps aside for the work. Unobtrusive. - App Store: each app’s page shows a privacy summary of the data it collects, before you download it. People see the cost up front. Honest. - iOS: drag past the top or bottom of a list and the content moves a little further, then springs back when you let go. It tells you that you reached the end, not that the app froze. Thorough down to the last detail.

entries.title: Train your eye
entries.summary: You train taste by looking closely at good work.

rules.title: Tag what you save by problem
Study whole flows, not showcase shots
Compare one property at a time

entries.tags: principle practice guide train eye taste looking closely good work rebuild screen admire detail name why there copying makes notice spacing
entries.search_text: Train your eye You train taste by looking closely at good work. Rebuild a screen you admire, detail by detail, and name why each detail is there. Copying makes you notice spacing, weight and color that you would otherwise skim past. Looking closely is not the same as collecting: a folder of screenshots trains nothing until you compare, rebuild and explain what you saved. Rules Four rules make close looking pay off. 1. Tag what you save by problem Screenshots saved under their default names are hard to find again, so when you design an empty state next month, you can’t search for one. Tag each shot by the problem it solves, like “empty state”, “bulk delete” or “long names”, so your collection answers the question you have. 2. Write down why it works A copy without a reason only fits the case you copied, so when the next case is different, you don’t know which part to keep. Write one line next to each copy on why it works, because the reason still helps when the picture doesn’t match. 3. Study whole flows, not showcase shots Showcase shots show only the happy path with perfect data, and much of the design work goes into the other states . Sign up, make mistakes on purpose, and capture every state you see. Tab through the flow and turn on a screen reader for a minute too. 4. Compare one property at a time Looking at two whole screens, you only notice that one “feels nicer”, and you can’t use what you can’t name. Compare one property at a time: spacing, then weight, then color, then corners. Small differences are easy to see once you look for one thing. In real products - Mobbin: a library of screenshots from real apps, filed by app, by flow and by pattern such as empty states. You can line up how many products answered the same problem. - Figma: select a layer and hold Option (Alt on Windows) while pointing at another to see the distance between them. Copying a design becomes measuring it, not guessing. - Chrome DevTools: inspect any element on a live site to read its exact spacing, font and colors, then change a value in place to see why it was chosen. - Pinterest: you save each image to a board you name. A board named for a problem, like “Empty states”, becomes a reference you can open when that problem comes up.

entries.title: Real material
entries.summary: Prototyping in the real material means building the risky parts of a design in code, early.

rules.title: Try the risky part in code early
Decide what “good” means before you tune
Try the messy cases on purpose

entries.tags: principle practice guide real material prototyping means building risky parts design code early mockup shows one still moment tidy text while
entries.search_text: Real material Prototyping in the real material means building the risky parts of a design in code, early. A mockup shows one still moment with tidy text, while code shows what happens when the message is long, the response is slow or the window is narrow. It also lets you test what a picture can’t: keyboard use, focus, screen readers and reduced motion. A prototype is not the feature. It answers one question, like “Can people read the toast before it goes?”, and then it’s thrown away. Keep mockups for what they answer faster, such as layout ideas and wording. Rules Four rules keep prototypes useful. 1. Try the risky part in code early A mockup uses short names and answers at once. The real build gets long names and slow responses, and nobody sees that until weeks later, when the design is signed off and changing it costs more. Build the risky part in code first, with real data and real timing, so problems show up while the design can still change. 2. Mark throwaway code as throwaway Prototype code is written fast, with fake delays, hard-coded colors and no tests. If nobody says so, it gets merged and ships, and months later someone has to work out which parts were real. Say it’s a prototype in the branch name and at the top of the file, then rebuild the idea properly. 3. Decide what “good” means before you tune Tuning without a goal never ends: each value looks a little off, so you keep nudging it and stop when you’re tired rather than when it works. Write down what has to be true first, like “people can read the caption before the slide changes”, then tune until it passes and stop. 4. Try the messy cases on purpose On your own laptop, with tidy sample data, everything looks fine, and people find the messy cases for you after launch: long names, empty lists, slow connections and small screens. Go through each one before you ship, and design what people see in it. In real products - Storybook: each state of a component is a story you can open on its own, like Long text or Error, and the Controls panel changes its data live. - Xcode: SwiftUI previews render the view next to its code and update as you type. Variants show it at several text sizes or orientations side by side. - Chrome DevTools: slow the network, narrow the viewport and turn on reduced motion, so a prototype meets slow responses and small screens before people do. - CodePen: code and result sit together and update as you type, so you can tune an animation’s timing by feel, then share a link others can fork.

entries.title: Design rationale
entries.summary: Design rationale is the reasoning behind a design decision, written down.

rules.title: Keep it where people will look
Lead with what changes for people

entries.tags: principle practice guide design rationale reasoning behind decision written down says what problem was which options considered one chose why next
entries.search_text: Design rationale Design rationale is the reasoning behind a design decision, written down. It says what the problem was, which options you considered, which one you chose and why. The next person reads it before they change the design. Without it, they guess, and may undo a choice that was made for a good reason. Rationale is not a description of how the design works, which the design itself shows. It records why it works that way, including the options you turned down. Record accessibility decisions too, like the keyboard path, because they are the first thing lost in a later rewrite. Rules Four rules keep design rationale useful. 1. Keep it where people will look Decisions are often made in a chat thread or on a call, and a month later nobody can find them, so a new teammate has to ask again or guess. Put the decision in the pull request description or a short doc, and link it from the issue so it’s one click from the question. 2. Include what you rejected A record that only names the winner answers “what”, not “why not”, so the next person suggests an option you already tried and the team argues it again. List each option you turned down, with one line on why, and the second discussion ends before it starts. 3. Write it while you decide Written weeks later, a record comes from memory. The reasons have faded, so it says “it seemed best”, which helps nobody. Write it while you’re still choosing, because spelling out each option’s trade-off often turns up a better option you hadn’t seen. 4. Lead with what changes for people Reviewers read the top of a pull request description and skim the rest. If it opens with refactors and file names, they can’t tell what people will notice, and the change people will feel gets the least review. Start with what changes for people, then why, then how it’s built. In real products - Material Design: guidelines pair a “Do” with a “Don’t” and a line on why, so the rejected option sits on the page next to the chosen one. - GOV.UK Design System: component pages say when not to use them and what research found, so teams see why a component works the way it does before they change it. - Python: a proposal to change the language, called a PEP, has a Rejected Ideas section that lists the alternatives raised and why each was turned down. - Wikipedia: every article has a talk page that keeps the discussion behind its wording, so a new editor can see what was already proposed and why it was turned down.

entries.title: Progressive disclosure
entries.summary: Progressive disclosure shows the settings most people need first and keeps the rest one step away, so people can start without judging every option on the screen.

rules.title: Let experts skip the extra click
Show what the hidden settings changed

entries.tags: pattern overload guide progressive disclosure shows settings most people need first keeps rest one step away start without judging every option
entries.search_text: Progressive disclosure Progressive disclosure shows the settings most people need first and keeps the rest one step away, so people can start without judging every option on the screen. Nothing is removed: the rest is there for the people who look for it. It works together with smart defaults , but where a default fills in a value for people, progressive disclosure decides what they see at all. Hidden settings should start on good defaults, so most people never need to open them. Ways to do it There are four common ways to keep the rest one step away. They differ in where the hidden part waits. - Show more. Use it when a few extra fields belong with the basics in one form. The button names what’s behind it. - Sections. Use it when there are many settings in a few clear groups. Closed sections still show their names, so people can scan for the one they need. - Separate page. Use it for settings few people change, which need room of their own. It costs a page change, so make the way back obvious. - When relevant. Use it when some options only matter after an earlier choice. Pick “Choose days” and the days appear. Rules Four rules keep progressive disclosure useful. 1. Say what’s hidden A button that says only “More options” gives no hint of what’s behind it, so people who need one of those settings don’t know it exists, and they give up or ask someone. Name what’s inside on the button and say how many, so people can tell whether it’s worth opening before they open it. 2. Let experts skip the extra click People who use the hidden settings every time pay for the split every time, and if the section closes again after each use, they open it over and over. Remember whether each person left it open, and give frequent users a keyboard shortcut or a setting to always show everything. 3. Split by what people change The line between basic and advanced is often a guess made before launch. If most people open the hidden part every time, the guess was wrong, and the split only adds a click. Look at what people actually change, and move anything most people need up into the basics. 4. Show what the hidden settings changed A hidden setting can still change the result, and people can’t fix a cause they can’t see. While the section is closed, show a short summary of every value that isn’t the default, and let people clear it from there. The most common case, a filter left on from an earlier visit, is covered in search with filters . In real products - Gmail: the search box is a single field. An icon in it opens fields for sender, subject and date, for the few searches that need them. - Lightroom: sliders are grouped into sections like Light and Color that open and close. Closed sections still show their names, so people know what’s inside. - VS Code: the settings editor opens on a short Commonly Used list. Every other setting is a search away, and experts can edit the settings file directly. - Google Maps: directions show the fastest route at once. Choices like avoiding tolls or highways wait in route options, for the trips that need them.

entries.title: Smart defaults
entries.summary: A smart default is a value filled in for people because it fits most of them, so they can accept it and move on, or change it.

rules.title: Base defaults on what people pick

entries.tags: pattern overload guide smart defaults default value filled people because fits most accept move change good removes one decision long form
entries.search_text: Smart defaults A smart default is a value filled in for people because it fits most of them, so they can accept it and move on, or change it. Each good default removes one decision, and on a long form that adds up. A default is a real value that will be used, shown in a field people can change. That separates it from a placeholder, which disappears when people type and is never used, and from a preset , which sets several linked values at once. Ways to do it Defaults differ in where the value comes from. - Most common. Use it when one answer fits most people. Base it on what people actually pick, not on what you hope they pick. - Last used. Use it when people repeat their own choice. Each person gets their own default, so it fits more people than one value can. - From context. Use it when the place, time or device already gives the answer. Say where the value came from, so a wrong guess is easy to spot and change. - From another field. Use it when one value follows from another, like an end time from a start time. Once people set it by hand, stop changing it for them. Rules Four rules keep smart defaults useful. 1. Base defaults on what people pick A default that’s wrong for many people is worse than none, because they have to notice it and change it on every visit. Look at what people actually choose and start there, then remember what each person used last, so someone with a different habit stops fixing it too. 2. Keep defaults in view Some defaults are applied where people can’t see them, so the result surprises people and they have no idea which setting caused it. Show every default in the form, in a field people can change. Mark values that differ from the default in words, not only with color, so people see what will happen before they press the button. 3. Start risky options off A default can quietly serve the business instead of the person, like a pre-ticked “public” box, and because most people never change defaults, they end up sharing what they meant to keep. Pick the safe, reversible option: anything that publishes, deletes, costs money or overwrites files should start off. 4. Use real values, not placeholders Gray text in an empty field looks like an answer, so people skip the field, and the form fails because it was empty all along. The gray text also vanishes as soon as they type. Put a real value in the field, or write the hint as a label or help text. In real products Notice where each default comes from: the spot you clicked, the most common choice, where you are, or what you already wrote. - Google Calendar: clicking a time slot starts an event right there, with the default length already set. Most events only need a title. - Figma: adding an export starts at PNG at 1x, the choice most people want. Both values sit right there to change. - Uber: pickup is already set to where you are, so the first question is only where to. - Google Docs: a document you never named takes its first line as its name. Files get a useful name without a question.

entries.title: Presets
entries.summary: A preset sets several linked values at once, under a name that says what you get, like “Fast” or “Best quality”.

rules.title: Offer a few, named by outcome

entries.tags: pattern overload guide presets preset sets several linked values once under name says what get like fast best quality people pick
entries.search_text: Presets A preset sets several linked values at once, under a name that says what you get, like “Fast” or “Best quality”. People pick the outcome they want instead of tuning each value, and the values stay in view, so people can still adjust one.
