Unlike a smart default , which fills in one field, a preset fills in a group of fields that only make sense together. Build the picker as a radio group, so arrow keys move between presets. Ways to do it Presets come in four common forms. They differ in how people choose one, and in whether it stays linked after it’s picked. - Picker. Use it when there are three to five outcomes people can name. The values each one sets stay in view. - Gallery. Use it when the result is easier to see than to describe. Each preset shows a small preview of what it will do to this photo. - Starting point. Use it when people pick once and then make it their own. The preset fills in the fields, and later edits don’t need to match it. - Linked style. Use it when the same look appears in many places. Changing the style once updates every heading that uses it. Rules Four rules keep presets useful. 1. Show what each preset sets A preset name alone doesn’t say what will change, so people pick one and find out what it did only when the result arrives, and careful people avoid presets. Show the values each preset sets next to the picker, and let people edit them. 2. Switch to “Custom” after an edit Once someone changes a value, the settings no longer match the preset, so a label that still shows the preset’s name is wrong, and people trust it. Switch the label to “Custom” as soon as a value changes, and mark what was edited. Picking the preset again brings its values back. 3. Offer a few, named by outcome A long list of presets is a new decision on top of the old one, and internal names make it worse, because people can’t tell what “JPG-80-2048” is for. Keep three to five presets, and name each one by what people want to do, like “Email” or “Print”. 4. Let people save their own Some people need the same mix of settings every time, and no built-in preset matches it, so without a way to save it they set each value again on every visit. Let them save their mix as a preset with their own name, next to the built-in ones. In real products - Photoshop: a new document starts from presets grouped by use, like Print or Web. Picking one fills in the size, resolution and color mode, which stay editable, and a custom setup can be saved as a new preset. - YouTube: on phones, video quality offers choices named by outcome, like higher quality or data saver. Exact resolutions are still there under Advanced. - Instagram: one tap on a filter changes several adjustments at once. Tapping it again shows a strength slider, so the look can be softened without starting over. - Google Docs: styles like Heading 1 set size, weight and spacing together. After restyling one heading by hand, “Update Heading 1 to match” gives every Heading 1 that look.

entries.title: Undo
entries.summary: Undo lets people act at once and take the action back afterwards.

rules.title: Keep a confirm for what can’t be undone
Give more than one way back

entries.tags: recovery delete remove unsaved tab close reversible time limit history undo toast
entries.search_text: Undo Undo lets people act at once and take the action back afterwards. The app deletes, moves or sends right away and keeps a way back open, so a wrong click costs a second instead of lost work. A confirm dialog asks “Are you sure?” before the action, when people haven’t seen the result yet, and after a few of them people click through without reading. Undo works after the action, when people can see what they did. Ways to do it Undo comes in four common forms. They differ in how long the way back stays open and where people find it. - Undo toast. Use it right after a single action, such as removing a song. A toast offers Undo for a few seconds, then leaves. - Undo history. Use it in editors where people make many small changes. Each Undo steps back one change, in order. Redo steps forward again, and the buttons name the step. - Trash. Use it when people may notice a mistake days later. Deleted items wait in the trash for a set time, and people can put them back from there. - Delay. Use it for actions that can’t be taken back once they happen, such as sending. The app waits a few seconds before it really acts, and Undo cancels it. Rules Four rules keep undo useful. 1. Plan where deleted things go Undo only works if the deleted thing still exists somewhere. If the app removes it for real and Undo is added later, Undo can only rebuild a rough copy, and people get back a name without the details they cared about. Plan for it in the data model from the start: mark items as deleted and keep them until the way back closes. Version history uses the same idea. 2. Keep Undo open long enough People often notice a mistake a few seconds late, after they look back at the screen, so an Undo that leaves after two seconds is already gone. Keep it until the next action, or for several seconds after people return to the page. Pause any timer while the pointer or focus is on the toast. 3. Keep a confirm for what can’t be undone Some actions can’t be reversed, such as emptying the trash, sending money or sharing with other people, and without a question one slip loses things for good. Ask first for these actions, and only these. Name the consequence in the question and put the action on the button, such as “Delete 12 files”. See Dialog . 4. Give more than one way back A toast is easy to miss and leaves after a while, so if Undo lives only there, people who missed it have no way back. Also support Ctrl+Z (⌘Z on Mac) and an Undo item in a menu that names what it will undo. After Undo, put focus on the restored item so keyboard users can carry on. In real products Notice where each way back lives: on screen, on the keyboard or in a menu. - Gmail: after Send, the message waits a few seconds with Undo on screen. Even sending, which is normally final, gets a way back. - macOS Finder: Move to Trash happens without a question. ⌘Z puts the file back, and the Edit menu names exactly what will be undone. - YouTube: choosing “Not interested” removes a video from the feed at once. The empty spot offers Undo, right where the tap happened.

entries.title: Preview
entries.summary: A preview shows what a change will do before it’s applied.

rules.title: Make the preview match the result

entries.tags: commit changes before after consequences apply cancel preview
entries.search_text: Preview A preview shows what a change will do before it’s applied. People try a setting on their own content, see the result, and then apply it or go back, and nothing changes until they say so. It suits changes that are slow, costly or hard to reverse. For quick changes that are easy to take back, undo is lighter: the change happens at once, and people step back if they don’t like it. Ways to do it Previews come in three common forms, which differ in where the result shows. - In place. Use it when trying an option is quick, such as styles or fonts. The real content changes while the pointer or focus rests on an option, goes back when it leaves, and only a click applies it. - Preview view. Use it when the result looks different from what people edit, such as formatted text. A separate view shows the result before anyone else sees it. - Summary. Use it when the result is something people can’t see yet, such as a price or what happens to their files. Say in words what will change before people confirm. Rules Four rules keep previews useful. 1. Make the preview match the result A preview is only useful if people can trust it. When it’s drawn differently from the real result, small differences slip in, like text that fits in the preview and is cut off in the result, and people stop trusting it. Draw the preview with the same code as the final output, and if it can’t match, label it “Approximate preview”. 2. Keep the preview fast People adjust a setting by watching the result, so if the preview trails behind the control, they overshoot, wait and adjust again, and the control feels sticky. Show a quick rough version right away and finish it when the full one is ready, and hold back slow work while a slider is still moving. 3. Show that it’s a preview People forget they’re in a preview, leave, and believe the change was applied, then find out later that it never happened. Mark the preview with a label and an outline, and keep Apply and Cancel in view the whole time. Put the label in text so screen readers announce it too, and ask before people leave with changes that aren’t applied. 4. Skip it for small changes A preview step on every setting turns each change into two clicks, so people get slower and stop reading the previews. Apply cheap, reversible changes at once and offer undo , and keep preview-then-apply for changes that are slow, costly or hard to reverse. In real products - Photoshop: filter dialogs show the effect on the image as values change, with a Preview checkbox to compare before and after. Nothing is applied until OK. - GitHub: comment boxes have Write and Preview tabs, so the formatting can be checked before anyone else sees it. - Word: resting the pointer on a style or font shows it on your text. Moving away puts it back, and only a click applies it. - Uber: before you confirm, each ride option shows its price and how soon it arrives.

entries.title: Version history
entries.summary: Version history keeps earlier versions of a document so people can go back to one.
entries.tags: recovery restore soft delete draft retention data loss version history
entries.search_text: Version history Version history keeps earlier versions of a document so people can go back to one. A trash does the same for deleted items, which wait there for a while before they’re gone. Both let people make big changes without fear of losing what worked. Where undo covers the last few seconds, version history covers days and weeks, and it still works after the app was closed. Ways to do it There are four common forms, which differ in what they cover: a whole document, one value or deleted items. - Automatic. Use it for documents people edit over days. The app saves versions on its own, lists them by time and author, and shows what each one changed. - Named. Use it when some moments matter more than others. People save a version with a name, and it stands out among the automatic ones. - One value. Use it when people care about one value more than the whole document, such as a cell in a spreadsheet. Its own history shows who changed it, when, and from what. - Trash. Use it for anything people delete. Each item in the trash shows how many days it has left. Rules Four rules keep version history useful. 1. Name versions by what changed A list of times says when something changed, not what changed, so people open one version after another to find the one they want. Describe each version by its change, such as “Added the menu”. Write that line automatically, and let people rename the versions that matter. 2. Restore as a new version If restoring an old version deletes everything newer, one wrong restore loses days of work, and people avoid restoring at all. Add the restored version on top as the newest one, so everything newer stays in the history and the restore itself can be undone. 3. Say what restoring will change A time doesn’t say what will happen to the current document, so people restore and then find parts missing that they wanted to keep. Show a short summary of the difference next to the Restore button, such as “Removes 2 slides and brings back the old title”. Put it in text, so screen readers read it too. 4. Say when the trash empties A trash that empties without warning removes things people still expect to find, and one that never empties grows until nobody can find anything in it. Empty it after a set time, such as 30 days, say so in the trash itself, and show how long each item has left. In real products - Google Docs: version history lists versions by time and author, and important ones can be named. Restoring one adds it as the newest version, so later edits stay in the list. - Figma: besides automatic saves, people can save a version with a title and a short description. The history then reads as named milestones, not just times. - GitHub: a merged pull request has a Revert button. It opens a new pull request that undoes the change, so the history keeps both. - iPhone Photos: deleted photos wait in Recently Deleted, and each one shows how many days it has left before it’s gone for good.

entries.title: Instant feedback
entries.summary: Instant feedback means the screen answers an action right away: a pressed button changes, a ticked box shows a tick, a save says “Saving…”.

rules.title: Leave the confirmation up long enough
Show it where the action happened
Match the strength to the action
Ignore repeat clicks while it works

entries.tags: status saving saved duplicate submission progress feedback
entries.search_text: Instant feedback Instant feedback means the screen answers an action right away: a pressed button changes, a ticked box shows a tick, a save says “Saving…”. People know their action registered, so they don’t click again or give up. The work itself may take seconds, but the sign that it started should take less than a tenth of a second. Put the new state in text as well, so screen readers announce it too. Ways to do it Feedback comes in four common strengths. The bigger or slower the action, the stronger the answer. - Pressed state. Use it for most clicks. The control itself changes the moment it’s pressed, and nothing else is needed. - Status line. Use it for work that runs in the background while people keep going, such as saving. A short status near the title says “Saving…”, then settles on “Saved” until the next change. - Change in place. Use it when the action changes the thing on screen. The item shows its new state at once: the button reads “Following” and the count goes up. - Toast. Use it when the result leaves the screen or matters more, such as archiving an email. The email is gone from view, so a short toast says where it went and offers Undo. Rules Four rules keep feedback useful. 1. Leave the confirmation up long enough A confirmation that flashes by is gone before people look at it, so they’re left unsure and do the action again. Keep a short confirmation on screen for one to two seconds, or better, switch to a state that lasts, like “Saved just now”, until the next change. 2. Show it where the action happened People look at the thing they just clicked, so a change in a far corner of the screen goes unseen and they click again. Show the answer on the button, row or card that was used. A counter elsewhere can update too, as a second sign. 3. Match the strength to the action When every small action gets a toast, the toasts pile up and people stop reading them, so they miss the one that matters too. A changed control is enough for most clicks. Keep toasts and other strong signals for actions that matter or take a while. 4. Ignore repeat clicks while it works When a button gives no sign during a slow action, people click again, and each click can run the action again: two comments, two orders. While it works, say so on the button and ignore further clicks. Use aria-disabled instead of disabled, so keyboard focus stays on the button. In real products - GitHub: the copy button on a code block turns into a check mark for a moment. The answer appears on the button that was just pressed. - Google Docs: next to the title, the status says it’s saving while you type, then settles on a saved state that stays until the next change. - Duolingo: pressing Check turns the bottom panel green or red right away, with a sound, and the same button becomes Continue.

entries.title: Optimistic UI
entries.summary: Optimistic UI shows the result of an action before the server confirms it.
entries.tags: async race server write stale response concurrency rollback optimistic
entries.search_text: Optimistic UI Optimistic UI shows the result of an action before the server confirms it. The app assumes the action will work, updates the screen at once, and sends the request in the background. If the request fails, it puts things back and says so. It goes one step further than instant feedback , which only shows that the action has started: here the result itself shows at once. That suits small actions that almost always succeed, such as a like, a star or a status change. Ways to do it Four kinds of actions often use it, and each needs its own way to show a failure. Tick “Make the next request fail” to see it. - Toggle. Use it for on and off actions, such as liking a song. The heart fills the moment it’s tapped. If saving fails, it empties again on that row, with a reason and Retry. - New item. Use it when people add something, such as a message. It appears in the list at once, slightly faded until it’s saved. If it fails, it stays in place, marked “Not sent”, with Retry. - Move. Use it when people move something, such as a task to Done. The card moves at once. If saving fails, it moves back to where it was, and a line under the board says so. - Rename. Use it when people edit text, such as an album name. The new name shows at once. If saving fails, the old name comes back and the typed name stays in the field, so nothing is lost. Rules Three rules keep optimistic UI honest. 1. Show failures where they happened Sometimes the request fails after the screen has changed. If nothing says so, the change quietly vanishes later or looks saved when it isn’t, and people find out much later, when it matters. Roll the change back where people can see it, say what failed, and offer Retry. Announce the rollback in text too, because a heart that empties again is invisible to a screen reader. 2. Wait when it matters Some actions often fail or carry a real cost, like payments or deletes. Showing success at once and taking it back a moment later is worse than waiting, because people may already have closed the app, sure it worked. For these, wait for the server’s answer and show progress. Keep optimism for small, reversible actions that almost always succeed. 3. Let the latest request decide Two quick clicks send two requests, and the answers can come back in the wrong order. If the screen follows whichever answer arrives last, it can show a state the person didn’t choose. Treat the server’s answer as the truth, but let only the latest request decide what’s shown. In real products - Linear: changing an issue’s status, assignee or priority shows at once, and the change syncs in the background. Nothing waits on a spinner. - Instagram: the heart fills and the count goes up the moment you tap. - iMessage: a sent message appears in the thread at once. If it fails, it stays in place, marked Not Delivered with a red icon, and tapping it offers to try again.

entries.title: Background work
entries.summary: Some work takes longer than people want to wait, such as an upload, an export or a backup.

rules.title: Keep finished work in a list

entries.tags: long task download upload notifications progress background
entries.search_text: Background work Some work takes longer than people want to wait, such as an upload, an export or a backup. Background work lets it run while people keep doing other things. A small indicator shows that it’s still going, a toast says when it’s done, and finished results wait in a list until people look at them. That is what separates it from a progress bar in a dialog, which makes people sit and watch: here people keep working while the progress stays on screen. Tell screen readers when the work starts and when it ends, not at every step of progress. Ways to do it There are four common ways to keep background work in view. They differ in how much room the work takes and in how people hear that it’s done. Many products combine two, like an indicator while it runs and a toast at the end. - Indicator. A small status in a bar that stays on screen. - Panel. A corner panel with one row per item, which people can shrink. - Toast when done. A short toast when the work finishes, with a way to open the result. - Email when ready. For work that takes many minutes or hours. Rules Four rules keep background work useful. 1. Keep progress on screen People rarely stay on the screen where they started a long job, and once they move on, progress that lived on that screen is gone. They can’t tell if the work is still running, stuck or done, so they go back to check or start it again. Put a small indicator in a bar that stays on every screen. 2. Keep finished work in a list A toast that says “ready” is easy to miss, because people look away or it fades before they finish what they’re doing. If that toast was the only way to the result, the result is lost to them. Keep finished work in a list they can open later, and mark new items until they’ve been opened. 3. Group notices that come together When many items finish close together, one toast per item piles up. The toasts cover the screen and all say nearly the same thing, and people have to read or close each one. Send one toast for the whole batch, with a link to the items. 4. Make failures louder than success A failure that looks like a success goes unnoticed until someone needs the file, and by then it may be too late to redo the work. Keep a failure on screen until it’s dealt with: mark it clearly, say what went wrong, and offer a way to fix it. In real products Notice where progress lives while the work runs, and where the result waits once it’s done. - Google Drive: uploads run in a small panel in the corner, one row per file, while you keep browsing. Finished files keep their check until you close the panel. - Lightroom Classic: imports and exports show a thin progress bar in the top-left corner, so you can keep editing photos while they run. - Instagram: after you share a post, you land back in the feed, and a strip at the top shows your photo with a progress bar until it’s posted. - Safari: the downloads button in the toolbar shows progress, and its list keeps finished files, so a download you missed is still one click away.

entries.title: Command palette
entries.summary: A command palette is a search box for actions.

rules.title: Give it a visible way in
Name commands as a verb and an object

entries.tags: pattern find guide command palette search box actions people press shortcut usually ctrl mac type what want enter don need know
entries.search_text: Command palette A command palette is a search box for actions. People press a shortcut, usually Ctrl+K (⌘K on Mac), type what they want to do and press Enter. They don’t need to know which menu holds the command, only a word for it. That is what separates it from search : search finds things, like a file or an email, and a palette runs commands, like “Export to PDF”. It adds a fast path for people who know what they want, and it doesn’t replace the menus. Ways to do it Palettes differ in what they search and when they open. - All commands. One box for every command in the app, opened with Ctrl+K or ⌘K. - Commands and pages. The same box also finds pages and files. - For the selection. Only the commands that fit the selected item. - Slash in text. Typing “/” at the start of a line opens a short menu of things to add. Rules Four rules keep a command palette useful. 1. Give it a visible way in A palette that opens only with a shortcut is hidden from anyone who doesn’t know the shortcut, so newcomers never find it and keep hunting through menus. Give the palette a button people can see, with the shortcut written on it. Keep the menus too, and show each command’s shortcut there, so people learn the keys over time. 2. Match the words people type People type the word in their head, not the command’s official name. With strict matching, “dark mode” finds nothing when the command is called “Change theme”, and people decide the app can’t do it. Match loosely: letters in order, plus a few synonyms for each command. Show why a result matched, so people learn the real name. 3. Name commands as a verb and an object A palette full of one-word entries is hard to scan: “PDF” and “Export” could each mean several things, so people try them one by one. Name every command as a verb and an object, like “Export to PDF”. Group them, and show recent commands first when the box is empty. 4. Use one well-known shortcut A shortcut that is also a normal key gets in the way of typing: if “/” opens the palette everywhere, people can’t type “and/or” in a note. Use the shortcut most apps share, Ctrl+K (⌘K on Mac), listen for it only where it applies, and never take keys people need for typing. In real products Notice what each palette teaches on the side: a shortcut, the current selection, or where the command lives in the menus. - VS Code: the Command Palette lists commands with their keyboard shortcuts beside them and puts recently used ones first, so using it slowly teaches the shortcuts. - Linear: with an issue selected, ⌘K offers actions for that issue, like changing its status or assignee, each with the one-key shortcut that does the same. - Notion: typing “/” in a page opens a menu of blocks you filter by name, so adding a heading or a table never leaves the keyboard. It’s a palette pointed at the things you can add. - macOS: the search field in an app’s Help menu finds menu commands by name, and pointing at a result opens the real menu with an arrow on the command, so you learn where it lives.

entries.title: Search with filters
entries.summary: Search with filters helps people narrow a long list fast, such as products, emails or files.

rules.title: Show recent items before anyone types

entries.tags: pattern find guide search filters helps people narrow long list fast such products emails files box takes words kind like size
entries.search_text: Search with filters Search with filters helps people narrow a long list fast, such as products, emails or files. The search box takes words, and filters narrow by kind, like size, date or type. Recent items cover the common case of coming back for something used before. Unlike a command palette , which runs actions, search finds things. It works only when people can see what the search and the filters leave out. Tell screen readers the result count once typing pauses, not on every key. Ways to do it There are four common shapes. Chips and a panel narrow the results, a scope picks where to search, and recents help before anyone types. - Filter chips. A row of toggles above the list. - Filter panel. Groups of checkboxes, each with a count of the items it matches. - Search scope. A choice of where to search, like this folder or everywhere. - Recents and suggestions. Places from before show as soon as the box gets focus, and suggestions narrow as people type. Rules Four rules keep search with filters useful. 1. Show what the filters hide Filters often stay on from an earlier visit, and if people can’t see them, they search, find nothing and decide the item doesn’t exist. Keep active filters in view and show the result count. Say how many matches sit outside the filters, and offer one click to see them. 2. Don’t stop at “No results” An empty page with only “No results” leaves people stuck, because they can’t tell if they misspelled a word, used the wrong term or filtered too much. Repeat what they searched for, offer a close spelling, and offer to clear filters. Empty state covers how “no results” differs from “nothing yet”. 3. Start with a few filters Each filter is one more thing to read, so with fifteen, the filter panel turns into a form and the results drop out of view. Start with three to five filters that match how people already choose, like price and breakfast for a hotel. Put the rest behind “More filters”, and add new ones when people ask for them. 4. Show recent items before anyone types People often search for something they used a short while ago, and an empty box makes them type the name again and remember how it’s spelled. Show recent items as soon as the box gets focus. When filters are on, show only the recent items that fit them. In real products - Spotify: the library has type chips, like Playlists or Artists, above a list sorted by Recents, so “the one I played yesterday” is near the top and “I know it’s an album” is one tap. - Airbnb: the button at the bottom of the filter panel says how many places match and updates as you change filters, so you see the effect before you apply it. - GitHub: the filters you pick are written into the search box as text, like “is:open label:bug”, so you can always see what’s applied and edit it. - Gmail: after a search, chips under the box, like “Has attachment” or a date range, narrow the results with one click, without learning search operators.

entries.title: Labels in people’s words
entries.summary: People scan menus and links for the word already in their head.

rules.title: Use people’s words, not the team’s
Name what’s inside, not the brand
Use one name for one thing
Test the whole path with a task

entries.tags: pattern find guide labels people words scan menus links word already head label matches click confidence doesn guess back try again
entries.search_text: Labels in people’s words People scan menus and links for the word already in their head. When a label matches it, they click with confidence, and when it doesn’t, they guess, go back and try again, or give up. This pull of matching words is called information scent. Labels in people’s words carry that scent: they name things the way customers do, not the way the team does inside the company. Each label should also make sense on its own, because many people, screen reader users among them, jump from label to label without seeing the layout around it. Ways to do it A label can carry more or less scent, and the more alike the options are, the more each label needs to say. - Name the thing - Name the task - Add a description - Show what’s inside Rules Four rules keep labels in people’s words. 1. Use people’s words, not the team’s Teams name things after how the system works: “entities”, “remittance”, a database field. People don’t know those words, so they read every option and guess. Collect the words people use in support questions, reviews and searches before you name things, and use those. 2. Name what’s inside, not the brand Clever or branded names are fun to write, but they don’t say what’s behind them, so people open each one to find out and remember none of them. Use plain names that say what each section holds, and keep personality for empty states and onboarding, where it doesn’t cost a click. 3. Use one name for one thing When one thing has two names, people assume they are two things and wonder whether the cart and the bag hold the same items. As with consistent naming anywhere in a product, pick one term for each concept, use it everywhere and keep a short glossary. 4. Test the whole path with a task A label can be right and still go unfound, because it sits under a parent nobody opens. People pick a top-level section first, and if that name doesn’t match their goal, they never see what’s inside. Give people a task, like “Where would you add your passport number?”, and watch where they click first, which is called tree testing. Move items to where people look. In real products - GOV.UK: pages are named for the task people come to do, like “Renew your passport”, not for the office that handles it. - Blender: menus use plain names like “Cube”. With Python tooltips turned on, the tooltip adds the scripting name under the description, for the people who need it. - Uber: the main box asks “Where to?”, the question already in your head, instead of a form label like “Destination”. - Windows: searching the old Control Panel name, “Add or remove programs”, still opens the newer Apps page in Settings, so people who learned the old words still get there.

entries.title: Templates
entries.summary: Templates and starter content give people a working example to start from, instead of an empty page.

rules.title: Keep a blank start one click away

entries.tags: pattern blank guide templates starter content give people working example start instead empty page see what finished result looks like change
entries.search_text: Templates Templates and starter content give people a working example to start from, instead of an empty page. People see what a finished result looks like and change it into their own, so they reach a first result faster and see what the product can do. Where a preset fills in settings, a template gives a whole starting document, with content people are meant to replace. After a template opens, move focus to the first thing to change. Ways to do it There are four common ways to give people a start. They differ in where the start comes from: a gallery of templates, a filled-in example in a new account, people’s own past work, or a few one-click starts on an empty page. - Gallery. Several templates, shown before people start. - Sample content. A new account comes with a filled-in example that teaches by doing. - Copy your own. People start from something they made before. - Starters on the page. A blank page with a few one-click starts on it. Rules Four rules keep templates useful. 1. Offer a few different starts If every template works the same way, people take it as the only way and fit their content into it, even when it doesn’t suit them. Offer a few starts that differ in kind, and say in one line what each is good for, so people pick by goal and see the range of what the product can do. 2. Keep templates up to date Templates go stale: an old year, renamed features, a chart type that no longer works. A broken template is often someone’s first experience of the product, so own templates like features: give each one an owner, check it with every release, and update or retire it. 3. Mark what to change A good example looks finished, so people can’t tell which parts are theirs to change, and the example text they miss ends up in what they send. Mark the parts meant to be edited with words and a border, not color alone, and add one line that names the first thing to do. 4. Keep a blank start one click away People who know what they want don’t need a template, and if every new file opens a gallery first, they click past it each time. Keep “Blank” as an equal choice next to the templates, one click away. In real products Notice that a blank start stays one click away, and each template already works before you change anything. - Google Docs: “Blank” is the first tile, in the same row as the templates for a resume or a letter. - Blender: a new file starts from a task, like Sculpting or Video Editing, and General opens with a cube, a camera and a light, so the first render works before you’ve built anything. - Instagram: a Reels template keeps another reel’s cuts and song, and leaves a slot for each of your clips, so it’s clear which parts are yours to fill.

entries.title: Contextual hints
entries.summary: A contextual hint teaches one thing at the moment people need it, next to the thing it explains.

rules.title: Show one hint at a time
Remember when people close a hint
Keep key help somewhere else too

entries.tags: pattern blank guide contextual hints hint teaches one thing moment people need next explains appears after related action such first click
entries.search_text: Contextual hints A contextual hint teaches one thing at the moment people need it, next to the thing it explains. It appears after a related action, such as a first click on an empty whiteboard, and stays away once people know the thing, so people who already know it never see it. A product tour works the other way round: it explains everything up front, before people have a reason to care. Most people skip it, and the rest forget it by the time they get stuck. Ways to do it Hints range from quiet to loud. Placeholder text sits inside an empty field. A help icon waits until people ask. A callout points at one control, once. A nudge appears after people do something the long way and offers the short way. Pick the quietest one that still reaches people at the right moment. - Placeholder. Use it for a short example of what goes in an empty field. - Help icon. Use it for detail only some people want. - Callout. Use it once, to point at a new or easy-to-miss control. - Nudge. Use it after people do something the long way, to offer the short way. Rules Four rules keep contextual hints useful. 1. Show one hint at a time When every feature gets its own hint, they all show up at once. People can’t tell which one matters, the bubbles sit on top of the things they wanted to use, and they close them all without reading. Show one hint, right after people do the related thing, and skip hints for things they already use. 2. Remember when people close a hint A closed hint that comes back tells people their choice didn’t count, and after the second time they close hints without reading them, new ones included. Remember every closed hint, ideally with the account so it holds on every device, and give people one place to see the tips again. 3. Keep the target in view A hint is about one control. If it sits on top of that control, people have to close the hint before they can try what it explains, and by then they have half forgotten it. Place the hint beside the control and point at it. Keep the control usable, and don’t move keyboard focus into the hint. 4. Keep key help somewhere else too Once a hint is closed, it’s gone, so if it was the only place that explained something, people who need it later have nowhere to look. Write the same help in the help pages or a help panel, and link there from the hint so people know where to find it again. In real products - Google Maps: on a map inside a web page, a one-finger swipe scrolls the page, and the map shows “Use two fingers to move the map” only when you try. If you already use two fingers, you never see it. - Notion: an empty line shows a faint hint to type “/” for commands, but only the line your cursor is on, and it’s gone the moment you type. - Slack: once you start typing, a small note in the corner of the message box says how to add a new line, right where people would otherwise send by mistake. - Photoshop: holding the pointer over a tool shows its name, one line on what it does and a short looping video of it in use, right when you’re wondering what the icon means.

entries.title: Constraints
entries.summary: A constraint makes a wrong value impossible to enter.

rules.title: Leave a way out for odd cases
Say why an option is off
Show the rule before people need it
Keep the rule in one place

entries.tags: pattern errors guide constraints constraint makes wrong value impossible enter instead free text field error afterwards people pick options all work
entries.search_text: Constraints A constraint makes a wrong value impossible to enter. Instead of a free text field and an error afterwards, people pick from options that all work, or set a number that stops at its limits. There is nothing to refuse, because every choice is valid. Validation works the other way round: it lets people type anything, then checks it and explains the mistake. Use a constraint when the valid values are few or follow a clear rule, and keep validation for values too varied to offer as choices. Ways to do it Constraints come in a few shapes. A list offers only the values that work. A number with limits stops at its smallest and largest value. Options that don’t apply right now stay visible but turned off. Split fields take one part of a value at a time, so its shape can’t go wrong. - List. Use it when the valid values are few and known. - Limits. Use it for a count or an amount within a range. - Turned off. Use it when some options exist but can’t be chosen right now. - Split fields. Use it for a value with a fixed shape, like a 6-digit code. Rules Four rules keep constraints useful. 1. Leave a way out for odd cases A short list covers most people, but not everyone. Someone with an odd-sized window has no way to enter the width they really need, so they give up or pick something wrong. Add a “Custom…” choice for those cases, check what people type there, and say so when you round it . 2. Say why an option is off A grayed-out option with no reason looks broken: people click it, nothing happens, and they don’t know whether to upgrade, free up space or give up. Put the reason next to the option, in plain text: what it needs and how to get it. Leave out options that can never apply to this person. 3. Show the rule before people need it Some values follow a rule that can’t be built into the control, like which characters a username may use. If people only learn the rule from an error, they have to guess again. Write the rule in the label or the help text under the field, so people get it right on the first try. 4. Keep the rule in one place The list, the help text and the final check often get written at different times. When they disagree, people pick a value the list allows and get refused at the end. Write the rule once and build the list, the help text and the check from it, so they can’t drift apart. In real products Notice that choices that can’t work are either never offered or visibly off. - Google Calendar: the end-time list only runs forward from the start time and shows each length, like “(1 hr)”, so an event can’t end before it begins. - Airbnb: dates that are already booked are grayed out and can’t be picked. - Duolingo: many exercises have you build the answer from word tiles, so every try is a sentence that can be checked, and you can switch to typing when you want it harder. - VS Code: the Settings editor builds each control from the setting’s definition, so a setting with fixed options gets a dropdown and an on/off one gets a checkbox.

entries.title: Forgiving input
entries.summary: Forgiving input accepts a value in the ways people actually write it.

rules.title: Ask only when it could mean two things
Say when the value itself changes

entries.tags: pattern errors guide forgiving input accepts value ways people actually write 1024 768 all mean same size field reads cleans spaces
entries.search_text: Forgiving input Forgiving input accepts a value in the ways people actually write it. “1024 x 768”, “1024×768” and “1024 by 768” all mean the same size, so the field reads all of them. It cleans up spaces, symbols and units on its own, and it shows how it read the input. Where a constraint limits what people can enter, forgiving input lets them enter a value their way and does the translating. Both prevent the same thing: an error about formatting that any person would have understood. Ways to do it A field can forgive in a few ways. It can accept several formats for the same value. It can clean up formatting, such as spaces and dashes. It can notice a likely typo and offer the fix. It can read plain words, like “tomorrow 9am”. Each way shows the result, so people can check it. - Many formats. Use it for values people write in different ways, like amounts. - Clean-up. Use it for values full of spaces, dashes and brackets, like phone numbers. - Typo fix. Use it when a small slip is likely and costly, like a mistyped email domain. - Plain words. Use it for dates and times, where people think in words. Rules Four rules keep forgiving input useful. 1. Show how you read it A field that guesses can guess wrong, and if it says nothing, people find out later, when the parcel costs seven times as much or the wrong thing arrives. Show the reading next to the field, in words, before the value is used, so a wrong guess is caught on sight. 2. Ask only when it could mean two things Most input has one obvious reading, and asking about it only slows people down. Some input really could mean two things, like “7” for a time, and a field that quietly picks one is sometimes wrong without anyone noticing. Take the obvious reading when there is one, and ask only in the real two-way cases, with each answer one click away. 3. Forgive the same way everywhere When one field accepts “12m 30s” and the next one rejects it, people can’t learn what works, so they fall back to the strictest format everywhere or give up on the shortcuts. Put the reading of times, sizes and amounts in one shared function and use it in every field, so a format that works once works everywhere. 4. Say when the value itself changes Cleaning up spaces or a “cm” is harmless, so do it without comment. Changing the number is different, because people get something they didn’t ask for. When you round to the nearest valid value, say so, and when the value is far outside what’s possible, refuse it and give the limit instead of picking one. In real products - Google Search: a misspelled search still gets results, with a line saying what it searched for instead and a link to search exactly what you typed. - Figma: size and position fields accept math, so typing “120 2” sets the width to 240 without leaving the field to work it out. - Todoist: as you type a task like “Call Sam tomorrow at 3pm”, the date words are highlighted and turned into a due date, so you see what it understood before you save. - Gmail: paste a list of addresses separated by commas or semicolons into the To field, and each one becomes its own recipient.

entries.title: Autosave
entries.summary: Autosave keeps people’s work without them asking.

rules.title: Offer recovery only when something was lost

entries.tags: draft persistence unsaved tab close restore storage write failure data loss autosave
entries.search_text: Autosave Autosave keeps people’s work without them asking. Each change is saved a moment after it’s made, and a small status says so. If the app crashes or the tab closes, the work is waiting when people come back. Autosave keeps only the latest state, so it belongs together with version history , which keeps the earlier ones. Ways to do it Autosave takes a few forms. A document saves as people type and shows the save state. A settings page saves each change the moment it’s made. A message box keeps unsent text when people move somewhere else. After a crash, the app offers the work it kept on the device. - As you type. Use it for documents people write over time. - Each change. Use it for settings, where each change is small and easy to reverse. - Unsent text. Use it for message boxes, where people often switch away mid-sentence. - After a crash. Use it for apps that keep work on the device between saves. Rules Four rules keep autosave useful. 1. Show that work is saved If people can’t see that their work is saved, they don’t trust it: they keep saving by hand, or they lose work when a save fails without a word. Show a save status where they already look. If a save fails, say so plainly, keep the work on the device and send it once the connection is back. 2. Keep earlier versions Autosave saves mistakes too: if someone deletes a paragraph by accident, the save goes through a second later and the old text is gone. Pair autosave with version history, so any earlier version is one step back. A recovered draft should also wait until people choose Restore or Discard. 3. Catch edits from another tab The same document can be open in two tabs or on two devices. Each copy saves its own text, so the last save replaces the other without a word, and people notice much later that what they added in the other place is gone. Detect the clash and ask before one copy replaces the other. 4. Offer recovery only when something was lost A recovery prompt that shows up every time teaches people to dismiss it, so the one time it matters, they press Discard without reading. Offer recovery only when the draft differs from what was saved. Clear old drafts after a while, and let Discard be undone for a moment. In real products Notice how each product shows that work is safe, and what comes back after a close or a crash. - Google Docs: saves as you type, so there’s no Save button to forget, only “Saved to Drive” next to the title. - Word: after a crash, a recovery pane lists the autosaved copy next to the last saved one, so you choose which to keep. - VS Code: quit with unsaved files and they reopen next time, still marked unsaved. Nothing is lost, and nothing is written to the file until you save. - Telegram: leave a chat mid-message and the chat list marks it as a draft. The text is still there when you come back, even on another device.

entries.title: Layered interface
entries.summary: A layered interface shows a simple set of controls first and keeps the full set one step away.

rules.title: Build both layers on one set of settings
Keep the way to more in sight
Show what changed out of sight
Decide where each new option goes

entries.tags: pattern layers guide layered interface shows simple set controls first keeps full one step away new occasional users get few choices
entries.search_text: Layered interface A layered interface shows a simple set of controls first and keeps the full set one step away. New and occasional users get the few choices that matter, and experts open the advanced layer to change the rest. Both layers change the same settings, so switching between them loses nothing. Where progressive disclosure tucks away the settings few people change, a layered interface gives newcomers and experts each a named layer of the same controls, and people pick the one they work in. Ways to do it There are a few ways to layer. Show more and a separate page work as in progressive disclosure . The other two split the work into two versions: a mode switch flips the whole screen between a basic and a full version, and a quick form handles the common case and opens the full form for the rest. - Show more. Use it when a few extra fields help some people, on the same screen. - Mode switch. Use it when a whole screen has a basic and a full version, and people stay in one for a while. - Separate page. Use it for settings few people ever need, kept out of the main screen. - Quick, then full. Use it when most people need only a title and a time, and some need everything. Rules Four rules keep a layered interface useful. 1. Build both layers on one set of settings If Simple and Advanced are two separate forms, they drift apart: a value typed in one is missing in the other, and some settings work in only one mode. Build Simple on top of the same settings as Advanced, so it only hides fields and keeps their values. 2. Keep the way to more in sight If the way to the full controls is hard to find, people assume the simple layer is all there is, and they scroll through everything or leave. Put the way in a fixed, visible place, as a named button or a segmented control , and say what’s behind it , such as “Filters: size, color, price”. 3. Show what changed out of sight Settings changed in the advanced layer still apply after people go back to the simple one, and a change nobody can see makes results look wrong for no clear reason. Show a short summary in the simple layer, such as “1 advanced setting changed”, with a way to show it and a way to reset it. 4. Decide where each new option goes When nobody decides where a new option goes, it lands in Advanced, which over time becomes a long, unsorted list where settings many people need get buried. For each option, choose the simple layer, the advanced layer, or a better default that makes it unnecessary. Keep Advanced for real expert choices, grouped in a sensible order. In real products - Gmail: the search options button opens fields like From, Subject and Date, and turns them into a query in the same search box. - VS Code: the searchable settings form and the JSON file that experts open from the corner icon edit one file. - Airbnb: the search bar asks only where, when and who. Price, type of place and amenities wait behind Filters for the people who care.

entries.title: Keyboard shortcuts
entries.summary: A keyboard shortcut runs a command from the keyboard, without the mouse.

rules.title: Show the keys where people look
Don’t take keys the browser already uses
Ignore single keys while people type
Keep a visible way to do it

entries.tags: keyboard single character speech dictation accessibility shortcuts
entries.search_text: Keyboard shortcuts A keyboard shortcut runs a command from the keyboard, without the mouse. People who repeat the same commands all day save a second or two each time, and that adds up. Shortcuts are for people who already know the command, while new people find it in a button or a menu and learn the key from there. Where a command palette lets people search for a command by name, a shortcut runs one they already know with a single key press. Ways to do it Shortcuts come in four shapes. A single key is the fastest, but it only works where people aren’t typing. A key with Ctrl or ⌘ works anywhere. A sequence of two keys gives room for more commands. A command palette lets people type the name of any command and shows its key on the way. - Single key. Use it for commands people repeat many times in one area, like moving through a list. It only works while focus is in that area, never in a text field. - With Ctrl or ⌘. Use it for commands that should work anywhere, even while people type, like sending. Click in the reply and press - Sequence. Use it when there are more commands than free keys. Gmail uses G then I to go to the inbox. The first key waits for the second, so show that it’s waiting. - Command palette. Use it when there are many commands. People type part of a name and pick from the list. The list shows each command’s key, so people learn it on the way. Rules Four rules keep shortcuts useful. 1. Show the keys where people look A shortcut nobody knows about saves nobody any time, and people don’t read help pages, so they never learn the key and keep clicking. Show each key next to its command, in buttons, menus and tooltips , and keep the full list behind “?”. 2. Don’t take keys the browser already uses People rely on keys like copy, paste, undo, find and close tab in every app. If your app uses one of them, either the browser wins and your command never runs, or your app wins and people lose a key they rely on. Pick keys that are free, and let people see and change all of them in one place. 3. Ignore single keys while people type A single-letter shortcut is fast in a list, but in a text field the same letter is part of a word. As with a palette that opens on “/” , a shortcut that still fires there runs commands people didn’t ask for. Turn single keys off while focus is in a text field, and give each shortcut a clear area where it works. 4. Keep a visible way to do it Some people never use the keyboard: they use a mouse, a touch screen or voice. Others haven’t learned the key yet, and if a command only has a shortcut, none of them can use it. Give every command a button or a menu item, and treat the shortcut as the faster path to it. In real products Notice how each product teaches its shortcuts on the slow path, and keeps single keys out of the way while people type. - macOS: every menu shows each command’s shortcut on the right. Using the menu once teaches the faster key. - VS Code: the command palette shows each command’s key binding beside it, and the Keyboard Shortcuts editor lets you search and remap any of them. - Gmail: single-key shortcuts like j, k and e are off until you turn them on in Settings. Once they’re on, ? opens the full list. - YouTube: k pauses, j and l jump back and ahead 10 seconds, and ? lists the rest. None of them fire while you type a search or a comment.

entries.title: Customization
entries.summary: Customization lets people shape a product around the few things they use most, such as starring a contact, pinning a chat or adding a button to a toolbar.
entries.tags: pattern layers guide customization lets people shape product around few things use most such starring contact pinning chat adding button toolbar
entries.search_text: Customization Customization lets people shape a product around the few things they use most, such as starring a contact, pinning a chat or adding a button to a toolbar. The full list stays as it was, and their own picks sit on top of it, one step away. It differs from personalization, where the product guesses, like a “Recently used” list that changes by itself. With customization people choose, so it only changes when they change it. Ways to do it There are four common ways, which differ in what people pick: an item to star, an item to pin at the top of a list sorted by date, the buttons a toolbar shows, or the sections of a home screen. - Favorites. Use it when people return to a few items in a long list. Starring adds a copy at the top. The item also stays in its usual place. - Pin to top. Use it in a list sorted by date, so one item doesn’t sink as new ones arrive. Pin a note, then write a new one. The pinned note stays first. - Toolbar. Use it when different people rely on different tools from a large set. Each person keeps the buttons they use and hides the rest. Every tool is still in the menu. - Home sections. Use it for a home screen made of sections that matter more to some people than others. People move the sections they read up, and hide the ones they don’t. Rules Four rules keep customization useful. 1. Fix the defaults first It’s tempting to leave a weak screen as it is, because “people can set it up themselves”, but most people never do: they keep the screen they were given and work around it. Make the default right for most people first, and offer customization on top for the rest. 2. Offer it when it helps A setting nobody finds doesn’t help anybody, and few people go looking in Settings. The best moment to offer customization is when someone keeps doing the same thing: after they share with the same person a few times, offer to make that person a favorite, right there. 3. Add on top, don’t reorder Help articles and support staff say things like “open the third item”. If customizing moves items around in the main list, those directions no longer match what people see. Keep pins in a separate place at the top and leave the full list in its usual order, with “Reset to default” in one obvious place. 4. Keep the pinned list short Pins are added in a second but often removed only from a settings page, so the pinned section keeps growing until it is as long as the list it was meant to shorten. Let people unpin right where the pin appears, and when nothing is pinned, show an empty state that explains how pinning works. In real products - Notion: add a page to Favorites and it shows up at the top of the sidebar. It also stays in its place in the page tree. - Chrome: the extensions menu lists everything installed. Pin the few you use often and they get their own button in the toolbar. - WhatsApp: pin a few chats and they stay at the top, even when newer messages arrive elsewhere. The rest keep sorting by the latest message.

entries.title: Jakob’s law
entries.summary: Jakob’s law says that people spend most of their time in other products, so they expect yours to work the same way.

rules.title: Use the control people already know
Adapt a convention to the task
Teach a break where it happens

entries.tags: pattern laws guide jakob law says people spend most time other products expect yours work same way search box magnifying glass
entries.search_text: Jakob’s law Jakob’s law says that people spend most of their time in other products, so they expect yours to work the same way. A search box has a magnifying glass, a link is underlined, and the cart sits in the top right corner. People use these without thinking and bring those habits to every new product they open. The law isn’t a ban on new ideas, but it tells you what one costs: every break from a convention is something people have to stop and learn. Sometimes that cost is worth paying, but it should be a choice. Rules Three rules help you work with people’s habits. 1. Use the control people already know A new kind of control can look fresh in a design review, but in use people try what works everywhere else, and it doesn’t work here. Some never find out how it works. Use the familiar control, which assistive tech understands too, and change it only when testing shows a clear win for a real task. 2. Adapt a convention to the task A convention that is right in one kind of product can be wrong in another. In a document, Enter starts a new line, but in a table people expect Enter to save the cell and move down. Find out how people do this work in the tools they already use, and test the result with them. 3. Teach a break where it happens Sometimes a product has a good reason to break a convention. If nothing explains the change, people try the usual way, nothing happens, and they don’t know why. Show a short hint at the moment they try the usual way, and keep the familiar path working where you can. In real products Notice what each product kept familiar. - Google Docs: menus, toolbar and shortcuts like Ctrl+B and Ctrl+Z (⌘B and ⌘Z on Mac) work like a desktop word processor. - Blender: selects with the left mouse button by default, like most software, and offers an Industry Compatible keymap for people coming from other 3D tools. - Instagram: stories work like stories in other apps. Tap right for next, tap left to go back, hold to pause.

entries.title: Fitts’s law
entries.summary: Fitts’s law says that the time it takes to hit a target depends on its size and its distance.

rules.title: Make the hit area bigger than the icon
Put the action near what it acts on
Keep risky actions away from common ones

entries.tags: pattern laws guide fitts law says time takes hit target depends size distance big close pointer thumb fast small far away
entries.search_text: Fitts’s law Fitts’s law says that the time it takes to hit a target depends on its size and its distance. A big target close to the pointer or the thumb is fast to hit. A small target far away is slow, and people miss it more often. It applies to every click and tap: buttons, links, menu items, close icons. The screen edges help too, because the pointer stops there and can’t overshoot. People with a tremor, on a touch screen or using zoom feel the difference most. Rules Three rules put Fitts’s law to work. 1. Make the hit area bigger than the icon Small icons look tidy, but a 12-pixel target is hard to hit, especially with a finger or a shaky hand, so people miss, try again, and sometimes hit the thing next to it. The icon can stay small if the clickable area around it is large, at least 24 by 24 pixels. See Icon button . 2. Put the action near what it acts on When the button sits far from where people are working, every use costs a long move across the screen. On a wide screen that adds up, and on a phone it can mean a stretch of the thumb. Put the action next to the field, at the end of the form, or in a menu that opens at the pointer. 3. Keep risky actions away from common ones If Delete sits right next to Reply and both are the same size, a fast move lands on either one, and a small slip deletes something. Make the common action the big, easy target, move the risky one away or into a menu, and let people undo it . In real products Notice how each one makes the target bigger, or puts it where the pointer or thumb already is. - macOS: the menu bar sits on the top edge of the screen. The pointer can’t overshoot it, so a quick flick up always lands on it. - Blender: pie menus open around the pointer. Every option is the same short move away, and you pick by direction, so each target is a whole slice. - YouTube: on phones, double-tap the left or right side of the video to jump back or ahead 10 seconds. Half the screen is the target. - Gmail: on phones, Compose is a large button in the bottom corner, where the thumb already rests, not a small icon at the top.

entries.title: Hick’s law
entries.summary: Hick’s law says that the more choices people see, the longer it takes them to pick one, because each extra option is one more thing to read and compare.

rules.title: Group long lists, or let people search
Make the likely choice stand out
Tuck rare options away, don’t delete them

entries.tags: pattern laws guide hick law says more choices people see longer takes pick one because extra option thing read compare effect
entries.search_text: Hick’s law Hick’s law says that the more choices people see, the longer it takes them to pick one, because each extra option is one more thing to read and compare. The effect is strongest when people don’t know the list yet and have to scan it. It doesn’t mean a product should offer less, but that it should show the likely choices first and keep the rest easy to reach. When people already know what they want, a search box beats any list. A screen reader reads options one at a time, so a long list costs even more there. Rules Three rules put Hick’s law to work. 1. Group long lists, or let people search In a long flat list, people read item after item until they find theirs, because nothing tells them where to look. Put recent choices first, group the rest, or add search that narrows the list as they type. See Combobox . 2. Make the likely choice stand out When every option looks the same, people have to read and weigh all of them, even when one is the usual answer, which slows them down and leads to wrong picks. Make the likely choice stand out: a sensible default, one primary button, the most used item at the top. 3. Tuck rare options away, don’t delete them Cutting options makes a menu shorter, but someone needed each one, and those people now can’t do their task at all. Keep the common options in view, and put the rare ones behind “More” or in an advanced section. In real products Notice how each one cuts a long list down to a few likely choices before people have to pick. - Slack: the quick switcher opens with your recent channels and people, and narrows to a few matches as you type. - Photoshop: the toolbar shows one tool from each group. Hold a tool to see its relatives, so dozens of tools fit in one short column. - Duolingo: the home screen is a path with one lesson marked as next. Opening the app leads to one obvious tap, not a menu of lessons.

entries.title: Tesler’s law
entries.summary: Tesler’s law says every task holds some complexity that can’t be removed, only moved.

rules.title: Solve it once in the product
Test the simple version with real data

entries.tags: pattern laws guide tesler law says every task holds some complexity removed only moved photo app imports pictures still save folder
entries.search_text: Tesler’s law Tesler’s law says every task holds some complexity that can’t be removed, only moved. When a photo app imports pictures, it still has to save them to a folder. Either people type the full folder path, or the app offers the folders they used recently. The design question is who carries that work: the system or the person. Usually the system should carry it, because the team solves the hard part once instead of every person solving it every time. But moved complexity always lands somewhere, such as an error message, the help pages or the next screen, so when you simplify a step, check where the work went. Rules Three rules help you put complexity in the right place. 1. Keep control within reach Some complexity exists because people need the choice. One fixed export size works for sharing a photo but not for a print shop that needs the full size, and if the app hides that choice, people can’t finish the task at all. Keep the simple path as the default, and put the full controls in an advanced layer one click away. 2. Solve it once in the product Some complexity lands on people only because the team didn’t handle it. A phone field that accepts one exact format makes every person reformat their number, often after an error. Accept the formats people type and tidy them up in the product, so the team does the work once. 3. Test the simple version with real data A simple flow often works only for the sample data it was built with. Real photos have odd names, other file types and huge sizes, and when those fail, the complexity comes back as error messages people can’t act on. Before you call a flow simple, try the messy cases : large files, unusual names, hundreds of items. In real products Notice which hard part each product carries for people, and where it still lets them take over. - Uber: sets the pickup point from your location, so the only thing to type is where you’re going. You can still change the pickup if it’s off. - iOS: when a sign-in code arrives by text, it’s offered above the keyboard. The security step stays, but nobody copies digits by hand. - Lightroom: Auto sets exposure, contrast and more in one click, and moves the regular sliders, so you can see what it did and adjust any of it.

entries.title: Inline message
entries.summary: An inline message is a short line of text right next to the thing it’s about.

rules.title: Bring the problem to where people look
Give each field one next step
Wait until people leave the field

entries.tags: component feedback guide inline message short line text right next thing about most often sits under form field says what wrong
entries.search_text: Inline message An inline message is a short line of text right next to the thing it’s about. Most often it sits under a form field and says what’s wrong and how to fix it. It can also give a hint before people type, or point out a value that looks like a mistake. Where a banner is about the whole page or app, an inline message is about one field or one item, and it sits right beside it. Forms Inline messages come in four kinds: a hint, an error, a warning and a success note. A hint is there before people type. The other three respond to what they typed, and only an error stops them from going on. - Hint. Use it to say what a field needs before people type. - Error. Use it when a value can’t be accepted and people must change it to go on. - Warning. Use it when a value is allowed but may be a mistake. - Success. Use it only when people wait to learn whether a value works, like a free username. Rules Four rules keep inline messages useful. 1. Bring the problem to where people look After a failed submit, the message often sits next to a field that has scrolled out of view, so people see nothing change near the button and press again or give up. Add a short summary at the top of the form that lists each problem, links to its field and gets focus when the form is sent. 2. Give each field one next step When every check adds its own red line, the form turns into a wall of errors: people can’t tell what to fix first, and several lines say the same thing. Show only the most useful message for each field. If something is still wrong after they fix it, the next message appears then. 3. Wait until people leave the field An error that appears on the first key press tells people they’re wrong before they’ve finished, when they’re only not done yet. Check the value when they leave the field or send the form, and if a message is already showing, clear it as soon as the value is right. 4. Say what to do instead “Invalid date” says that something is wrong, but not which date or why, so people guess and often change the wrong field. A good message names the field and the rule in plain words, and offers the fix as a button when it’s obvious. In real products - VS Code: a squiggle marks the exact spot, and hovering it shows the message. A count in the status bar opens the full Problems list, so the markers stay small and one list holds them all. - Google: when a new account’s username is taken, the message appears right under the field and says what to do next. What you typed stays, so the fix is one edit. - Stripe Checkout: the card number is checked when you leave the field, and the message under it says what’s wrong, like “incomplete”. You fix it before you press Pay, not after.

entries.title: Toast
entries.summary: A toast is a short message that appears near the edge of the screen after people do something.

rules.title: Don’t put errors in a toast
Don’t make it the only way to act
Offer Undo instead of asking first

entries.tags: undo recovery notification time limit toast
entries.search_text: Toast A toast is a short message that appears near the edge of the screen after people do something. It confirms that the action worked, such as “Email archived”, and often offers Undo. It leaves on its own after a few seconds, and people can keep working while it’s there. Where a banner describes a state that lasts, like being offline, and stays until the state ends, a toast reports one moment and fades. So it can’t carry anything people must see. Forms Toasts come in three common forms: a plain toast only confirms, a toast with Undo lets people reverse what they just did, and a progress toast reports a short task while it runs. All three leave on their own. - Plain. Use it to confirm something that worked, when nothing else needs doing. - With Undo. Use it after an action people may want to reverse, like removing something from a cart. - Progress. Use it for a short task that runs in the background, like sending invitations. Rules Five rules keep toasts useful. 1. Don’t put errors in a toast A toast leaves after a few seconds, whether anyone read it or not, so people who looked away never learn that the photo didn’t upload. Put the error next to the file it’s about, or in a banner that lasts until the problem is solved, where it has room to explain the limit and offer a way forward. 2. Don’t make it the only way to act When a toast holds the only Restart button, the button leaves with it, and people who miss it have no way left to finish the update. Put requests like this in a banner or a notification that stays until people choose, so “Later” is a real choice and not a missed chance. 3. Combine messages into one When several things finish at once, each can fire its own toast, and they pile up, cover the page and repeat the same news. Use one toast that updates as things finish, such as “3 photos uploaded”, so people get one clear result and the page stays usable. 4. Leave a trace that lasts A toast only helps if people are looking when it appears. If the export finishes while they’re in another part of the app, they come back to no sign that it’s done. Also mark the result somewhere that waits, such as a badge on Files or an entry in a notifications list, where people find it whenever they look. 5. Offer Undo instead of asking first A confirm dialog on every delete gets clicked through without reading, as the Undo pattern explains. For actions that can be reversed, act right away and show a toast with Undo: it takes fewer clicks, and a mistake is one press to fix. In real products - Gmail: after you send, a toast offers Undo for a few seconds, and the email only goes out once that time is up. A slip costs one click instead of a follow-up email. - macOS: after a screenshot, a thumbnail slides into the corner. Click it to mark up or share, or ignore it and it saves on its own a few seconds later. - Spotify: adding a song to a playlist from a menu shows a short toast with the playlist’s name. The menu has already closed, so the toast is how you know it worked.

entries.title: Banner
entries.summary: A banner is a strip across the top of an app or page.

rules.title: Use it only for what’s happening now

entries.tags: persistent notice restore draft recovery banner
entries.search_text: Banner A banner is a strip across the top of an app or page. It describes a state that lasts and changes what people can do: they’re offline, the file is read-only, the trial is ending. It stays while the state lasts and leaves when it ends, where a toast reports one moment and fades. Forms Banners come in three tones, set by how serious the state is: info, warning and error. The tone also decides whether people can close it. A fourth, smaller form covers only one part of a page. - Info. Use it for a state that changes what people can do, when nothing is wrong. - Warning. Use it when something will become a problem soon unless people act. - Error. Use it when something is wrong right now and affects the whole app. - In a section. Use it when the state only affects one part of the page. It sits at the top of that part. Rules Four rules keep banners useful. 1. Use it only for what’s happening now People learn fast what the top of the screen means. If a banner there always means “something is going on right now”, they read it. If it also carries news and offers, they learn to skip it, and then they skip the offline notice too. Put news somewhere people can open when they want, such as a “What’s new” entry. 2. Let information be closed Some banners are only information, such as a tip or a note that this is a shared copy, and once read they’ve done their job. If they can’t be closed, they keep taking space and turn into a stripe people look past. Let people close them, and remember that they did. 3. Show one at a time Several states can be true at once: offline, read-only, a tip. Each banner is short, but stacked they push the page down, and people rarely read past the first. Show the most serious one and put the rest in a notifications list. 4. Don’t move the page Like content that loads late , a banner that appears or leaves pushes everything below it, and a click aimed at a button lands on the wrong thing. Lay the banner over the top edge, or keep its space reserved, so nothing under the pointer moves. In real products - Gmail: while the vacation auto-reply is on, a bar above the inbox says so and offers End now. It’s a mode people forget they switched on. - Notion: a page opened from the trash gets a red bar across the top, with buttons to restore it or delete it for good. - GitHub: an archived repository shows a notice at the top saying it’s read-only, which explains why you can’t push or open issues.

entries.title: Badge
entries.summary: A badge is a small mark on another item: a dot or a number on an icon, a tab or a button.
entries.tags: component feedback guide badge small mark another item dot number icon tab button tells people glance something there new needs like
entries.search_text: Badge A badge is a small mark on another item: a dot or a number on an icon, a tab or a button. It tells people at a glance that something there is new or needs them, like 3 unread messages or 1 update. It goes away once they’ve looked. Where a toast interrupts to say something just happened, then fades, a badge doesn’t interrupt. It waits on the item until people are ready to look. Forms Badges come in four forms, set by what people need to know. A dot says only that something is new. A count says how many. A label names the kind of thing, like “New” or “Beta”. A status mark shows a live state, like who is online. - Dot. Use it when “something new is here” is all people need to know. - Count. Use it when the number changes what people do, like unread messages. - Label. Use a short word, like “New” or “Beta”, when the kind of thing matters more than how many. - Status. Use it for a live state, like who is online. Rules Four rules keep badges useful. 1. Clear it once people look A badge that still says 3 after someone has seen all 3 is out of date, so people stop trusting it and miss the next one that matters. Remove it as soon as they view what it points to, so a badge always means there’s something they haven’t seen yet. 2. Badge only what needs attention When every row has a bright number, none of them stands out, and people open folders one by one to find what changed. Keep badges for what’s new or needs action, and show totals as plain text next to the item, where they don’t compete. 3.
