Cap the number A big number makes the badge wider than the icon it sits on and crowds the icons next to it. Past a point, nobody reads the exact number anyway: it just means “a lot”. Show “99+” instead, and put the exact count at the top of the list it opens. 4. Say what the number means A red 3 on a gear could mean errors, warnings or updates, and red also reads as danger, so people either worry or ignore it. Put what it counts in the button’s label and a tooltip, like “3 updates available”, so people can decide whether to look now without opening anything. In real products Notice that each badge stays small, and only shows a number when the number matters. - Slack: a channel with new messages turns bold, and only mentions and direct messages get a number. Bold says something’s new, and a number says someone wants you. - GitHub: the notifications icon shows a small dot when something’s unread, not a count. The exact number waits in the inbox it opens. - YouTube: the count on the bell stops at 9+. Past that, the exact number wouldn’t change what you do, so the badge stays small. - iOS: apps can put a count on their home screen icon, like unread mail. People can turn badges off for each app in notification settings, so a noisy app loses its badge.

entries.title: Spinner
entries.summary: A spinner is a small turning circle that says “working on it”.

rules.title: Use a progress bar for long waits
Keep the rest of the app working

entries.tags: component progress guide spinner small turning circle says working short waits about ten seconds sending message loading search results saving change
entries.search_text: Spinner A spinner is a small turning circle that says “working on it”. It’s for short waits, up to about ten seconds: sending a message, loading search results, saving a change. It sits on the thing that’s busy. Where a spinner says only that work is happening, a progress bar also shows how much is done, so it’s the better choice for longer waits. Forms Spinners come in four forms, set by how much is waiting: in a button, inline next to a field, in one section, and over the full page. Use the smallest one that covers what’s loading, so the rest of the page stays usable. - Button. Use it when one action is waiting, like sending an email. - Inline. Use it next to a field or a line that’s updating, like a search box. - Section. Use it when one part of the page is reloading. - Full page. Use it only when there’s nothing to show yet, like while an app first opens. Rules Four rules keep spinners useful. 1. Wait before showing it When results come back in a fraction of a second, the spinner only blinks, which looks like a glitch and makes the app feel slower than it is. Hold it back for about 400 ms, so fast results just appear and a spinner means there’s a real wait. 2. Use a progress bar for long waits A spinner can’t say how much is done or how long is left, so after a while people wonder if it’s stuck, and they cancel or reload. Once a wait can run past about ten seconds, show a progress bar and what’s happening, so people can choose to wait or go do something else. 3. Keep the rest of the app working A spinner over the whole screen locks everything, even the parts that aren’t loading, so someone writing a reply has to stop and wait for a folder list. Put the spinner on the part that’s loading, so it shows what’s busy and everything else stays usable. 4. Hold the content’s space A spinner is usually smaller than the content that replaces it, so the page jumps when the content arrives, like any content that loads late . Show a skeleton in the shape of the coming content instead, so nothing below it moves. In real products - Chrome: a loading tab swaps its icon for a small spinner. Only that tab is busy, so you keep reading in the others. - Stripe Checkout: after you press Pay, the button itself shows a spinner, then a check mark. The feedback sits where you clicked, so you know the press landed. - iOS Mail: pull the inbox down and a spinner shows above it while it checks for new mail. The messages already there stay put and readable.

entries.title: Progress bar
entries.summary: A progress bar is a line that fills as long work gets done: an upload, a download, an export, a backup.

rules.title: Show stages when you can’t measure

entries.tags: component progress guide bar line fills long work gets done upload download export backup shows how far along often what
entries.search_text: Progress bar A progress bar is a line that fills as long work gets done: an upload, a download, an export, a backup. It shows how far along the work is, and often what it’s doing and how much is left. Unlike a spinner , it lets people decide whether to wait or do something else. Forms Progress bars come in four forms. A bar of known length fills as work gets done, and a bar of unknown length moves without filling. A small ring sits on one item in a list, and a background strip tracks long work while people do something else. - Known. Use it when the work can be counted, like songs in an album. - Unknown. Use it when the total isn’t known yet, like a search across many airlines. - Ring. Use it when several things download at once, like podcast episodes. - Background. Use it for long work people don’t need to watch, like a photo backup. Rules Four rules keep progress bars useful. 1. Show stages when you can’t measure Some work has nothing to count, so the bar sits at 0% and then jumps to done, and until then people can’t tell if it’s working or stuck. Use a moving bar to show it’s alive, with a label that names each stage as it starts, so people see it’s getting somewhere. 2. Count real work A bar that isn’t tied to real work often races ahead, then sits at 99% for most of the wait, so people think it froze and stop believing it. Move it by real units, like photos exported, and if one part can’t be counted, say so with a label like “Finishing up…”. 3. Let people keep working When an export locks the whole app, people can only sit and watch the bar, and if they change their mind, there’s no way to stop it. Run long work in a small strip, as background work , let people carry on, always offer Cancel, and tell them when it’s done. 4. Put it on the item A new file can look ready in the list while it’s still uploading, and a tiny bar in a corner goes unseen. Show progress on the item itself, where people are already looking, and add a summary, like an uploads count in the top bar. In real products - Blender: while rendering, the render window counts samples and shows the time left. Samples are real units of work, so the count is honest, and Esc stops the render. - Finder: a long copy shows how much is done, about how long is left, and a button to stop it. You can keep using Finder while it runs. - YouTube: while a video uploads, the dialog shows the percent and time left at the bottom, and you fill in the title and description meanwhile. - WhatsApp: a photo or video you send shows a ring around a cancel button, right on the message, so stopping takes one tap.

entries.title: Skeleton
entries.summary: A skeleton is a gray outline of content that is still loading, with the same boxes and lines as the content that will replace it: a box for each photo, a bar for each line of text.

rules.title: Skip it when loading is quick

entries.tags: component progress guide skeleton gray outline content still loading same boxes lines replace box photo bar line text arrives drops place
entries.search_text: Skeleton A skeleton is a gray outline of content that is still loading, with the same boxes and lines as the content that will replace it: a box for each photo, a bar for each line of text. When the content arrives, it drops into place and nothing moves. Unlike a spinner , which only says “wait”, it shows what is coming and where it will go. Forms Skeletons take the shape of what they stand in for. The common forms are a grid of tiles, a list of rows and a block of text. A fourth, smaller form holds the place of one value on a page that has already loaded. - Grid. Use it for photos, products or videos, with one box for each tile. - List. Use it for rows like messages, songs or orders. - Text. Use it for an article, a description or a review. - One value. Use it when the page is ready but one number or name is still on its way. Rules Four rules keep skeletons useful. 1. Match the real layout A skeleton is there to hold the space of content that loads late , so if its shape is wrong, the page still jumps when the content arrives. Give each placeholder the size and place of what will fill it, and if you can’t know the shape in advance, use a spinner instead. 2. Skip it when loading is quick When content arrives almost at once, a skeleton shows for only a split second, too short to read as loading, so people see a flicker and the app feels jumpy instead of fast. As with a spinner , wait about 400 ms before showing it, so fast content just appears. 3. Replace it if loading fails A skeleton tells people that content is on its way, so if loading fails and it stays, they keep waiting for something that will never come, then reload or give up without knowing why. As soon as loading fails, replace it with what went wrong and a way to try again. 4. Keep the motion calm Fast shimmer on every part of the screen is tiring to look at, and it covers parts that are already known, like the account name, so nothing can be read until everything arrives. Show what you have at once and load the most important part next. Give only the parts still loading a slow, soft pulse, and stop it for people who turn off motion. In real products - YouTube: the home page first shows gray boxes where thumbnails go and bars where titles go, so the videos drop in without moving anything. - Facebook: the feed shows gray posts before the real ones arrive, with a circle for the profile photo and bars for the name and text. - Google Photos: when you scroll fast, each photo’s spot is held by a plain tile of the right size and shape. Photos fill in where they belong, so the grid doesn’t reflow.

entries.title: Tooltip
entries.summary: A tooltip is a small label that appears when people point at something or move to it with the keyboard.

rules.title: Don’t hide what people must know
Don’t put links or buttons in it

entries.tags: hover focus supplementary help noninteractive tooltip
entries.search_text: Tooltip A tooltip is a small label that appears when people point at something or move to it with the keyboard. It answers a quick question, like what an icon button does. It goes away as soon as the pointer or focus moves on. Where a tooltip only adds a name or a short note, with nothing in it to click, a popover opens on a click, stays open and can hold buttons and links. Forms Most tooltips name an icon button, and some also show its keyboard shortcut. Others explain a word in one short sentence, or show the full text of a name that is cut off. All of them hold a few words of plain text and nothing else. - Name. Use it for icon buttons that have no text. - With shortcut. Use it when the button also has a keyboard shortcut. - Explanation. Use it to explain a word some people won’t know, in one short sentence. - Full text. Use it when a long name is cut off to fit. Rules Four rules keep tooltips useful. 1. Don’t rely on hover Phones and tablets have no hover, so a tooltip there never appears, and people decide without the information, such as what an extra fee pays for. Put the text on the page where people can see it. If there isn’t room, add an info button that opens a popover when tapped, which works the same with a finger, a mouse or a keyboard. 2. Don’t hide what people must know Most people never point at a small info icon, so if a warning hides there, they find out what the setting does only when their old messages are already gone. Put anything people need for a decision on the page, as helper text right under the choice. 3. Don’t put links or buttons in it A tooltip closes as soon as the pointer moves off the icon, and the keyboard can’t move into it, so a link inside can be seen but not used. When the note needs a link, use a popover instead. It stays open until people close it, so they can reach the link with a mouse, a finger or the Tab key. 4. Don’t repeat the label A tooltip that repeats a visible label tells people nothing new, but it still pops up over nearby content, such as the price next to the button, and screen readers read the same words twice. If the label already says it, leave the tooltip out. In real products Notice that tooltips only add a name or a detail, and that on touch screens the name has to be visible instead. - Figma: hovering a tool shows its name and its key, like Rectangle R. The toolbar stays compact, and the key teaches a faster way for next time. - GitHub: relative times like “3 days ago” show the exact date and time on hover. Most people only need the rough age, and the precise one is there for those who wonder. - Spotify: the phone app has no hover, so its tab bar puts a word under each icon instead of hiding the names in tooltips.

entries.title: Popover
entries.summary: A popover is a small box that opens next to the button people pressed.

rules.title: Keep it to a few controls
Don’t lose work when it closes

entries.tags: component overlays guide popover small box opens next button people pressed holds few related controls details such view options guest count
entries.search_text: Popover A popover is a small box that opens next to the button people pressed. It holds a few related controls or details, such as view options, a guest count or a contact card. It stays open until people click outside it, press Esc or press the button again. Unlike a tooltip , it opens on a click and can hold buttons, fields and links. Unlike a dialog, it doesn’t block the page behind it. Forms The common forms are options, a picker, a details card and a tip. Options and pickers change something on the page, a details card shows more about a person or a link, and a tip points at something new once. - Options. Use it for a few settings that change the view, like size or filters. - Picker. Use it to set one value, like dates or the number of guests. - Details. Use it to show more about a person, a place or a link without leaving the page. - Tip. Use it once, to point out something new right where it is. Rules Four rules keep popovers useful. 1. Keep it to a few controls A popover has room for only a few controls, so with seven fields in it, people scroll inside the box to find a field, then scroll again to find Save. When a task needs more fields than that, use a side panel or a page, where the fields can be grouped and Save stays in view. 2. Don’t lose work when it closes People close popovers by clicking outside them, often without thinking, so if that also throws away what they typed, their work is gone without a word. Save each change the moment it’s made, so nothing is lost however the popover closes. If people need to review changes before they count, use a dialog with Save and Cancel instead. 3. Don’t open popovers from popovers Each popover that opens another adds a layer on top, so people lose track of where they are, and one choice can close every layer at once. The next change then starts again from the first button. Put related choices side by side in one popover or panel, and apply them as people click. 4. Keep the result in view When a popover covers what it changes, people adjust blind: they close it to see the result, then open it again to adjust some more. Place it beside the thing being changed, or, if there isn’t room, use a side panel and leave the thing itself in full view. In real products - Figma: clicking a fill swatch opens a small color picker beside the properties panel. The selected shape updates as you drag, and clicking away just closes the picker. - Google Docs: putting the cursor in a link shows a small card under it, with the address and buttons to copy, edit or remove the link. The page around it doesn’t change. - Airbnb: the guests field opens a small panel of plus and minus steppers. Each change shows up in the search bar right away, so there’s nothing to confirm before closing it. - YouTube: in the player’s settings panel, picking playback speed swaps the list for the speeds, with a back arrow, instead of stacking a second layer. The new speed applies at once.

entries.title: Menu
entries.summary: A menu is a short list of commands that opens from a button.

rules.title: Keep the main action in view
Put options to compare on the page

entries.tags: component overlays guide menu short list commands opens button holds actions people need now like rename duplicate delete don crowd screen
entries.search_text: Menu A menu is a short list of commands that opens from a button. It holds actions people need now and then, like Rename, Duplicate or Delete, so they don’t crowd the screen. Picking an item runs it and closes the menu. Where a select fills in a value, like a size or a country, and the field keeps showing that value, a menu runs a command, and then it’s gone. Forms Most menus open from a button: a “More” button with three dots, or a button with a name like Sort, which may let people pick one setting. A context menu opens when people right-click or long-press an item, and a menu bar along the top of a window holds all of an app’s commands. - More button. Use it for the actions people need now and then on one item. - Pick one. Use it for one setting with a few short choices, like sort order. - Context menu. Use it for shortcuts on items people can right-click or long-press. - Menu bar. Use it in a large app with many commands, like a document editor. Rules Four rules keep menus useful. 1. Keep it short In a menu of more than about a dozen items, people have to read every item to find the one they want, and if it’s out of view at the bottom, they scroll past it or give up. Split the list into small groups with the common actions on top. Move rare actions out, or let people type a few letters to find them. Very large sets need a command palette . 2. Keep the main action in view Every trip into a menu costs a click and a search. That is fine for rare actions, but for the action people take most, like Reply in email, they pay it every time. Give the one or two most used actions their own buttons, and keep the menu for the rest. 3. Put options to compare on the page A menu shows names only, and only while it’s open, so to compare prices or dates, people open it again and again and keep the numbers in their head. When options differ in price, time or size, lay them out on the page with those details, for example as radio buttons or cards, so people can compare them in one look. 4. Don’t nest submenus Each submenu opens on hover and switches when the pointer slips onto a neighbor, so people retrace their steps or pick the wrong item without noticing. Keep a menu to one level, two at most. When a choice needs more steps, open a dialog that shows every option at once and has room to explain them. In real products Notice that the most common actions stay in view, the rest wait in a short grouped list, and very large sets get a search. - Slack: pointing at a message shows a few buttons for what people do most, like reacting or replying in a thread. Everything else waits in a More menu. - VS Code: the editor’s right-click menu groups commands with dividers and shows each shortcut on the right, so the menu also teaches the faster way. The full set of commands lives in the Command Palette. - macOS: the Help menu has a search field that finds commands across every menu. Pointing at a result opens its menu and points to the command, so people learn where it lives. - iOS Photos: pressing and holding a photo lifts a preview with a menu of actions under it. Delete comes last, in red.

entries.title: Dialog
entries.summary: A dialog is a box that opens over the page and asks the person something.

rules.title: Give long tasks a page or a panel
Name the action on each button

entries.tags: modal confirm unsaved close cancel save focus dialog
entries.search_text: Dialog A dialog is a box that opens over the page and asks the person something. The page behind it is dimmed and can’t be used until they answer. Use it for a decision they have to make before they go on, such as deleting something for good. A popover also opens over the page, but a click anywhere else closes it. Forms Dialogs come in four common forms, set by what they ask for: a confirmation, a choice about unsaved work, a short form and a notice. They differ in how many buttons they have and which button gets focus first. - Confirm. Use it before an action that can’t be undone. - Unsaved work. Use it when people close something with changes they haven’t saved. - Short form. Use it to ask for one or two things that belong to one action, like a new name. - Notice. Use it only when people can’t go on without knowing, like after they’ve been signed out. Rules Five rules keep dialogs useful. 1. Don’t use it for news People open an app to do something, like read their mail, so a box with news or a tip stands in their way, and most close it without reading. Put the news where people can open it when they want, such as a “What’s new” entry or a short note they can close. They can read it now, later or never, and the mail works right away. 2. Offer Undo instead of asking If every action asks “Are you sure?”, people learn to press OK without reading, so the one time it matters, the dialog doesn’t protect them. Let actions that can be undone happen at once, and offer Undo. Keep the dialog for the rare action that can’t be undone, and say what will be lost. 3. Give long tasks a page or a panel A dialog is a small box that covers the page, so a long form inside it hides what people need to look at, like the chart behind it. To check a number they have to close the dialog, and they lose what they typed. A page or a side panel gives them room to scroll and look things up, and keeps what they entered. 4. Name the action on each button “OK” and “Cancel” don’t say what will happen. When someone leaves a photo they were cropping, “Cancel” could mean cancel the crop or cancel leaving, so people have to read the whole question, and many guess wrong. When each button names its action, the buttons alone answer the question, and the one that throws work away stands out. 5. Don’t open it on load A dialog that opens with the app stands between people and what they came for. They haven’t done anything yet, so they close it unread. Ask at the moment it matters, like after they press Download, when the question is about what they just asked for and they read it. In real products Notice which actions get a dialog at all, and that the buttons say what will happen. - macOS: when an app asks before closing a document with unsaved changes, the buttons say Save, Don’t Save and Cancel, so people can answer without reading the message. - GitHub: deleting a repository can’t be undone, so the dialog spells out what will be lost and asks people to type the repository’s name before the delete button works. - WhatsApp: deleting a message you sent asks who it should disappear for. Each button names its outcome, so the choice is clear without any extra text. - Gmail: archiving or deleting an email doesn’t ask first. It happens at once, and a toast in the corner offers Undo for a few seconds.

entries.title: Side panel
entries.summary: A side panel opens along the left or right edge of the screen.

rules.title: Give the main task the full width
Use the whole screen on phones
Don’t dim a page people still use

entries.tags: component dialogs guide side panel opens along left right edge screen holds second task next main view such comments doc details
entries.search_text: Side panel A side panel opens along the left or right edge of the screen. It holds a second task next to the main view, such as comments on a doc, the details of a photo or search filters. In most forms, people can keep using the main view while it’s open. Unlike a dialog , it shares the screen, so people can look at both and move between them. Forms Side panels come in three forms, which differ in what happens to the page: a docked panel makes it narrower, an overlay panel covers its edge, and a modal panel dims it and blocks it. - Docked. Use it for a panel people keep open for a while, like the play queue in a music app. - Overlay. Use it for details people open and close often, like a place on a map. - Modal. Use it when people should finish one task before going back, like checking their cart. Rules Four rules keep side panels useful. 1. Give the main task the full width A panel is narrow, which is fine for a side task. When the task in it becomes the main job, like writing a long reply, lines wrap every few words and the draft is hard to read back. Give that task a full page or a mode of its own, with a clear way back. 2. Use the whole screen on phones On a phone, a side panel takes half the screen, so the page next to it shrinks to a sliver and neither half is big enough to use. Let the panel cover the whole screen while people choose, with a clear Close or Back. When they’re done, the page comes back at full size. 3. Keep one panel per side Each panel takes another slice of the screen, so with three open, the document people are editing becomes a thin strip. Allow one panel on each side, and use tabs inside it for the rest. Switching tabs changes what’s in the panel, and the document keeps its room. 4. Don’t dim a page people still use A dimmed page tells people it’s off-limits, so they don’t think to click the photos behind the panel, and if they do, the click only closes it. If the page is meant to stay usable, keep it bright and clickable, so picking another photo updates the panel in place. In real products Notice that the main view stays visible and usable while the panel is open, and what changes when space runs out. - Slack: opening a thread puts it in a panel on the right. The channel stays readable beside it, and people can reply in either place without losing their spot. - Figma: the panel on the right always shows the selected layer’s properties. Select another layer and it updates in place, while the canvas stays fully usable. - VS Code: the icons on the far left swap which view fills the one side bar, such as files or search, instead of opening a new panel for each. - Google Maps: on a computer, a place’s details open in a panel beside the map, which you can still pan. On a phone, the same details come up as a sheet you drag up from the bottom.

entries.title: Switch
entries.summary: A switch turns one setting on or off.

rules.title: Don’t use it in a form with Save
Name the setting and show its state
Use it only for on and off

entries.tags: on off setting immediate commit checkbox switch
entries.search_text: Switch A switch turns one setting on or off. The change takes effect the moment it’s flipped, with nothing to save, so people expect to see the result at once. That is what separates it from a checkbox, which marks a choice in a form and does nothing until people press Save or Submit. Forms Switches come in four common forms. Most sit in a settings list, one per row, and some add a line that explains the setting. One switch can also turn a whole group of settings on or off, and in a toolbar a switch changes how the page is shown. - In a list. Use it for a list of settings, one per row. - With a description. Use it when the name alone doesn’t say what will change. - For a group. Use it to turn a whole group of settings on or off at once. - In a toolbar. Use it for a view option people change often, like showing only unread mail. Rules Four rules keep switches useful. 1. Don’t use it in a form with Save A switch slides to On at once, so the setting looks done. In a form that still needs Save, people leave without pressing it, and the change is lost. Use a checkbox there, because it reads as a choice that waits for Save. 2. Name the setting and show its state A label like “Turn off emails” reads as a command, and with the switch off it becomes a double negative. A vague label like “Notifications” doesn’t say which kind. Either way, people have to puzzle out what’s on, and many get it wrong. Name one setting per row, and write “On” or “Off” next to the switch, so the answer doesn’t depend on color. 3. Show what really happened Some changes take time or can fail, like turning on backup while the phone is offline. If the switch says On at once, people trust it and find out when a photo is lost. Show a small busy state while the change runs, and if it fails, flip the switch back and say why. 4. Use it only for on and off A switch has two positions. When a setting has three choices, “Off” could mean either of the others, and one of them can’t be reached at all, which people only find out by flipping it. Use a segmented control or a radio group , so every choice is in view with its name. In real products - iOS Settings: Airplane Mode is a switch right in the list, while rows that open their own page, like Bluetooth, show their state in words. - YouTube: the autoplay switch sits in the player’s controls. It decides whether the next video starts on its own, and its tooltip says which way it’s set. - Gmail: the full settings page has a Save Changes button at the bottom, so it uses radio buttons and checkboxes instead of switches.

entries.title: Checkbox
entries.summary: A checkbox marks a yes or no choice.

rules.title: Use radio buttons for one choice
Use a switch when it applies now
Add search and Select all to long lists

entries.tags: selection independent boolean commit form checkbox
entries.search_text: Checkbox A checkbox marks a yes or no choice. In a group, people can check any number of boxes, from none to all, and nothing happens until they press a button such as Save or Place order. That separates it from a switch , which acts the moment it’s flipped, and from radio buttons, which allow only one choice in a group. Forms Checkboxes come in four common forms: a single box, a group, a card and a box on each row of a list. They differ in how many choices there are and which button acts on them. - Single. Use it for one yes or no question, like getting emails about an order. - Group. Use it when people can pick any number of options from a short list. - Card. Use it for extras that need a price or a short detail, like add-ons for a flight. - In a list. Use it to pick items for one action, like moving or deleting files. Rules Four rules keep checkboxes useful. 1. Use radio buttons for one choice Square boxes say “pick any”, so when only one option is allowed, checking a second one leaves the first checked too, and people learn the rule only when the next step shows an error. Radio buttons say “pick one”, and choosing one clears the other by itself. 2. Use a switch when it applies now Checkboxes usually wait for a Save or Done button, so when a change happens at once with no button, people aren’t sure it worked. Use a switch there, with “On” next to it to confirm the change. 3. Make checked mean yes With a label like “Don’t send me updates”, people have to leave the box empty to say yes, so people who skim see “send me updates”, check it, and get the opposite. Write the label as the thing they can choose, like “Send me updates”, so checking the box gives them what they want. 4. Add search and Select all to long lists In a long list, people have to scroll and read every name to find the ones they want, which is slow and makes it easy to miss one. A search box cuts the list down, and Select all checks what’s left in one click. When only some are checked, Select all shows a dash. In real products - Gmail: checking emails only selects them, for an action like Archive or Delete. The box at the top shows a dash when just some are checked. - Lightroom Classic: the export dialog lists independent options, like resizing, sharpening and adding a watermark, as checkboxes that apply when you press Export. - Google Photos: each photo has a check circle, and the one beside a date selects every photo from that day. The top bar counts what’s picked.

entries.title: Radio group
entries.summary: A radio group is a short list of options where people pick exactly one.

rules.title: Keep it to a few options
Make long options easy to compare
Don’t use it to switch views

entries.tags: mutually exclusive choices default deliberate answer radio
entries.search_text: Radio group A radio group is a short list of options where people pick exactly one. Every option is visible, so people can compare them before they choose, and picking one clears the one picked before. Its round buttons say “pick one”, where checkboxes allow any number. Forms Most radio groups are a stacked list. Two or three short options can sit side by side on one line. When each option needs a price or a detail, the options become cards. Picking one option can also open a follow-up field, such as “Tell us more”. - List. Use it for three to six options. One under the other, they’re the easiest to read, and the labels can be as long as they need. - Inline. Use it for two or three short options that fit on one line. Keep each label to a word or two, or the row wraps and gets hard to read. - Cards. Use it when each option needs a price or a short detail to choose well. The whole card responds to a click, not just the small circle. - With a follow-up. Use it when one answer needs more detail. The extra field appears right under that option, and only once it’s picked. Rules Four rules keep radio groups useful. 1. Keep it to a few options Past about six options, the group becomes a long column: people read down it to find their country, and the Continue button ends up far below. A field that filters as people type, or a select , keeps the form short, and a few typed letters bring up the right answer. 2. Preselect the safe choice With nothing picked, people can’t tell if they have to answer. If they skip it, the app has to choose for them, and it may pick the least safe option, like sharing the file with anyone who has the link. Pick the safest common option up front, so skipping still gives a safe result, and if no option is safe, leave it empty and ask for an answer. 3. Make long options easy to compare When each option is a long sentence, the price, the billing and the rules run together, and people have to read every word to see how two plans differ. Turn each option into a card, with the name and the one fact people compare first, and the details on a short line below. 4. Don’t use it to switch views Radio buttons look like a form setting, so people expect to press Save before anything changes, and a calendar that jumps to Month the moment they click doesn’t match that. Stacked in a column, the buttons also push the calendar down. For a view that changes at once, use a segmented control in the toolbar, like other calendar apps. In real products - Google Calendar: changing a repeating event asks how far the change should reach. This event, the safest choice, is preselected, so a quick OK can’t rewrite the whole series. - Duolingo: the daily goal options are listed together, each with its minutes per day, so people can compare the effort. - Uber: ride options are large rows with a car picture, seats, arrival time and price, and picking one deselects the others.

entries.title: Segmented control
entries.summary: A segmented control is a row of two to five buttons joined into one.

rules.title: Keep it to a few short labels
Use it only for changes that apply at once
Make the selected segment stand out

entries.tags: component inputs guide segmented control row two five buttons joined one exactly segment picking another changes view mode right away save
entries.search_text: Segmented control A segmented control is a row of two to five buttons joined into one. Exactly one segment is on, and picking another changes the view or mode right away, with no Save button. That is what separates it from tabs , which move between different content, like Overview and Reviews. A segmented control shows the same content in another way, like a day, a week or a month of the same calendar. Forms Most segmented controls use short text labels, and well-known views can use icons instead. On a phone, the control often spans the full width under the page title. With exactly two options, it works like a switch that names both sides. - Text. Use it for two to five views of the same thing, like Years, Months and All in a photo library. Keep each label to one short word so the row fits on one line. - Icons. Use it when the icons are well known, like list and grid. Give each segment a name that shows on hover and is read out by screen readers. - Full width. Use it on a phone, where a row of small segments is hard to tap. The segments share the width equally, so each one is a big target. - Two options. Use it for a pair of choices, like monthly and yearly billing. People can read both, so they know what they’ll get before they switch. Rules Three rules keep segmented controls useful. 1. Keep it to a few short labels Long labels or more than five options don’t fit on one line, so the control wraps into a block of buttons that is hard to scan and no longer looks like one switch. Use tabs for views like these, because they stay on one line and scroll sideways. For a value rather than a view, use a select . 2. Use it only for changes that apply at once People expect a segmented control to take effect the moment they click it, so if the choice waits for a Save button, they leave and the change is lost. When a choice needs saving, use a radio group , which reads as part of a form. 3. Make the selected segment stand out The selected segment is the only thing that tells people what they’re looking at. With a faint tint, they can’t tell if the chart shows a day, a week or a month, and on a dim screen or in bright light the tint disappears. Give the selected segment a solid fill and bold text, so it reads at a glance. In real products - macOS Calendar: four short segments switch the same events between day, week, month and year. - Blender: four small buttons in the viewport header switch how the same scene is drawn, from wireframe to fully rendered. They change only the view, never the model. - Google Maps: the travel modes at the top of directions switch the same trip between driving, transit, walking and cycling. Each shows its time, so people can compare before they pick. - Google Calendar: with six views to choose from, the view switch is a dropdown in the header instead of a long row of segments.

entries.title: Select & combobox
entries.summary: A select shows the current choice in a closed field, and people open it to see the list and pick one option.

rules.title: Let people pick several when they need to

entries.tags: component inputs guide select combobox shows current choice closed field people open see list pick one option adds text type narrow
entries.search_text: Select & combobox A select shows the current choice in a closed field, and people open it to see the list and pick one option. A combobox adds a text field, so people can type to narrow a long list down. Where a radio group shows every option all the time, a select hides them until it’s opened, which saves space but costs a click and makes options hard to compare. Forms There are four common forms. A plain select opens a short list. A combobox adds typing to filter a long list. A multi-select lets people pick several. An autocomplete suggests answers but also accepts text that isn’t in the list. - Select. Use it for about six to fifteen known options, like a language. There’s no search box, so the list has to be short enough to scan. - Combobox. Use it for a long list where people know the name they want, like an airport. Only an item from the list can be picked, so the answer is always valid. - Multi-select. Use it when people pick several, like labels on an email. Each pick shows as a chip with its own remove button. - Autocomplete. Use it when the list helps but can’t cover every answer, like a street address. People can pick a suggestion or keep their own text. Rules Four rules keep selects and comboboxes useful. 1. Show short lists in full With only a few options, a dropdown hides them for no reason, and every change takes two clicks. Show them as a segmented control or a radio group , so they’re all in view and a change takes one click. 2. Make long lists searchable In a long list, people scroll through the whole alphabet to find one name, which is slow and makes it easy to scroll past the one they want. Let people type a few letters to filter. Put the items they use most at the top and group the rest, so common picks are one click away. 3. Show previews when looks matter Some options differ in how they look, like themes or photo filters. A name like Atlas or Juno says nothing about that, so people open the list again and again to try each one. Use a gallery or a panel that shows a small preview of each option, so people can compare them side by side and pick once. 4. Let people pick several when they need to A single-choice list replaces the old pick without saying so: someone adds a second person, the first one drops off, and they find out only when that person never gets the email. When people may pick several, use checkboxes, or a multi-select that keeps every pick in view. In real products Notice how each product fits the control to the choice: a filter for long lists, previews when looks matter, chips for several picks, and an open list when people compare. - Linear: fields like status and assignee open a short list with a filter on top. Type a few letters and press Enter, so a change never needs the mouse. - Google Docs: the font menu writes each font name in its own typeface and keeps recently used fonts at the top. - Gmail: each recipient in the To field becomes a chip with its own remove button, and typing suggests contacts. - Uber: ride types are an open list, not a dropdown, so every price and arrival time stays in view.

entries.title: Slider + number
entries.summary: A slider sets a value by dragging a handle along a track.

rules.title: Let people type the exact value
Make the handle easy to grab

entries.tags: component inputs guide slider number sets value dragging handle along track shows whole range people see where sits between lowest highest
entries.search_text: Slider + number A slider sets a value by dragging a handle along a track. The track shows the whole range, so people see where the value sits between the lowest and the highest. Dragging is quick, but it’s hard to land on one exact number. A number field is the opposite: exact, but it doesn’t show the range, and people can’t try values by feel. Many settings show both, side by side. Forms Sliders differ in what they let people set. A plain slider moves smoothly. Adding a number field makes it exact. A range slider has two handles for a minimum and a maximum. A stepped slider snaps to a few fixed values. - Plain. Use it when people judge the result by eye or by ear, like brightness or volume. Show the effect live while they drag, because the number itself matters less. - With a number. Use it when people sometimes need an exact value, like a quality setting. Typing a number moves the slider, and dragging updates the number. - Range. Use it to set a minimum and a maximum, like a price filter. Show both values, and how many results are left, while people drag. - Steps. Use it when only a few values make sense, like text size. The handle snaps to each step, and tick marks show where the steps are. Rules Four rules keep sliders useful. 1. Let people type the exact value When the range has more values than the track has pixels, one pixel covers several values, so landing on exactly 37 takes many tries, and with a finger it’s worse. Put a number field next to the slider, so people can drag to get close and type the exact value. 2. Spread out a huge range On a straight track from $1 to $10,000, all the small amounts share the first few pixels, so setting $50 by dragging is nearly impossible. Use a number field, or a slider where $1 to $10, $10 to $100 and so on each get the same room, with a field beside it for any exact amount. 3. Make the handle easy to grab A tiny handle is hard to hit with a mouse, and a finger covers it completely. If clicking the track does nothing and the keyboard can’t reach it, some people can’t set the value at all. Make the handle and its hit area bigger, let a click on the track move it there, and let arrow keys move it too, with Shift for bigger steps. 4. Show what the value does When only a number changes, people can’t tell if higher is stricter or looser, so they guess or leave it alone. Label both ends with what they mean, and show the effect while people drag, like which emails would go to Spam. In real products Notice how each product pairs dragging with something exact or something you can see: a typed number, a live result, or a preview of where you’ll land. - Figma: number fields double as sliders. Drag sideways on a field’s label to scrub the value, or click into it and type the exact number. - Lightroom: every edit slider shows its value, and the value can be typed. The photo changes while you drag, so people judge by the result, not the number. - YouTube: hovering or dragging along the seek bar shows a small frame and the time at that point. People see where they’ll land before they let go. - Airbnb: the price filter shows a bar chart of prices above a two-handle slider, with minimum and maximum fields below. Drag for a rough range, or type an exact one.

entries.title: Text field
entries.summary: A text field is a box where people type their own words: a name, an address, a message, a search.
entries.tags: component inputs guide text field box where people type own words name address message search label above says what goes hints
entries.search_text: Text field A text field is a box where people type their own words: a name, an address, a message, a search. A label above it says what goes in, and hints and errors appear below it. That is what separates it from a picker , which offers only valid values, like the days on a calendar. A text field accepts anything people type, so it has to say what it expects and help when the text doesn’t fit. Forms Text fields come in four common forms, set by what people type. A single line holds a short value, like a name or an email. A multi-line box holds longer text, like a message. Search and password fields are single lines with a control of their own. - Single line. Use it for a short value, like a name or an email. - Multi-line. Use it for text that runs past a sentence, like a message. - Search. Use it to find things in a list or a whole app. - Password. Use it for a secret that shouldn’t show on screen, like a password or a PIN. Rules Four rules keep text fields useful. 1. Say back what you understood Some values can be written in more than one way: “12/11” is 11 December in the US and 12 November in most other places. If the field guesses without saying so, people find out at the hotel desk. Use a picker for values like this, or read the typed text back in words and ask when it could mean two things. 2. Keep the label visible A placeholder disappears as soon as there’s text in the field, and after that nothing on screen says what the field is for. People can’t check a filled form without clearing it, so a value in the wrong field gets through. Put the label above the field, where it stays while people type. 3. Show long text in full In a small fixed box, people only see a slice of what they wrote, so they can’t reread it before they post. If typing also stops at a hidden limit, the end of their text is lost. Use a box that grows as they write, and show a count when there is a limit. 4. Say how to fix it “Invalid username” has the same problem as a bare “Invalid date” : people can’t tell whether it’s the dot, the length or a name someone else has, so they change things at random. Say what’s wrong in plain words and offer a value that works, one click away. In real products Notice how each field fits the text it holds: a label that stays, a box that grows, a count near the limit, and the value shown back the way it will be saved. - Google sign-in: the field’s label sits inside the box, then moves up into the border once you type. Unlike a placeholder, it never disappears. - Slack: the message box grows line by line as you write, up to a set height, then scrolls. Short messages stay compact and long ones stay readable. - YouTube Studio: the title and description fields show a running count against their limits, like 31/100. People see the limit before they hit it. - GitHub: if a new repository name has spaces or other characters it can’t use, the form shows the name it will create instead, like portrait-tools. People see the fix, not just an error.

entries.title: Structured picker
entries.summary: A structured picker lets people enter a value with a set format by pointing at it: a day on a calendar, a time from a list, a color from a row of swatches.

rules.title: Put the context in the picker

entries.tags: component inputs guide structured picker lets people enter value set format pointing day calendar time list color row swatches every offers
entries.search_text: Structured picker A structured picker lets people enter a value with a set format by pointing at it: a day on a calendar, a time from a list, a color from a row of swatches. Every value it offers is valid, so people can’t enter a date that doesn’t exist or a color the app can’t use. Where a text field takes any text and checks it afterwards, a picker shows the possible values up front, so people choose one instead of remembering the format. Forms Pickers take the shape of the value they hold. A calendar picks one date, and a range calendar picks a start and an end. Times often come as a set of slots. Colors from a short list come as swatches. - Calendar. Use it for one date in the near future, like a delivery day. - Date range. Use it when the value has a start and an end, like a hotel stay. - Time. Use it when only some times work, like table bookings every 30 minutes. - Swatches. Use them when only a few colors are allowed, like label colors in a mail app. Rules Three rules keep pickers useful. 1. Let people type too A calendar is quick for a date next week, but slow for a date people know by heart, like a birthday: March 1988 is hundreds of clicks back. Put a text field next to the picker and accept the common ways of writing the value. The picker follows what people type, so they can still check it or click instead. 2. Show every allowed value Sometimes only a few values are allowed, like the 8 colors a calendar keeps for events. A free color strip suggests that any color will do, so people pick one, save, and get a different one with no reason given. Show the allowed values as swatches, chips or radio buttons, so what people pick is what they get. 3. Put the context in the picker A bare calendar doesn’t say which day is today, so to pick “a week from now”, people have to work out today’s date and count squares. Mark today in the calendar, offer presets for the usual choices, like “In 7 days”, and spell out the result in words, so people can check it before they move on. In real products Notice how each picker gives a fast path for the common case and a way to be exact: presets, context inside the calendar, or plain typing. - Gmail: Schedule send offers a few presets like tomorrow morning, each with its exact date and time, and a full picker for anything else. Most picks take one click. - Google Flights: the date picker shows a price under each day, with the cheaper days in a different color. People pick dates with the cost in view. - Figma: the color picker pairs a color area with a hex field and an eyedropper. People can point, type the exact code, or take a color from the canvas. - Todoist: typing a date in plain words, like “tomorrow 3pm”, highlights it and sets the due date. People who know the date never open a calendar.

entries.title: Button hierarchy
entries.summary: A button starts an action: save, send, pay, delete.
entries.tags: primary secondary destructive action submit cancel button
entries.search_text: Button hierarchy A button starts an action: save, send, pay, delete. Its style shows how important that action is, so people can find the main step without reading every label. That is what separates it from a link , which takes people to another page or place. A button does something where they are. Forms Buttons come in three styles, set by how important the action is: primary, secondary and tertiary. A fourth, destructive style marks actions that delete or lose something. - Primary. Use it for the one main action on a screen or in a dialog, like Pay. - Secondary. Use it for other likely actions next to the main one, like Save for later beside Add to bag. - Tertiary. Use it for rare or low-stakes actions, like Not now or Show more. - Destructive. Use it for actions that delete or lose something, like Delete photos. Rules Four rules keep buttons useful. 1. Keep one primary button When two buttons are filled, neither one stands out, and people have to read both labels before they know which one takes them forward. Give each screen or dialog one filled button for the main step, and make the others secondary or tertiary, so they’re still there but quieter. 2. Say what the button does As with dialog buttons , OK, Yes and Cancel only make sense next to the question: during an upload, “Cancel” could mean stop the upload or close the question. Use a verb and an object, like “Stop upload”, so each button makes sense on its own. 3. Set the risky action apart People press familiar buttons by habit, often by where they sit, so if Delete looks like Save and sits where Save usually goes, one quick click removes a folder and all its files. Make the destructive button red and move it away from the main button’s spot. Where you can, let people undo it instead of asking them to be careful. 4. Explain why it won’t work A grayed-out button shows that something is missing, but not what, and when every field looks filled in, people recheck the whole form or give up. Keep the button enabled, and when it’s pressed, say what’s missing and move the cursor there. Or show the reason next to the button before it’s pressed. In real products Notice how each screen has one strong action, and how the risky one is set apart and named for what it does. - Gmail: in the compose window, Send is the only filled button. Formatting tools are small icons, and discarding the draft is a trash icon at the far end, away from Send. - Airbnb: the booking card has one wide, filled Reserve button, and a short note under it says nothing is charged yet. - GitHub: deleting a repository sits in a red-bordered Danger Zone at the bottom of settings. The final button names the action and only works after you type the repository’s name. - iOS Photos: deleting a photo opens a sheet with a red Delete Photo button, and Cancel sits apart in its own block.

entries.title: Icon button
entries.summary: An icon button is a button that shows a small picture instead of a word: a magnifier for search, an × to close, a heart to like.

rules.title: Make them big enough to hit

entries.tags: component actions guide icon button shows small picture instead word magnifier search close heart like fits tight spaces toolbars photo overlays
entries.search_text: Icon button An icon button is a button that shows a small picture instead of a word: a magnifier for search, an × to close, a heart to like. It fits in tight spaces like toolbars and photo overlays, and suits actions people use again and again. That is what separates it from a button with a label. A word can be read the first time, but an icon has to be recognized, so it only works for actions people already know or quickly learn. Forms Icon buttons come in four common forms. Plain ones sit in a toolbar and do one thing each. Toggles stay on or off, like bold or mute. A floating button holds the main action on a phone screen, and a More button opens a list of the actions that don’t fit. - Plain. Use it in a toolbar for actions people repeat, like zoom in and out. - Toggle. Use it for something that’s on or off, like bold text. - Floating. Use it for the one main action on a phone screen, like writing a new email. - More. Use it to hold actions people need now and then, like Download or Move to trash. Rules Three rules keep icon buttons useful. 1. Label icons people don’t know Only a few icons mean the same thing to everyone, like search, close, settings and home. Most others, like crop, could mean several things, so people click around to find out, and some never find the right one. Give those buttons a word, and keep bare icons for the few that everyone knows. 2. Keep the row short In a row of ten look-alike icons, every action gets the same weight, so people hover them one by one to find the one they want. Group related icons, give the main action a word, and move rare actions into a More menu, so there is less to scan. 3. Make them big enough to hit A 16 px button is smaller than a fingertip, and with no gap between buttons, one tap covers all three, so people hit Close when they meant Add. Make each button at least 24 px (the WCAG 2.2 minimum), ideally 40 to 44 px, with space between, and keep Close a little apart from the rest. In real products Notice which icons stand alone and which get help: a label, a tooltip with the shortcut, or a menu with words. - Instagram: like, comment, share and save sit under every post as bare icons. People see them on every post, so they learn them fast and labels would only add clutter. - Spotify: each tab at the bottom of the app has a short label under its icon, because a library icon alone could mean many things. - VS Code: the activity bar down the side is icons only, but hovering one shows its name and keyboard shortcut. People learn the icon and the faster way at the same time. - Gmail: the message toolbar groups its icons into small clusters, and less common actions sit in a More menu with text labels. The row stays short and easy to scan.

entries.title: Link vs button
entries.summary: Links and buttons are both things people click, but they do different jobs.

rules.title: Use a button when something changes
Use a link to go somewhere

entries.tags: component actions guide link button links buttons both things people click different jobs takes another page place something where saves sends
entries.search_text: Link vs button Links and buttons are both things people click, but they do different jobs. A link takes people to another page or place. A button does something where they are: it saves, sends, adds or deletes. The difference matters because browsers treat them differently: a link has an address, so people can open it in a new tab, bookmark it and come back with Back, and a button has none of that. So choose by what happens on click, not by how it should look. Forms Each comes in a few forms. A link can sit inside a sentence or stand on its own, and a button can be a full button or a lighter text button. A link can also look like a button when it’s the main next step: the look follows how important it is, but whether it’s a link or a button still follows what it does. - Inline link. Use it to point to another page from inside a sentence. - Standalone link. Use it for a way to another page that sits on its own, such as “See all orders”. - Button. Use it when pressing it changes something here: add, save, send, delete. - Button-style link. Use it when the main next step is another page, such as “Go to checkout”. - Text button. Use it for a small action that shouldn’t compete with the main one, such as “Remove”. Rules Three rules keep links and buttons clear. 1. Use a button when something changes People open links in a new tab just to look, so if a link deletes or sends something, opening it is enough to do it, with no warning and no way back. A button tells people that pressing it does something, so they press it on purpose. Put Undo next to the result to cover a slip. 2. Use a link to go somewhere People open pages in a new tab to keep their place, and use Back to return. A button that only swaps the view breaks both: the address doesn’t change, so there’s nothing to bookmark or share, and Back can’t return to the page they came from. A link keeps all of this working, the same as on every other site. 3. Underline links in text A link that differs from the words around it only by color is easy to miss, because people with color blindness or low vision, or anyone on a dim screen, see plain text. An underline marks it without relying on color, so it still shows in grayscale. Links that stand on their own, like “See all orders”, can do without it, because their place already says what they are. In real products Notice that in each product a link and a button sit side by side. - Google Docs: links in the text are underlined. In the card that opens on one, the address is a link, while copy, edit and remove are buttons. - GitHub: in a comment, issue numbers like 42 and @mentions are links to other pages. Comment and Close issue change things here, so they are buttons. - YouTube: under a video, the channel name is a link to the channel’s page. Subscribe is a button: it changes something without leaving the video. - Amazon: in search results, each product title is a link, so it can open in a new tab for comparing. Add to cart is a button that acts right where you are.

entries.title: Tabs
entries.summary: Tabs split one thing into a few parts and show one part at a time.

rules.title: Put things to compare side by side
Keep short content on one page

entries.tags: component containers guide tabs split one thing few parts show part time hotel page might overview rooms reviews tab names sit
entries.search_text: Tabs Tabs split one thing into a few parts and show one part at a time. A hotel page might have Overview, Rooms and Reviews. The tab names sit in a row with the selected one marked, and picking a tab swaps the panel below it while the rest of the page stays where it is. Each tab holds different content, where a segmented control changes how the same content is shown, such as a list or a grid. Forms Tabs come in three common forms, which differ in who decides what the tabs are and in what each tab remembers. Line tabs split one section of a page, a tab bar holds the main sections of a phone app, and document tabs are ones people open and close themselves, like browser tabs. - Line tabs. Use them when one section of a page has a few parts people read one at a time. - Tab bar. Use it for the three to five main sections of a phone app. - Document tabs. Use them when people open their own items side by side, like web pages. Rules Four rules keep tabs useful. 1. Put things to compare side by side Tabs show one panel at a time, so when people need to compare, such as rooms and their prices, they flip back and forth and keep the numbers in their head. That is slow and easy to get wrong. Put the options side by side, or in one table with a column per option, so the eye does the comparing and the answer takes one look. 2. Keep to a few tabs Only so many tabs fit in a row, so the rest hide past the edge, often behind a faint fade, and people miss them or scroll sideways to look. For more than about six sections, list them top to bottom in side navigation , where every section is visible and the list has room to grow. Or keep a few tabs and put the rarely used sections in a select. 3. Use a stepper for steps Tabs tell people they can open them in any order, so when the parts have to happen in order, people jump ahead and only learn at the end that something earlier was needed. A stepper shows the order and where people are, and it checks each step before the next one, so nothing fails at the last moment. 4. Keep short content on one page When each tab holds a field or two, checking them all costs a click per tab, and people never see the whole thing before they save. On one short page with headings, they check everything at a glance and save with one click. In real products Notice when products use tabs, and what they do instead when there are too many. - Figma: the right panel splits into Design and Prototype tabs. Both describe the same selection, and people work in one at a time. - Instagram: a profile has a row of icon tabs for posts, reels and tagged photos, each a different collection from the same person. - GitHub: a repository’s tabs show counts, like open issues. When the window is narrow, the tabs that don’t fit move into a menu at the end of the row instead of being cut off. - Slack: preferences have many sections, so they’re a list down the side instead of tabs.

entries.title: Accordion
entries.summary: An accordion is a stack of headers.

rules.title: Don’t fold what people read in full
Don’t hide what people must see

entries.tags: component containers guide accordion stack headers header opens show content under closes hide again which keeps long page short most people
entries.search_text: Accordion An accordion is a stack of headers. Each header opens to show the content under it and closes to hide it again, which keeps a long page short when most people need only part of it, like the answers on a help page or the filters in a shop. Where tabs keep their names in a row and show one panel at a time, an accordion keeps its headers in a column, opens each section in place, and can show several at once. Forms Accordions differ in how their sections open and in what a closed header shows. In the most common form, each section opens on its own. In another, opening one section closes the others. In a filter panel, each closed header also shows what’s chosen inside it. - Several open. Use it for a list of separate topics, like the questions on a help page. - One at a time. Use it when people need only one section at a time, as on a phone. - Filter panel. Use it for groups of filters or settings in a narrow side panel. Rules Four rules keep accordions useful. 1. Show what people come for Most people open an order page to see when it arrives, so if that sits behind a closed header, every visit costs the same extra click. Show the part people come for as soon as the page loads, either open or above the accordion, and leave behind headers only what few people need. 2. Don’t fold what people read in full Some pages are read from top to bottom, like the details of a home before booking it. In an accordion, people open the sections one by one, and a closed header doesn’t show what’s inside. Put it all on one page instead, with headings to guide the eye and a few links at the top that jump to each part. 3. Keep it one level deep Each level of nesting costs another click and pushes the content further in, so a setting three levels down is hard to find and people lose track of where they are. Open one level, and group what’s inside with small headings. If that is still too much, split it into separate pages. 4. Don’t hide what people must see People read what’s open and skip what’s closed. If a problem sits in a closed section, such as an expired card, the page looks fine and people leave, and they find out later, when something stops working. Show the problem where people look first, with the fix next to it, and keep the accordion for extra detail. In real products Notice what stays open: the part people use most is shown, and the rest folds into headers that open in place. - VS Code: the Explorer keeps the file tree open and folds Outline and Timeline into headers at the bottom. They open in place when you need them. - Lightroom Classic: the Develop panel stacks Basic, Tone Curve, Detail and more as sections. Solo mode keeps just one open, so the panel stays short. - Gmail: in a long thread, older messages shrink to one-line headers and the newest stays open. A count stands in for the ones in between, and any of them opens with a click. - Google Search: “People also ask” lists related questions. Each one opens in place to show a short answer, so the results page stays short.

entries.title: Card
entries.summary: A card is a box that holds one item: a photo album, a home to rent, a product.

rules.title: Give each card one main action
Make the whole card one target
Don’t put everything in a card

entries.tags: component containers guide card box holds one item photo album home rent product shows just enough tell items apart such picture
entries.search_text: Card A card is a box that holds one item: a photo album, a home to rent, a product. It shows just enough to tell items apart, such as a picture, a name and a detail or two, so people can scan a set of cards, compare them at a glance, and open one to see the rest. A row in a list lines up the same details in columns, which is better for comparing dates or prices. A card gives each item room for a picture instead, which helps when people know items by how they look. Forms Cards come in a few forms, and the form decides what a click on the card does. A media card leads with a picture, and a horizontal card puts the picture beside the text, so it fits in a list. A summary card shows a few key figures, like an account balance. A choice card is picked instead of opened, like a plan. - Media. Use it when people know items by their picture, like photos, videos or homes to rent. - Horizontal. Use it when the text matters as much as the picture, like hotels in search results. - Summary. Use it on a home screen to show a few key figures, like an account balance. - Choice. Use it when people pick one option that needs a few details to compare, like a plan. Rules Four rules keep cards useful. 1. Give each card one main action Every button on a card takes space from the name and the picture, so a page of busy cards is hard to scan. Risky actions like Delete also end up next to everyday ones, one slip away. Let a click anywhere on the card open it, and put the rarer actions in one ⋯ menu. 2. Put the cards in order With no order and no dates, every card is a guess, and people open them one by one to find the right one. Sort or group them the way people remember the items, such as newest first for albums, and show the date. For comparing details like photo counts, offer a list view, where the values line up in columns. 3. Make the whole card one target When a card holds several click targets, one inside another, people can’t predict what a click will do: a shop name might open the shop, and a heart might save the item and open it too. Make the card one link that always opens the item, and keep the one extra action, like save, outside that link, so it does only its own job. 4. Don’t put everything in a card Cards are for separate items of the same kind, like albums or homes to rent. When every setting sits in its own box, the page fills with borders and shadows, nothing groups, and the boxes look clickable when they aren’t. Use plain rows under headings, and let the space between them do the grouping. In real products Notice how little each card shows, and that none has more than one extra action. - YouTube: each video card is a thumbnail, a title, the channel and how old it is. The whole card opens the video, and other actions wait in one ⋮ menu. - Airbnb: every listing card puts the same facts in the same order, photo, place, dates, price, so they’re easy to compare. Saving is the one extra action, a heart on the photo. - Trello: a card shows only its title, labels and small badges for things like due date and checklist progress. Open it to see everything else. - Spotify: album and playlist cards are mostly cover art. A play button appears on hover, so you can play without opening, and the card stays clean the rest of the time.

entries.title: Side navigation
entries.summary: A side navigation is a list of an app’s main places, down the left edge: Home, Documents, Shared, Settings.
entries.tags: component navigation guide side list app main places down left edge home documents shared settings people use move between those
entries.search_text: Side navigation A side navigation is a list of an app’s main places, down the left edge: Home, Documents, Shared, Settings. People use it to move between those places, and it always marks the one they’re in. It stays in the same spot while the page beside it changes. Where tabs split one thing into parts, like the details and the reviews of a product, a side navigation moves between separate areas of the app, and it can hold more of them. Forms Side navigation comes in four common forms. A full sidebar shows an icon and a label for each place. A nested one lets places open to show their own pages. A rail is a narrow strip of icons with short labels, for pages that need the width. On phones, the list moves into a drawer that opens over the page. - Full. Use it when the app has a handful of main areas and the screen has room. - Nested. Use it when areas have their own pages, like a help center or a big settings page. - Rail. Use it when the page needs most of the width, like a photo grid or a map. - Drawer. Use it on phones, where there’s no room to keep the list open. Rules Four rules keep side navigation useful. 1. Keep it to places People read every item in the sidebar as a place to go, so when one of them runs an action instead, like New folder, pressing it takes them away from the page they were on. The new folder then lands somewhere else, and they have to go looking for it. Put actions on buttons in the page, where they act on what people are looking at. 2. Group long lists When every area sits in one long list, all of them look equally important, so people read the whole list each time, and daily work sits next to setup pages they open once a year. Group items under short headings so people can skip to the right group, fold away the groups people rarely need, and move setup pages into Settings. 3. Show labels with icons Most icons don’t say what they are, so with icons alone people point at one after another to read the tooltips, and next time they do it again. A short label with each icon lets them find a place at a glance and remember it. If space is tight, let the rail expand to show the labels. Icons alone can work in a tool people use all day, like VS Code, where there are few icons to learn and the open view’s name heads the panel beside them. 4. Mark the current place If nothing in the sidebar is marked, people have to work out where they are from the page, and when the page title also uses different words from the item, they can’t match the two at all. Highlight the current item and give the page the same name, so people can tell where they are from either side of the screen. In real products Notice how each one marks the current place and makes room for more items. - Gmail: the open folder gets a filled background and bold text, unread counts sit beside each name, and rarely used labels wait under More. Compose is a button above the list, not a place in it. - Slack: channels sit in sections you can name and collapse. Unread channels turn bold and the open one is highlighted, so a long list stays easy to scan. - VS Code: the activity bar is icons only, but the active view is marked on its edge and its name heads the side bar. Badges add counts, like changed files. - YouTube: on narrower windows the side menu shrinks to a rail but keeps a short label under each icon, so places stay findable without hovering.

entries.title: Breadcrumbs
entries.summary: Breadcrumbs are a short line of links above a page title, like My drive / Family / Holidays.
entries.tags: component navigation guide breadcrumbs short line links above page title like drive family holidays show where sits structure top level down
entries.search_text: Breadcrumbs Breadcrumbs are a short line of links above a page title, like My drive / Family / Holidays. They show where the page sits in a structure, from the top level down, and let people jump to any level above in one click. A Back link goes up one level at a time. Breadcrumbs show every level at once, so people can skip several in one go. Forms Most breadcrumbs show the full path, with a link for each level. Some add a small menu after each level, so people can move sideways to a neighbor as well as up. On phones, many show only the level above. - Full path. Use it when pages sit three or more levels deep, like folders or a shop’s departments. - With menus. Use it when people often move between neighbors, like cities in one country. - Parent only. Use it on phones, where a full trail would wrap onto several lines. Rules Three rules keep breadcrumbs useful. 1. Skip them in flat structures With only one or two levels, the trail mostly repeats the page title: one more line to read that doesn’t take people anywhere new. A clear title says where people are, and a Back link covers the one way up. 2. Show location, not history A trail made of the pages people visited changes every time and says nothing about where the page belongs, so finding more things like it means starting again from the top. Leave the visited pages to the Back button, and make the trail show where the page sits in the structure, so its category is one click away however people got there. 3. Shorten long paths A deep path wraps onto a second line and pushes the page down, and people have to read every level to find the one they want. Keep the top level and the current one, and put the middle behind a “…” button, where the middle levels are still one click away. In real products Notice that every level above the page is one click away, and that long paths get shortened in the middle. - GitHub: above a file, the path names the repository and each folder down to the file. Every folder is a link and the file name is plain text, so you can jump up any number of levels in one click. - Notion: the top bar shows where a page lives. When the path gets deep, the middle levels fold into “…”, which lists them when clicked, so the first and last levels stay readable. - Windows File Explorer: each folder in the address bar is a button, and the arrow after it lists that folder’s subfolders. You can jump up, or up and across, in one move. - Amazon: a product page shows its category trail, like Electronics › Headphones. It shows where the product sits in the store, not how you got there, and each level opens a broader category.

entries.title: Stepper
entries.summary: A stepper, also called a wizard, splits a long task into a few steps in a fixed order, such as Delivery, Payment and Review.

rules.title: Use as few steps as you can

entries.tags: component navigation guide stepper also called wizard splits long task few steps fixed order such delivery payment review row top names
entries.search_text: Stepper A stepper, also called a wizard, splits a long task into a few steps in a fixed order, such as Delivery, Payment and Review. A row at the top names the steps, marks the current one and ticks off the ones that are done, so people answer a little at a time and can always see how much is left. Where tabs open in any order and are never finished, a stepper has an order, and each step is done before the next one starts. Forms Steppers come in three common forms. A horizontal stepper names each step in a row across the top. A vertical one stacks the steps and opens the current one in place. On phones, many show only a count and a progress bar. - Horizontal.
