Use it for three to five steps on a wide screen, like a checkout. - Vertical. Use it when steps need room to explain, or when the page is narrow. - Step count. Use it on phones, or when the task is a run of short questions. Rules Four rules keep steppers useful. 1. Let people jump back In a strict stepper, changing one answer means going back through every screen and forward again, which costs so many clicks that people stop checking their answers. Make finished steps clickable, and put an Edit link next to each answer on the review step. If people need to move around freely, use one page with sections instead. 2. Give regulars a shortcut A guided path helps the first time, but someone who sends the same invoice every month still has to sit through the welcome screen and every step. Offer templates or a one-page form next to the guided path, so newcomers keep the guide and regulars finish in a couple of clicks. 3. Keep answers on Back Losing answers on Back is the most common stepper bug. People have to choose everything again, and they may miss that a value was reset, like the number of copies going back to 1, and order the wrong number of prints. Hold on to every answer until people finish or cancel the whole task, so checking a step costs nothing and people check more. 4. Use as few steps as you can Past about five steps, people lose count of how much is left, and some give up before they pay. Most of the extra screens only confirm an answer that was already picked. Cut steps, merge them, or fill them with smart defaults that people can change in one place. Three named steps fit on one line, so the end is always in sight. In real products Notice how each one shows how far along you are and asks for a little at a time. - macOS Installer: a list on the left names every step from Introduction to Summary and marks the current one, so people always know how much is left. - Airbnb: listing a home is many short screens grouped into a few big steps, with a progress bar at the bottom. Save & exit keeps the answers so hosts can finish later. - Duolingo: setup asks one short question per screen, with a progress bar on top. Each screen takes seconds, so the whole thing feels light. - VS Code: the Get Started walkthrough lists its steps with checkmarks. You can open any step in any order, and finished ones stay ticked.

entries.title: Interaction states
entries.summary: Interaction states are the different looks one control takes as people use it: hover, focus, pressed, selected, disabled, loading, and the result after.

rules.title: Design every state, not just the default

entries.tags: component states guide interaction different looks one control takes people use hover focus pressed selected disabled loading result after state
entries.search_text: Interaction states Interaction states are the different looks one control takes as people use it: hover, focus, pressed, selected, disabled, loading, and the result after. Each state tells people something they need in that moment: that the control reacts, that it heard the click, that it’s working, or that it’s done. A state lives on the control itself, so people see it exactly where they acted. A message, like a toast or an inline message , is for anything that needs more words than a control can hold. Forms States fall into four kinds, by what they report. Hover and pressed follow the pointer, focus shows where the keyboard is, selected shows what’s chosen, and disabled and loading say what the control can do right now. - Hover and press. Use them on anything people can click: hover says it reacts, and pressed says the click landed. - Focus. Use it to show which control the keyboard is on. It moves with Tab. - Selected. Use it to show what’s chosen or switched on, like photos picked for sharing. - Disabled. Use it when a control can’t work yet, like Continue before there’s an amount. - Loading. Use it when an action takes more than a moment, like exporting a file. Rules Four rules keep interaction states useful. 1. Design every state, not just the default A button that looks the same while it sends, after it fails and when there’s nothing to send gives people no answer, so they press again or give up. Give each state its own look and words, such as “Sending…”, “Sent” and “Retry”. Before building, list every state (default, hover, focus, pressed, disabled, loading, error, success) and check each one in the browser. 2. Say why it’s off A disabled control shows that people can’t act, but not why, so they check every field and guess. Put the reason right next to it, or keep it enabled and explain when it’s pressed, the same fix as for a disabled button . 3. Keep the focus ring Without a focus ring, keyboard users can’t see which button they’re on, so they press Enter and hope. As in Keyboard and focus , restyle the ring to fit the design instead of removing it. :focus-visible shows it only when people use the keyboard, so it never shows on mouse clicks. 4. Block the second click If a button still works while it’s loading, a nervous double-click places two orders. Once it’s pressed, ignore repeat clicks and show that it’s working. Keep its width fixed too, because a button that grows to fit “Placing your order…” moves the buttons next to it, like content that loads late . In real products - Figma: hovering a layer draws a thin outline; selecting it adds handles and its size. “I’m pointing at it” and “I’ve picked it” never look the same. - YouTube: Subscribe is a strong filled button; once pressed it becomes a quieter Subscribed button. The color and the label both say which state you’re in. - Spotify: hovering a track swaps its number for a play icon, and the playing track is highlighted with small moving bars. The main button shows pause while music plays. - Slack: the send button stays dimmed while the message box is empty and turns on as soon as you type. The reason it’s off is right there: there’s nothing to send.

entries.title: Empty state
entries.summary: An empty state is what a screen shows when there’s nothing in it: no albums yet, no search results, no tasks left.

rules.title: Match the message to the cause

entries.tags: component states guide empty state what screen shows there nothing albums yet search results tasks left instead blank space says belongs
entries.search_text: Empty state An empty state is what a screen shows when there’s nothing in it: no albums yet, no search results, no tasks left. Instead of a blank space, it says what belongs here and how to get the first one. Loading means content is on its way, and an error means something failed. Empty means everything worked, and there’s nothing to show. Forms Empty states come in three common kinds, set by why the screen is empty: first use, no results and all done. Each kind needs different words and a different action. - First use. Use it when people haven’t added anything yet. - No results. Use it when a search or filter matched nothing. - All done. Use it when people cleared the list themselves, like an inbox or today’s tasks. Rules Three rules keep empty states useful. 1. Say what goes here “No items” doesn’t say what belongs on the screen or how to add it, so people have to find the small + in the corner on their own. Name what will show up here, and put the button for the first one inside the empty space, where it takes one press. 2. Offer one way to start Five equal buttons make a new person stop and compare them, and none of them looks like the place to start. Give one main action, and at most one quieter one beside it, such as a link to templates for people who look for them. 3. Match the message to the cause If an empty search and an unstarted wishlist both say “No items”, people can’t tell which problem they have, and a search that’s too narrow needs a different fix than a list that’s new. For no results, name the filter and offer to clear it. For first use, explain how to add the first item. In real products Notice that each empty screen says what belongs there and puts the first step inside the empty space. - GitHub: a new, empty repository shows the setup commands to copy, so the first push is one paste away. - Trello: on a new board, the spot where the first list will go is itself the Add a list button. - Spotify: a new, empty playlist puts a song search right where the songs will appear, so adding the first one doesn’t mean going anywhere else. - Gmail: a search with no results says nothing matched and points to search options like sender and date. It’s a no-results state, not a first-use one, so it helps you change the search.

entries.title: Error state
entries.summary: An error state is what a screen, or part of one, shows when something failed: a page didn’t load, a save didn’t go through, a link is broken.
entries.tags: component states guide error state what screen part one shows something failed page didn load save through link broken says went
entries.search_text: Error state An error state is what a screen, or part of one, shows when something failed: a page didn’t load, a save didn’t go through, a link is broken. It says what went wrong in plain words and offers the next step. It sits where content would be, like an empty state , but it means the opposite: something failed, and people need to know what and what to do about it. Forms Error states come in four common kinds, set by what failed: content that didn’t load, an action that didn’t go through, a link to something that’s gone, and a page people aren’t allowed to open. Each kind needs a different next step. - Couldn’t load. Use it when part of a page can’t get its content, often because of the connection. - Couldn’t send. Use it when something people did didn’t go through, like sending an email. - Not found. Use it when a link leads to something that was deleted or never existed. - No access. Use it when the thing exists but people aren’t allowed to open it. Rules Four rules keep error states useful. 1. Say what failed When every problem gets the same words, people can’t tell if they made a mistake, lost their connection or hit a bug, so they don’t know what to fix. Name the thing that failed, and say where the cause lies: in what they entered, in the connection, or on the product’s side. People then know whether to change their input, wait for the connection or try again later. 2. Offer the next step An error with only an OK button closes and leaves the problem where it was. Put the next step on buttons in the message, such as Try again or Get help, as in Error messages . Most failures go away on a second try, and help is there when they don’t. 3. Keep people’s work When an upload of 40 photos fails halfway and the error clears the selection, people have to pick all 40 again, and the 18 that already uploaded get sent a second time. Keep what people chose and what already finished, so Retry continues from where it stopped. 4. Don’t lead with the code “Error 500” means nothing to most people, who can’t tell whose fault it is, or whether to retry or wait. Lead with plain words : say what didn’t load, that it isn’t their fault, and what to do. The code can stay below in small text, for when they contact support. In real products Notice that each one names what failed, keeps the work, and offers the fix right there. - Figma: a file that uses fonts you don’t have still opens. Figma lists the missing fonts and lets you pick replacements, so nothing is lost and the fix is one step. - GitHub: when a pull request can’t merge, it says the branch has conflicts, lists the files, and offers a Resolve conflicts button. Merge stays off until they’re fixed. - iPhone Messages: a message that fails keeps its text, gets a red mark and “Not Delivered”, and tapping the mark offers Try Again. Nothing has to be retyped. - Chrome: when a page can’t load, it says why in plain words, lists a few things to check, and keeps the error code small at the bottom, for support.

entries.title: The loop
entries.summary: Every change goes through the same loop.

rules.title: Frame the problem before you build
Choose yourself, and write down why
Try it in the real app
Frame a hunch as a question

entries.tags: loop frame explore decide build check learn agent workflow cycle brief guide part4 effective every change goes through same problem work come what finds
entries.search_text: The loop Every change goes through the same loop. Problem and Brief frame the work, then come Explore, Decide, Build and Check, and what Learn finds starts the next round. Each stage takes something in and hands something on, so a skipped stage leaves the next one guessing. Agents make Build fast, so the stages around it matter more: framing the problem before, and checking the result after. Each stage at a glance. What you own, what agents do shows how the split moves with the kind of work. Table: Stage Takes in Hands on Who owns it Problem A signal: a support thread, a ticket, something you hit yourself. One sentence: who has the problem, and what stops them. You Brief The problem statement and what you know about it. A short brief: the goal, limits, what’s out of scope and how you’ll know it worked. You (agents can draft) Explore The brief. Several real options, each with its trade-offs. Agents, you steer Decide The options, checked against the brief. One direction, and why, written down. You Build The decision and the brief. A pull request with tests. Agents, you review Check The PR and the brief’s “how you’ll know”. Pass or fail against the brief, plus the gaps. Both Learn What the check found, and feedback after release. A note, and the next problem or a sharper brief. You Rules Five rules keep the loop useful. 1. Frame the problem before you build A ticket that names a fix sends the agent straight to Build, and it builds that fix quickly and well. If the fix doesn’t solve the real problem, people still have it and the fast build was wasted. Frame the problem and write a short brief first, so the agent explores answers to the right question. 2. Close the loop A merged pull request means the change shipped, not that it worked. When shipping is the last step, nobody checks, and the problems it didn’t solve come back weeks later as support requests. Check the change against the brief and write down what you learned, because that note becomes the problem for the next round. 3. Choose yourself, and write down why Agents are quick to build the first idea that fits. If you merge it because it’s already built, the agent made the choice, and later nobody can say why it was done this way. Ask for several options, pick one yourself, and write the reason in the ticket or the PR. 4. Try it in the real app Tests an agent wrote check what the agent thought of, so they can all pass while the change fails people in a case nobody listed. Open the change in the real app and walk through the brief yourself. A problem found before the merge costs minutes, not a bug report. 5. Frame a hunch as a question Some work starts from a hunch, with no evidence yet and a goal that’s still moving. Written as a spec, the hunch gets built as if it were known, and a whole round passes before anyone learns it was wrong. Write the brief as a question instead: what you want to find out, what you believe now and what would change your mind. Keep the rounds short, and let each Learn rewrite the brief. In real products Notice how long a round runs in each: a week, eight weeks, or as long as one test takes. - Google Ventures: the design sprint fits the loop into one week. Map the problem, sketch, decide, build a prototype, then test it with five customers on Friday. What the tests show decides the next step. - Basecamp: in Shape Up, ideas are shaped into pitches, a betting table picks which to build, and a team builds for six weeks. A two-week cool-down follows, and the next bets are placed then, so every round has a clear end and a fresh start. - Duolingo: many changes ship first as A/B tests. Some learners get the new version and the rest keep the current one. The result decides what ships, and it suggests what to test next.

entries.title: Ownership
entries.summary: Agents are good at wide, repeatable work: searching a codebase, writing test scaffolds, making many variations.

rules.title: Ask for trade-offs, not a verdict
Hand over the wide, repetitive work
Review the plan before the build

entries.tags: ownership agent judgment framing decide human accountable design role workflow loop guide part4 effective agents good wide repeatable work searching codebase writing test scaffolds making many variations keep problem
entries.search_text: Ownership Agents are good at wide, repeatable work: searching a codebase, writing test scaffolds, making many variations. You keep the judgment: framing the problem, choosing between options and checking the result. Between agent steps, put a checkpoint where you read what came back before the next step starts. Where the loop names the stages of a change, this entry says who owns each one. Agent output often sounds sure, but confident wording isn’t evidence, so ask for the file, the test or the screenshot behind each claim before you build on it. An agent can draft any part of a brief, and any option or check, as long as it says where each part came from, such as a support thread, a ticket or a file. Confirming who has the problem, the evidence and the problem itself stays with you, and so do the choice between options and every judgment call. The table shows the split from the demo for each kind of work. Table: Stage Small fix New feature Open exploration Problem Reproduce it yourself. Is it really one line? You confirm people really lose work, and when. A hunch to test, not a spec. Brief Expected and actual, in one sentence. An agent can draft from the ticket; you cut and sharpen. What question should the prototypes answer? Explore An agent finds the cause. Usually one obvious option. Subagents sketch three options in parallel. Many quick prototypes as artifacts. Decide You approve the fix, or notice it isn’t small after all. You pick one and write why. You choose what to learn more about, or stop. Build The agent writes the fix and a test that failed before. Claude Code builds in a worktree, plan first. Throwaway build; speed over code quality. Check Tests run; you check the real app once. Agents run tests; you close real tabs. You watch people try it. That part is yours. Learn Is it a pattern? Note it, or close it. You decide what becomes the next problem. Write down what you now believe. Rules Four rules keep the split between you and agents useful. 1. Ask for trade-offs, not a verdict When you ask an agent to pick the best design, it picks one and sounds sure about it, so you get a choice with nothing to check and can’t explain it later. Ask for the options and what each one is good at and costs, then make the choice yourself. If you already lean one way, write it down first, so the agent’s confident answer doesn’t become yours, as Hear their read first explains. 2. Hand over the wide, repetitive work Some tasks are long only because there is a lot of the same thing: every use of a color token, every form to update, ten variations of a layout. Doing them by hand takes hours that framing and checking needed. Agents can do that work, several at once, and you spend the time you get back reading what they found. 3. Stop after each agent step If exploring flows straight into planning and building, an early misreading carries all the way through, and you find out at the end, when many files have changed. Stop after each step and read what came back. Claude Code’s plan mode, where the agent proposes a plan and changes no files until you approve it, is one built-in checkpoint. 4. Review the plan before the build A wrong approach takes a minute to fix in a short plan, but in a finished diff (the changed lines of code) it runs through many files, and fixing it means building again. Read the plan before the agent builds, as Plan, then take small steps explains. In real products Notice where each tool stops and hands over to a person: before the merge, at the sliders, before Send. - GitHub: Dependabot opens pull requests that update dependencies, with release notes inside, and the repo’s checks run on each one. It does the dull, repeated part in every repo; a person still reads and merges. - Lightroom: Auto sets the basic tone sliders in one click. The sliders stay in view and editable, so the photographer starts from a good guess and keeps the final call. - Gmail: Smart Reply suggests a few short answers under a message. Picking one only drafts the reply; you can edit it, and nothing goes out until you press Send.

entries.title: Problem brief
entries.summary: A problem brief is a short note written before anyone builds.

rules.title: Describe the problem, not the fix
Say how you’ll know it worked
Replace vague words with what you’d see

entries.tags: brief problem who goal constraints non-goals success criteria ticket agent workflow guide part4 effective short note written before anyone builds says what should change off limits how know worked
entries.search_text: Problem brief A problem brief is a short note written before anyone builds. It says who has the problem, what should change, what’s off limits and how you’ll know it worked, so an agent can explore answers without guessing what you meant. Where a ticket often names a fix, a brief names the problem, so better fixes can still turn up. Its neighbors do other jobs: a context pack holds the materials the agent works with, and a definition of done lists the checks the change must pass. Keep a brief to one page. A longer one likely covers more than one problem, so split it. Say where each part came from, and leave what you don’t know empty . The brief check in the demo flags four things. Passing it doesn’t make a brief clear, but each flag is worth fixing. Table: Flag Shows when Fix Missing A field is empty: who, problem, goal, constraints, non-goals or success criteria. Fill it in. Without non-goals , an agent may widen the scope, and without success criteria , nobody can say when it’s done. Vague A field uses a word from the vague-word table , such as “better” or “intuitive”. Say what you’d see happen. Too broad Who is only “users”, “user”, “everyone”, “everybody”, “people”, “all users” or “anyone”. Name the people and the moment, like “people editing in several tabs”. Solution The problem names a control: dialog, modal, popup, pop-up, button, toggle, banner, toast, checkbox or menu. Describe what goes wrong instead. Rules Four rules keep a brief useful. 1. Describe the problem, not the fix An agent builds the fix a brief names, and nothing else, so a simpler answer never comes up. Frame the problem instead: state the problem and the goal, and list any fix you have in mind as one option. 2. Say what’s out of scope An agent that sees nearby problems tends to fix them too. The change grows, you review work you didn’t ask for, and some of it may undo choices made on purpose. List the non-goals, such as the page layout or the button wording, so the change stays the size you meant. 3. Say how you’ll know it worked Without success criteria , “done” means whatever the agent or the reviewer feels, so the review turns into opinions and gaps slip through. Write criteria you can check in the app, such as a time, a step count or a key that must work, and turn them into the definition of done. 4. Replace vague words with what you’d see Words like “better”, “cleaner” and “intuitive” mean something different to every reader, so each agent fills them in its own way, and none of the results is wrong by the brief. Replace each vague word with something you could watch happen, such as “people pay in three steps or fewer”. In real products Notice that each format makes the writer state the problem and the limits before anyone builds. - Amazon: in “working backwards”, teams write the press release and FAQ they’d publish at launch before they build. It forces a plain answer to who the customer is and what problem goes away. - Basecamp: a Shape Up pitch names the problem, the appetite (how much time it’s worth), a rough solution, rabbit holes and no-gos. The no-gos are its non-goals, set before anyone starts. - GitHub: issue templates can ask for steps to reproduce, expected and actual behavior before an issue is filed. Whoever finds the bug writes the brief, so nobody has to guess later.

entries.title: Context pack
entries.summary: A context pack is what a new teammate would need on their first day: design tokens, components to reuse, copy rules, examples of good screens, repo conventions and the design frames.

rules.title: Point to the design system by path
Show the look, don’t only describe it
Keep the stable parts in one file

entries.tags: context pack tokens components copy repo conventions examples materials agent workflow brief guide part4 effective what new teammate would need first day design reuse rules good screens
entries.search_text: Context pack A context pack is what a new teammate would need on their first day: design tokens, components to reuse, copy rules, examples of good screens, repo conventions and the design frames. An agent that doesn’t get these makes up its own, and the result may work but doesn’t look or read like the rest of the product. Where the problem brief says what to solve, the context pack says how things are done here. Include the accessibility rules too: focus order, labels, and which color tokens pass contrast. An agent may skip rules that aren’t in the pack, and the gap only shows up in review. Rules Four rules keep a context pack useful. 1. Point to the design system by path An agent doesn’t know your design system unless you show it where it lives, so it writes a new button with its own color, shape and focus style. Each one is small, but they add up to a product that looks patched together. Give the path to the token file and the components to reuse, and name the ones it must not rebuild. 2. Pick what this task touches Pasting the whole repo or every design page seems thorough, but the agent then has to guess which parts matter, and it may copy an old screen instead of the current one. The brief itself can get lost in the pile. Pick what this task touches: one or two similar screens, the frames for this flow, the rules that apply. 3. Show the look, don’t only describe it Words leave room for guessing: “a small image on the left” can mean many sizes and positions, and the agent picks one. Link the design frame instead, or attach a screenshot of a similar screen. Claude Code can read Figma frames through the Figma MCP connector (MCP is a standard way to plug tools into an agent). 4. Keep the stable parts in one file Tokens, copy rules and conventions rarely change between tasks. Pasting them into every request takes time, and sooner or later one part gets left out, so that task breaks a rule the others followed. Keep the stable parts in a file the agent reads every session, such as CLAUDE.md, the project notes file Claude Code loads on its own. Add only the task-specific parts to each brief. In real products - Figma: Dev Mode shows a frame with its spacing, the variables and the components it uses. Whoever builds it gets the rules behind the pixels, not just a picture. - Storybook: every component has stories for its states and a docs page with its props. A newcomer, or an agent, can see what already exists before building something new. - Airbnb: hosts write check-in steps, Wi‑Fi details, house rules and a house manual once, and every guest who books gets them, like the stable part of a context pack.

entries.title: Definition of done
entries.summary: A definition of done is the list of checks a change must pass before you call it finished.

rules.title: Ask for proof, not a report
Put the tests in the brief

entries.tags: definition of done checks finished acceptance criteria verification agent workflow brief guide part4 effective list change must pass before call write one something could see run such behavior
entries.search_text: Definition of done A definition of done is the list of checks a change must pass before you call it finished. Write each one as something you could see or run, such as a behavior, a state or a test that passes, and mark who checks it. An agent can prove many of them with a test run or a screenshot, but some need your judgment, such as whether the wording reads well. Where Define “good” before building decides what a good result is, this entry turns it into checks for one change, so you and the agent agree on when it’s finished. Rules Four rules keep a definition of done useful. 1. Ask for proof, not a report An agent says a change is done when it believes it is, and that message doesn’t tell you whether any check passed. If you approve on its word, the bugs reach people first. Ask for the test run and the screenshots in the pull request, and look at them before you approve. 2. Name what you’d see “It feels intuitive” can’t pass or fail, so it gets marked done without a check. Write what you’d see instead, as in the problem brief , such as which result shows first. Keep the calls that need judgment, labeled as yours, and look yourself: a screenshot proves a state exists, not that it reads well. 3. Cover the other states Criteria often describe only the path where everything works, so nobody checks what happens when a save fails or several tabs are unsaved, which is where people lose work. List the other states too: several unsaved tabs, a failed save, keyboard only, a narrow window. 4. Put the tests in the brief Tests planned for later rarely get written, so the next change can break this one without anyone noticing, and people find out first. Name the tests in the brief, such as a Playwright spec (a test that clicks through the app in a real browser) for the new behavior, so they ship in the same pull request. In real products - GitHub: branch protection can require passing status checks and an approving review before a pull request merges. Machines prove the tests pass; a person approves the change itself. - Chromatic: visual tests compare each Storybook story with its last accepted screenshot. The tool finds what changed, and a person accepts or denies it, because only they know if the change was meant. - DoorDash: when an order is left at the door, the courier takes a photo at drop-off and the app shows it to you. “Delivered” comes with proof you can check, not just a status.

entries.title: Explore wide
entries.summary: Before you build one answer, ask for several different ones.

rules.title: Give each one its own bet

entries.tags: explore wide directions alternatives subagent options cheap variations workflow guide part4 effective agent before build one answer ask several different ones give direction own short brief helper
entries.search_text: Explore wide Before you build one answer, ask for several different ones. Give each direction its own short brief and its own subagent (a helper agent that works alongside the others), then lay the results side by side and choose. With agents a rough direction costs minutes, so the first idea doesn’t have to be the one you build. How the directions should differ, so that each one teaches you something, is the subject of Vary along named axes . Rules Four rules keep exploring wide useful. 1. Ask for several at once If you ask one agent for one answer, you get the obvious idea, and every round of polish after that makes the same idea neater, not better. Ask for several directions at the same time instead: one subagent per direction, or one git worktree (a separate working copy of the code) each when a direction needs real code. 2. Give each one its own bet Agents given the same prompt tend to land on the same answer, so you get three versions of one idea, differing only in wording or layout, and think you’ve explored. Write each brief around a different bet about what people need, such as “never interrupt” or “make it fixable in one step”. If two results still differ only in layout, rewrite one brief with a different bet. 3. Keep them equally rough When one direction looks finished and the others are sketches, the finished one wins, and you end up choosing the polish, not the idea. Ask for every direction at the same level of detail, so the only difference left is the idea. 4. Set the number first Asking for “a few more” has no natural end. The pile grows, each new card adds less, and nothing gets chosen. Decide before you start how many directions to ask for, say three to six, then keep two or three and drop the rest. In real products - Google Ventures: in the design sprint’s Crazy 8s step, each person folds a sheet into eight panels and sketches eight ideas in eight minutes. The time limit keeps every idea rough, so people compare ideas, not drawing skill. - Lightroom Classic: a virtual copy is a second edit of the same photo, without duplicating the file. Survey view shows the copies side by side, so you remove the weak ones and keep the best. - Midjourney: each prompt returns a grid of four different images at once. You pick the ones worth taking further and ask for variations or a larger version of just those. - Google Maps: directions show a few different routes at once, each with its time on the map. You see the trade-offs side by side and tap the one you want, instead of taking the first answer.

entries.title: Named axes
entries.summary: When you ask for options, name what should change between them.

rules.title: Name the axis and its ends
Vary what people notice or do
Change two things at a time

entries.tags: axes named dimensions vary options explore tradeoffs loud silent workflow guide part4 effective agent ask name what should change between axis one dimension two ends such how message
entries.search_text: Named axes When you ask for options, name what should change between them. An axis is one dimension with two ends, such as how loud a message is, from silent to blocking. Lay two axes out as a grid, one across and one down, and each cell becomes a direction. The options then differ in ways you chose, so each difference tells you something. Where Get many directions cheaply asks for many directions, this entry decides how they should differ. Rules Four rules keep axes useful. 1. Name the axis and its ends “Make three versions” gives no direction, so you get the same idea three times with small changes. Name the dimension and its two ends instead, such as “how loud, from silent to blocking”, and ask for one direction per point along it. 2. Vary what people notice or do Color, label and corner radius are easy to vary, but people using the app barely notice them, so options that differ only there can’t teach you anything about the experience. Vary how loud it is, where it shows up and when it happens. If both ends of an axis would look the same to someone using the app, pick another axis. 3. Change two things at a time When every option differs in every way, a test shows a winner but not the reason. Vary two axes at a time and hold the rest fixed. Then two options that differ on only one axis, such as neighbors in the same row or column, show what that axis does. 4. Look at the odd cells Some cells look wrong at first, such as a blocking dialog after the fact, and it’s tempting to drop them unread. Look at each one before you drop it, because a strange corner often shows why its neighbor works. In real products - Figma: a component’s variants are set by named properties, like Size and State, each with its values. The set is usually laid out as a grid, one property per direction, so a missing or odd combination is easy to spot. - Tailwind CSS: every default color is named by two axes, a hue and a shade from light to dark, like blue-500. The palette is the full grid, so choosing a color means choosing a position, and its neighbors are easy to compare. - Optimizely: a multivariate test names the parts of a page that change, like the headline and the image, with a few options each. It then tests every combination, so you can tell which part made the difference.

entries.title: Prototype in code
entries.summary: A prototype answers a question about a design.

rules.title: Write the question at the top
Decide what happens to the branch

entries.tags: prototype code fidelity clickable artifact real material build explore workflow guide part4 effective agent answers question about design needs higher page questions feel timing branch app
entries.search_text: Prototype in code A prototype answers a question about a design. Build it in code, at the fidelity the question needs and no higher. A clickable artifact page answers questions about feel and timing, and a branch in the app answers questions about real storage, real data and real speed. Code also lets you try the prototype with a keyboard and a screen reader, which a static mock can’t. Do that before you pick a direction, not after it ships. Rules Four rules keep prototypes useful. 1. Make timing questions clickable Some questions are about time: is a toast up long enough, does a reply feel slow. A static mock can show a toast, but not how long it stays. Make a clickable page with a real timer and real keyboard behavior, and try it yourself. 2. Sketch before you branch A branch in the app takes days and is slow to throw away, so if you build one per direction just to compare them, most of that work goes in the bin. Compare directions as sketches first, and build in the app once the question is about the real thing. 3. Write the question at the top A prototype without a question has no point where it’s finished, so it keeps growing and nobody can say what it showed. Write the question at the top of the prototype, add only what helps answer it, and stop when it’s answered. 4. Decide what happens to the branch A prototype branch is built to answer a question fast, so it skips tests and takes shortcuts. If it ships as it is, those shortcuts reach people. Decide on purpose: rewrite it with tests, or keep it only after it passes the same review as any other change. In real products Notice how far each one goes: one page, one component, a real branch, real people. - CodePen: a pen is one page of HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the result running underneath. It’s enough for a question about feel, like how long a toast should stay, without touching the real app. - Storybook: each story renders one real component in one state, outside the app. You can check the error and long-text states in real code, and change props live, before any screen uses it. - Vercel: every pull request gets its own live preview link. Reviewers click through the real branch in a browser instead of judging screenshots. - Instagram: it tested hiding like counts with real accounts in several countries before deciding, because how people would feel about it could only be learned from real use, not from a mock. It later became a setting people can turn on.

entries.title: Decision matrix
entries.summary: A decision matrix scores each direction from 1 to 5 against each criterion in the brief.

rules.title: Score against the brief, not the polish
Set the weights before you score
Use the total to start the decision

entries.tags: decision matrix mandatory requirements eligibility alternatives tradeoffs score weight criteria brief workflow decide guide part4 effective agent scores direction against criterion gets things problem about count more weighted total starts doesn
entries.search_text: Decision matrix A decision matrix scores each direction from 1 to 5 against each criterion in the brief. Each criterion gets a weight, so the things the problem is about count more. The weighted total starts the decision, but it doesn’t make it. A score of 4 against a 3 is a judgment, not a measurement. Write one line of why next to each score, so a reviewer can argue with the reason instead of the number. Rules Four rules keep a decision matrix useful. 1. Score against the brief, not the polish Agents make every direction look finished, and the most polished one draws the eye, but polish says little about whether it solves the problem. Score every direction against the brief’s criteria before you pick. 2. Set the weights before you score Once you’ve seen the scores, it’s easy to nudge the weights until your favorite wins, and the matrix only confirms what you already wanted. Write the weights down from the brief first, then score on your own before you read anyone else’s scores, an agent’s included, so their read doesn’t become yours . 3. Use the total to start the decision A total of 24 against 23 looks like an answer, but the numbers are judgments. If one small change to a weight flips the winner, the directions are close, so decide on the risk you care about most and say which one it is. 4. Keep three to five criteria With many criteria all weighted the same, the one the problem is about counts as little as “looks modern”, so a direction can win while failing the problem. Keep three to five criteria from the brief, and weight the ones the problem is about higher. In real products - Intercom: its RICE method scores each idea by reach, impact, confidence and effort. Confidence pulls down scores that rest on guesses, and the score is meant to inform the call, not make it. - Aha!: a team sets up a scorecard once, with its criteria and an equation for how much each counts. Every idea is then rated on the same card, so scores compare like with like. - Google Flights: the top results are ranked by a mix of price and convenience, and each row shows the price, duration and stops. If price matters most to you, you re-sort by price.

entries.title: Spot the plausible
entries.summary: Agent-made screens often look finished and still have problems: vague copy, a broken keyboard path, a missing state, or a color a little off the design tokens.

rules.title: Use it, don’t just look at it
Collect problems, then send one list

entries.tags: plausible finished looking agent critique keyboard accessibility state polish workflow decide guide part4 effective spot agent-made screens often look still problems vague copy broken path missing color little
entries.search_text: Spot the plausible Agent-made screens often look finished and still have problems: vague copy, a broken keyboard path, a missing state, or a color a little off the design tokens. A screenshot hides all of these, so you find them by using the screen the way people will. In Let agents prove their work the agent runs checks and shows you the results; here you use the result yourself and catch what no check covered. Rules Four rules keep this check useful. 1. Use it, don’t just look at it A screenshot shows how a screen looks, not how it works: it can’t show that Tab skips a button, that an empty name gets saved, or that text is too faint to read. If you approve from the picture, people find these problems after release. Open the real thing: Tab through it, trigger the errors and read the copy out loud. 2. Look at every state Agents build the state they were shown, usually the one with data, but people also see the screen empty, loading and failing. A blank panel on a first visit looks broken, and a spinner that never stops leaves people stuck. Ask for each state and look at each one before you approve. 3. Check values against the tokens A padding of 15 instead of 16, or a color that’s almost the brand color, looks fine by eye. Each one is small, but the next change copies it, and the product slowly stops matching itself. Check spacing, corners and color against the design tokens. Ask the agent for token names, not raw values. 4. Collect problems, then send one list Sending problems to the agent one at a time takes many rounds, and a fix for one can bring back an earlier one, so you end up checking the same thing again. Collect everything you found in one list first, and send it back with the checks the agent should run, such as a Playwright test for the keyboard path and screenshots in both themes. In real products - GitHub: a repository can require status checks, like tests and lint (automatic checks for code mistakes), to pass before a pull request can merge. A change that looks right in review still can’t land until they pass. - Chromatic: it highlights the pixels that changed in every Storybook story since the last accepted version, so a small shift in spacing or color can’t slip in unseen. - Lighthouse: an audit built into Chrome’s developer tools checks a page for problems a screenshot hides, like low contrast or buttons with no name. Each failed check lists the exact elements to fix. - Gmail: if a message says something is attached but nothing is, it asks before sending. The email reads as finished, and the check catches the one thing it promised but doesn’t have.

entries.title: Cut and combine
entries.summary: When you have several design directions, the best answer is often none of them whole: it takes the strongest part of each and cuts the rest.

rules.title: Cut what the problem doesn’t need
Read the result as one story
Write down why parts were cut

entries.tags: cut combine best parts directions synthesize choose decide workflow guide part4 effective agent several design answer often none whole takes strongest part cuts rest check kept
entries.search_text: Cut and combine When you have several design directions, the best answer is often none of them whole: it takes the strongest part of each and cuts the rest. Then you check that the parts you kept still work together as one design. Agents make it cheap to get many directions, so the work that’s left is choosing which parts solve the problem and which only add to it. In the demo, each direction has three parts: the trigger (what starts it), the surface (what people see) and the recovery (how they get their work back). Rules Four rules keep this choice useful. 1. Take directions apart Each direction is usually strong in one place and weak in others, so if you pick one whole, you keep its weak parts too. Split every direction into the same parts, such as trigger, surface and recovery, and pick the best version of each part. 2. Cut what the problem doesn’t need Good ideas pile up fast, and each one sounds worth keeping, but every part is something to build, test and explain, and people have to work out what each control does. Write the problem down and keep only the parts that solve it. The rest can wait until people ask for it. 3. Read the result as one story Parts from different directions can contradict each other. A design can keep both a confirm dialog and an Undo toast: each makes sense alone, but together they ask people to decide twice. Describe the combined design in one sentence, from trigger to surface to recovery. If the sentence needs an “or”, cut one side. 4. Write down why parts were cut A few weeks later, nobody remembers why a part was cut, so someone suggests it again and the team repeats the discussion or adds it back. Write one line per cut part in the ticket or the pull request, so it comes back only with new evidence. In real products - GV’s design sprint: people put dot stickers on the parts they like in each sketch, not on whole sketches. The team then draws one storyboard from the best parts, which shows whether they still fit together. - Basecamp’s Shape Up: a pitch ends with “No-gos”, the parts left out on purpose, so they don’t creep back in during the build. - VS Code: for each merge conflict you can keep one side, the other, or both. Keeping both still needs a read, because two good changes can contradict each other, like a save prompt and an Undo on the same close. - Google Pixel: Best Take works from a few group shots taken seconds apart. You pick each person’s best face, and because the shots are so close, the result still looks like one moment.

entries.title: Small steps
entries.summary: Before an agent writes code, agree on a plan with it, for example in Claude Code’s plan mode.

rules.title: Finish one step before the next

entries.tags: small steps plan mode reviewable incremental build agent workflow guide part4 effective before writes code agree example claude one change time check next starts
entries.search_text: Small steps Before an agent writes code, agree on a plan with it, for example in Claude Code’s plan mode. Then build one small change at a time, and check each change before the next one starts. Small steps keep mistakes cheap: when a step fails review, only that step goes back. In one big change, a problem in one part sends the whole change back, and it’s harder to find. Rules Four rules keep small steps useful. 1. Plan before code If you ask an agent to build a whole feature from one prompt, it makes every decision on its own, and you find the wrong ones in review, after the code is written. Ask for a plan first and read it, because changing a step in the plan takes a sentence, and changing it in code can take a day. 2. Slice so each step works Steps sliced by layer, such as database, then server, then screen, leave nothing to try until the last step lands. Problems then show up all at once, and nobody knows which step caused them. Slice so each step leaves the app working and gives you something to try. If a step can’t stand on its own, merge it behind a feature flag, a switch that keeps new code turned off for people, until the step that completes it lands. 3. Give every step a check Without a check, a step is “done” when the agent stops typing, so a broken step looks the same as a working one, and the next step builds on it. Write the check into the plan next to each step: a unit test, an end-to-end spec, a screenshot or you trying it. A step is done when its check passes. 4. Finish one step before the next Open questions about a step don’t go away when the next step starts. Later steps build on the answer, so a late answer can undo several steps of work. Finish the review of one step, open questions included, before the next one starts. In real products Notice that each step is small, leaves things working, and gets checked before the next one builds on it. - Basecamp’s Shape Up: a project is split into scopes, each a slice that works end to end. A hill chart shows each scope moving from “figuring things out” to “making it happen”, so a stuck one is easy to spot. - Google’s code review guide: each change should be small and do one self-contained thing. Small changes get reviewed faster and more carefully, and a bad one is easy to roll back. - LaunchDarkly: each step can merge behind a feature flag that’s off for most people, so the app keeps working in between. When the last step lands, you can turn it on for your team first, then a few percent of people, then everyone. - Duolingo: a course is a path of short lessons. Each takes a few minutes and opens the next one when you finish, so you always know where you are and never face a whole unit at once.

entries.title: Agent checks
entries.summary: When an agent says it’s done, ask it to show the proof: which unit tests ran, the end-to-end specs for the screens it changed, screenshots before and after, and a clean type check.

rules.title: Ask what ran, and see the output
Run the end-to-end specs for visible changes
Get screenshots for each theme, width and state

entries.tags: agent verification proof tests screenshots e2e unit check done workflow build guide part4 effective checks says ask show which ran end-to-end specs screens changed before after
entries.search_text: Agent checks When an agent says it’s done, ask it to show the proof: which unit tests ran, the end-to-end specs for the screens it changed, screenshots before and after, and a clean type check. Then you can see what was checked and what wasn’t. Proof isn’t the same as trying the change. Checks cover only what someone thought to test, so the proof tells you where the agent looked. Trying the change yourself, as in Check output that looks finished , covers the rest. Rules Four rules keep this proof useful. 1. Ask what ran, and see the output “All tests pass” is also true when no tests ran. A new test file can be empty, or the agent can run a folder that doesn’t touch the change. Ask which tests ran and have the agent paste the output. Also read the test diff: an agent can make a failing test pass by changing what the test expects. 2. Run the end-to-end specs for visible changes Unit tests check logic, not screens, so a change can pass every unit test and still move a button people rely on, or break a flow another screen depends on. For anything people see, run the end-to-end specs that touch the changed screens, and compare screenshots from before and after. 3. Get screenshots for each theme, width and state A screenshot in one theme at one width shows only the case that was easiest to check. Ask for light and dark, wide and narrow, and the states that matter, such as empty, error and long names. Each one catches different problems, as Let an agent run design QA shows. 4. Try it yourself anyway Green checks only mean that nothing tested broke, so a case nobody thought of still gets through. Before you approve, try it in the real app for a few minutes, the way people will. In real products Notice that “done” comes with proof anyone can open: a list of checks, a link, a picture. - GitHub: each pull request lists its checks, like tests and a type check, with a pass or fail and a link to the output, so anyone can see what ran. - Vercel: the preview link on each pull request lets anyone open the real change, instead of reading that it works. - Chromatic: each change comes with snapshots of every Storybook story and any differences side by side, so a visual change can’t pass as “no change”. - Amazon: a “Delivered” status can come with a photo of the package where it was left. You don’t have to take the status on trust, and you know where to look.

entries.title: UX calls
entries.summary: Every change people will see is a design decision: the wording, the spacing, which kind of dialog appears.

rules.title: Lead with what people will notice

entries.tags: ux calls design decision copy spacing dialog visible change call out workflow build guide part4 effective agent every people see wording which kind appears makes these choices let
entries.search_text: UX calls Every change people will see is a design decision: the wording, the spacing, which kind of dialog appears. An agent makes these choices for you if you let it, so treat each one as a proposal: decide on it, then name it in the pull request. This keeps the decisions with the people who own them. When the pull request describes each visible change, reviewers can judge it, but a change it doesn’t mention gets approved without anyone deciding on it. Rules Four rules keep these calls visible. 1. Decide on each visible choice An agent fills every gap with a default: generic wording, the nearest dialog, a button that says OK. Each default looks reasonable on its own, so it ships without anyone choosing it. List the choices people will see and decide on each one: keep it, change it or drop it. 2. Keep side changes out Agents often change things on the way: a font size, a color, a label in another screen. Buried in a bigger pull request, these changes ship without review, because the description doesn’t mention them. Drop them, or move them into their own pull request with their own note. 3. Lead with what people will notice Reviewers and teammates read the first lines of a description. If those lines list files and functions, they have to work out from the code what changes for people. Start with what people will notice, in their words, and put the code notes under it. 4. Check before saying “no visible change” Refactors and shared components often change how things look by a few pixels or a color, and saying “no visible change” without checking hides that from reviewers. Compare screenshots from before and after, and skim the diff for new strings, styles and components. If anything differs, describe it as a visible change. In real products Notice that each change people will see is shown on its own, in plain words, where someone can decide on it. - Google Docs: in Suggesting mode, each edit shows up marked in the text with its own accept and reject. Nothing changes for good until someone decides, one edit at a time. - GitHub: a repo can add a pull request template, so every description starts from the same sections. Teams use it to put what people will see, with before and after screenshots, above the code notes. - App Store: every app update comes with a “What’s New” note. The good ones name each change people will notice, in plain words, instead of “bug fixes and improvements”.

entries.title: Watch people
entries.summary: Watching people use a design is the quickest way to see where it fails.

rules.title: Describe the goal, not the feature
Stay quiet when they get stuck

entries.tags: research severity single observation sampling usability watch people sessions workflow evaluate guide part4 effective agent watching use design quickest way see where fails give few real task stay quiet while try
entries.search_text: Watch people Watching people use a design is the quickest way to see where it fails. Give a few real people a task, stay quiet while they try it, and note where they stall. Five people usually show the problems that matter, because the big ones come up again and again. Analytics are different: they show where many people drop off, but not why. A session shows the why, one person at a time. An agent’s review can’t stand in for one: it predicts what people might do, and a session shows what they do. Rules Four rules keep these sessions useful. 1. Watch what people do Ask people whether they’d use something, and most will say yes, because they want to be kind and can’t know what they’ll do later. What they do with a real task is better evidence, so give them the task and watch where they go. 2. Describe the goal, not the feature If the task names the feature, people look for that word on screen and find it, so you learn that they can read, not that they’d find their way. Describe what they want to get done, in their own words, and you see where they look first. 3. Stay quiet when they get stuck Silence feels awkward, so you’ll want to help as soon as someone stalls. But the stall is the finding, and if you help, you never learn why it happened. Note where it happened and wait. Ask “What did you expect?” at the end, and only step in if they want to give up. 4. Fix what repeats One person’s trouble may be theirs alone. If you change the design after each session, every person sees a different version, and you can’t tell which problems repeat. Run all the sessions on the same version and tally what went wrong, then fix what more than one person hit. In real products Notice that each one watches what people do, not what they say, and looks for problems that repeat. - GV’s design sprint: on the last day, five customers each try the prototype in a one-on-one interview while the team watches from another room. Notes go on a grid, one column per person, so problems that repeat stand out. - UserTesting: you write the tasks, and people record their screen and voice while they try them on their own. You watch the recordings and clip the moments where they get stuck. - Maze: you give testers a task on a clickable prototype and mark the path you expect. It shows how many finished, where they left that path, and a heatmap of clicks on each screen. - FullStory: replays real people’s sessions and flags rage clicks, many quick clicks on one spot. Searching for them across sessions shows which stuck point hits many people, not just one.

entries.title: Measure
entries.summary: Measuring against the brief means choosing, before you build, the numbers that will show whether the brief’s goal was met.

rules.title: Count the outcome, not the activity
Add a number that must not get worse
Pick the numbers before you build
Read the number with what people say

entries.tags: measure metrics success criteria brief numbers evaluate workflow guide part4 effective agent measuring against means choosing before build show whether goal was met criterion gets one
entries.search_text: Measure Measuring against the brief means choosing, before you build, the numbers that will show whether the brief’s goal was met. Each success criterion gets one number that moves only if people got what they needed. You add one number that must not get worse, and read both next to what people say. Without this, teams count what is easy to count, and a banner can be seen a million times and still help nobody. Rules Four rules keep these numbers useful. 1. Count the outcome, not the activity Views and clicks are easy to count, so they end up on the dashboard, but they rise with traffic whether or not anyone got what they came for. Count the outcome instead, as a share of the people who could have reached it, such as finished reorders out of everyone who opened a past order. Then more visitors alone can’t move the number. 2. Add a number that must not get worse A change can raise one number by hurting something else, so if you only watch the number you want to raise, you’ll pick the version that does the most harm. Add a guardrail: one number that must not get worse, with a limit you set before looking. In an A/B test, where each group of people gets a different version, a version that crosses the limit is out, however good the main number looks. 3. Pick the numbers before you build If you choose the number after release, the event you need is often missing, so you can only look at what happens to be logged, and that rarely answers the brief. Write the numbers in the brief and add their events in the same pull request. An event only needs to record that something happened, such as a suggestion being picked, so never log what people typed or made. 4. Read the number with what people say A number tells you that something changed, not why. A drop can mean people stopped wanting a feature, or that they can’t find it anymore. Read it next to support threads and a few watched sessions , which usually explain the change. In real products Notice that each team counts a number that moves only when people get what they came for, and some add one that must not get worse. - YouTube: recommendations count watch time, not just clicks. A misleading thumbnail wins the click, but people leave early, so watch time shows whether they found what they wanted. - Google: the HEART framework starts from a goal, then names the signal that shows it, then the metric. It has a slot each for happiness, engagement, adoption, retention and task success, and teams fill only the ones that fit the goal. - Microsoft: experiments are judged on one main measure agreed before the test, plus guardrails like page load time. A win on the main number isn’t enough if a guardrail slips. - PageSpeed Insights: speed is measured the way people feel it: when the main content appears, how fast a tap gets a response, and whether the layout jumps. A page can fire its load event early and still look blank.

entries.title: Design QA
entries.summary: Design QA means checking a change everywhere people will see it before it ships: in light and dark, on narrow and wide screens, and in every state it can be in.
entries.tags: design qa light dark responsive states agent check evaluate workflow guide part4 effective means checking change everywhere people see before ships narrow wide screens every state render
entries.search_text: Design QA Design QA means checking a change everywhere people will see it before it ships: in light and dark, on narrow and wide screens, and in every state it can be in. An agent can render all of those and list what looks wrong much faster than you can. You still read the list, open the important findings yourself and decide what to fix. The agent does the looking, which is slow and easy to skip, and you keep the judgment that tools lack: what matters to people, and what is a false alarm. Rules Four rules keep design QA useful. 1. Check every theme and width You build in your own theme on your own screen, so that’s where the change looks right. Other people use dark mode and phones, and that’s where text goes faint and buttons get cut off. Have the agent take screenshots in light and dark, at 360px and at a desktop width, every time. It takes the agent seconds. 2. Render every state The state you designed is usually the one that works. Problems hide in the others: while it loads, when it fails, when a name is long. List every state the change can be in, and have the agent render each one with real, messy data , because it is longer than the sample. 3. Open the findings yourself An agent can misread a screenshot, or flag something that is meant to look that way. If you apply every finding without looking, you can break what was right. Open at least two findings yourself and check them against the brief. Dismiss the wrong ones and say why. 4. Test with the keyboard yourself An automated scan checks things like contrast and missing labels, but it can’t tell whether the focus moves in a sensible order, or whether a screen reader reads the page in a useful way. Tab through the change once and try a screen reader once. Only then call it accessible. In real products Notice that the tool renders every state, theme or size and points at what changed or failed, but a person makes the call. - Chromatic: every Storybook story is captured on each change, in the browsers and widths you choose, and changed snapshots wait for a person to accept or deny them. - Xcode: SwiftUI previews have a variants mode that shows one screen in each color scheme, orientation or text size, side by side. A label that only breaks at the largest text size is in view while you work. - Lighthouse: besides what a tool can measure, the accessibility audit lists items to check by hand, like a sensible tab order, because a scan can’t judge them. - Chrome DevTools: device mode resizes the page to a phone width, and the Rendering panel can switch it to dark mode or reduced motion. You can confirm a finding yourself in seconds, without a phone or a change to system settings.

entries.title: Worked example
entries.summary: This entry follows one problem from brief to release: people lose unsaved work when they close a workflow tab.

rules.title: Scale the stages to the problem

entries.tags: worked example end to unsaved tab brief release walkthrough workflow guide part4 effective agent entry follows one problem people lose work close stage ends small
entries.search_text: Worked example This entry follows one problem from brief to release: people lose unsaved work when they close a workflow tab. Each stage ends with one small thing someone else can read: a brief, a context pack, directions, a decision, a plan, checks and a note on what you learned. The stages follow the loop , with Problem folded into the brief and the context pack as a step of its own. With those artifacts, anyone can pick up the problem at any stage and see why it went the way it did, including you a month later. The rule demos below use smaller problems of their own. Stage 1 · Brief Sample brief · Linear ticket People lose unsaved work when they close a workflow tab. - Who : People with several workflows open, tidying their tabs. - Trying to : Close what they don’t need without thinking about it. - In the way : A tab with changes can close before they meant to keep them. - Evidence : Three support threads this month, and you lost work the same way in your own runs. To check: how often it happens. - Done when : Closing a tab never throws away changes without a choice the person made. - You : Name the person, the moment and what stops them. Write “done when”. - Agents : Draft the brief from threads you paste in. You cut it down. Stage 2 · Context pack Sample context pack · one page, linked from the ticket - How the tab bar closes a tab repo · subagent - How saving and the unsaved marker work repo · subagent - Related tickets and threads Linear · you - Tab, dialog and toast frames, plus tokens Figma connector - Patterns: dialog , undo , autosave this book Out of scope: closing the whole app. Note it, don’t solve it here. - You : Say what’s in scope and what isn’t. - Agents : Read the repo, tickets and Figma in parallel, and summarize each in a few lines. Stage 3 · Three directions - A · Ask on close : A dialog before the tab closes. - B · Close, then Undo : Close right away, offer Undo for a while. - C · Keep a draft : Close right away, offer the changes back on reopen. Three subagents each prototyped one direction. All three went on one shared page. - You : Ask for directions that differ, not three versions of one idea. - Agents : Each subagent prototypes one direction. One page shows all three. Stage 4 · Decision Sample scores · 1 to 5, criteria from the brief Criterion A · Ask B · Undo C · Draft Never loses work 3 of 5 1 of 5 5 of 5 No extra step 1 of 5 5 of 5 5 of 5 Pattern people know 5 of 5 5 of 5 3 of 5 Small to build 5 of 5 5 of 5 1 of 5 Totals: A · Ask 14, B · Undo 16, C · Draft 14. Counting “never loses work” twice: A · Ask 17, B · Undo 17, C · Draft 19. Counted once: B wins on points, but its work is gone once the toast fades. The brief says never lose work, so that criterion should count more. Counted twice: C wins: nothing is lost, even after the toast is gone. Keep B’s Undo for the moment right after closing. Record why in the ticket. - You : Pick the criteria from the brief, score the directions yourself, then decide. - Agents : Score them separately. You look again wherever the two disagree. Stage 5 · Build plan and checks Build plan · agreed in plan mode 1. Work in its own git worktree, so main stays clean. 1. Save a draft when a tab with changes closes. Restore it on reopen. Clear it on save. 1. Show “Tab closed · Undo” right after closing. 1. Write the checks first: they should fail before the change. Sample PR description Keep unsaved changes when a workflow tab closes What changes for people - Closing a tab with changes closes it right away and offers Undo. - Reopening that workflow offers to restore the changes. - Tabs without changes close as before. Checks - Vitest: draft saved on close, restored on reopen, cleared on save. - Playwright: close with edits, Undo, edits are back. Close, reopen, Restore. - You : Approve the plan and the PR’s behavior list. - Agents : Build in a worktree, write the tests, open the PR. Stage 6 · Evaluation plan Sample evaluation plan · in the PR, under the behaviors We’ll know it worked when… - No silent loss. Closing a tab with changes never discards them without a choice. Playwright spec on every PR - Found without help. People get closed work back on their own. Watch five people close and reopen tabs - Fewer reports. No new threads about work lost on close. Read support threads a month after release - You : Say what you’ll watch for, and when you’ll look. - Agents : Run the checks on every change. Stage 7 · What was learned Sample session tally · written in the ticket when it closes - 3 directions explored - 1 kept, plus B’s Undo - 4 subagent runs - 1 worktree - 5 checks added - 2 review rounds Learned: drafts need a limit, or old ones pile up. Next time: ask in the brief what happens when the whole app closes. - You : Write one lesson for next time. - Agents : Count what happened in the session. Rules Four rules keep the stages useful. 1. Explore directions before you build An agent builds fast, so it’s tempting to go from the brief straight to code. Then the first idea is the only idea, and a better one turns up in review, after the work is done. Spend that speed on directions instead: ask for three different ones, and pick one before anything is built for real. 2. Leave one artifact per stage If each stage lives in your head or in a long chat, nobody else can follow it: when someone asks why you chose this design, the answer is somewhere in hundreds of messages. Leave one small artifact per stage: the brief in the ticket, the directions on a page, the decision and checks in the pull request. 3. Scale the stages to the problem Agents make every stage cheap, so it’s tempting to run all of them at full size. For a typo, three directions and a scoring table waste a day and bury a one-word change. Ask what each stage is for, and if its artifact wouldn’t change a decision, keep it to a line. 4. Check the result after release Merged isn’t done : the evaluation plan only helps if someone reads it after release. Go back to it once people have used the change, check each line, and write down one thing you learned. In real products Notice that each story moves through clear stages, and each stage leaves something others can read or try. - Gmail: Undo send began as an opt-in Labs experiment for people who hit Send too soon. People could try it for years before it became a standard setting, where you choose how long to wait before the message goes. - Basecamp: in Shape Up, each stage leaves something others can read: the written pitch, the bet leaders place on it, and the hill chart the team updates while it builds. - Amazon: in “working backwards”, the press release and FAQ are the first thing the team reads and revises together, before anything is built. - GV: each day of the design sprint leaves something the team can see: a map and a target on Monday, sketches on Tuesday, a storyboard on Wednesday, a prototype on Thursday and interview notes on Friday.

entries.title: Toolkit
entries.summary: Design work has separate jobs: frame the problem, gather context, explore, decide, build, check and share.

rules.title: Ask for a test that fails first
Share a link people can click

entries.tags: toolkit tools frame explore decide build check share agent workflow example guide part4 effective design work separate jobs problem gather context job tool fits splitting
entries.search_text: Toolkit Design work has separate jobs: frame the problem, gather context, explore, decide, build, check and share. Each job has a tool that fits it, and splitting the work by job keeps each step small enough to check, with a result the next step can use. One long chat can do all of it, but then the decisions are buried and nobody can check them. Whatever the agents make, the brief, the decision and the pull request’s list of behaviors should read as yours, because you’re the one answering for them. - Frame the problem (Linear, Claude Code): Write the brief in the Linear ticket: who, what they’re trying to do, what stops them. Claude Code can draft it from threads you paste in. For the tab-close problem: one paragraph naming people who tidy tabs and lose changes, with a “done when” line. - Gather context (Claude Code, Figma connector, Linear): Send Claude Code subagents in parallel to read the repo and past tickets. Pull frames and tokens from Figma through its connector. For the tab-close problem: a one-page pack: how tabs close, how saving works, related tickets, the tab frames. - Explore directions (Claude Code, Claude artifacts): Ask subagents for clearly different directions, one each, and put them side by side on one artifact page. For the tab-close problem: ask on close, close then Undo, and keep a draft. - Prototype (Claude artifacts, Claude Code): Make a clickable page as an artifact and share the link. If it needs the real app, prototype in a git worktree instead. For the tab-close problem: a page where you close a tab and see each direction play out. - Decide (Claude artifacts, Linear): Score the options against criteria from the brief on a shared page. Record the decision and why in the ticket. For the tab-close problem: C, with B’s Undo, once “never loses work” counted twice. - Build (Claude Code): Start in plan mode and agree on the plan. Then build in a worktree, so several agents can work at once without clashing. For the tab-close problem: one worktree, draft on close, restore on reopen, Undo toast. - Check (Vitest, Playwright, Claude Code): Vitest for the logic, Playwright for the flow people use, with screenshots. Claude Code can run both and report what failed. For the tab-close problem: three unit tests for the draft, two end-to-end specs for close and reopen. - Review (GitHub PRs, Claude Code): Open a GitHub PR that leads with what changes for people, then the checks. Claude Code can read review comments and make the fixes. For the tab-close problem: reviewers checked the behavior list first, then the code. - Share (Claude artifacts, Linear, GitHub PRs): Publish a short artifact page with before and after, and link it from the ticket and the PR. For the tab-close problem: a before and after page linked from the ticket, so support knows what changed. Rules Four rules keep the tools working for you. 1. Split the work by job One chat asked to explore, decide and build does all three at once: it builds the first idea, and the choice between directions is never made in the open. Explore with parallel subagents, decide on a shared page, then build in a worktree with tests, so each step leaves something you can check. 2. Read the real design values A screenshot shows how a design looks, not the values behind it. An agent that rebuilds from one guesses the colors, spacing and corner radius, and each guess is a little off. Read the frames and tokens through the Figma connector instead, so the build uses the same values as the design. 3. Ask for a test that fails first An agent says “done” when the code runs, not when the behavior works, so if you take that on trust, the bug turns up when someone uses it. Ask for a test that fails before the change and passes after, then run the Playwright specs that touch the changed screens. 4. Share a link people can click A screen recording shows one path, at the pace of whoever made it. People can’t try the other buttons, so their questions stay open. Publish the prototype as an artifact link people can click through, and link it from the ticket so it’s still there next week. In real products Notice that each tool does one job well and hands its result to the next, instead of one tool doing everything. - Linear: the issue holds the problem and the plan. When a branch or pull request names the issue, Linear links them and moves the issue along as the PR opens and merges, so the plan follows the code without anyone updating it. - Figma: designers mark frames “Ready for dev”, and the build takes its exact spacing, colors and variables from Dev Mode instead of guessing them from a screenshot. - Vercel: a bot posts a preview link on every pull request, and each new push updates it, so the link people click always shows the latest build. - GitHub: a pull request gathers a separate tool for each check, like tests, lint, a preview and visual review, so each job reports its result in one place.
